# Changelog

## soilKey 0.9.399 (2026-11-10)

### The AfSP loader reads drainage, parent material and landform; two old regular expressions fixed

[`load_afsp_pedons()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/load_afsp_pedons.md)
now reads the site fields of AfSP by the words of its dictionary
(`AfSP012Qry_DictioClassValues.dbf`, when it is in `afsp_dir`; without
it ParMat and LndForm are not read):

- `Drain` into `drainage_class` (excessively, somewhat excessively,
  well, moderately well, imperfectly, poorly, very poorly drained).
- `ParMat` into `parent_material`, the words of the code composed with
  those of its ancestors (“volcanic rocks, acid”; “clayey, fluvial,
  calcareous”; an ancestor whose words the next one repeats is left out,
  so MA1 is “acid metamorphic rocks, quartzite”). The codes of the
  unconsolidated deposits that the dictionary does not list (U: U00C,
  U00L, U00M, U00FC, US00, Ux0F, U02F, UT00, UY2 …) are decoded by the
  dictionary’s own pattern; “unknown” and “unspecified” are left out. Of
  the 8082 AfSP profiles that record a ParMat, 40 stay unread (A, Hilly,
  IS1C, MI1, U000, UC0F, UF02, UQUC, US11, UY2A, UYOC); of the 1752 that
  also have a WRB 2006 group (the profiles
  [`load_afsp_pedons()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/load_afsp_pedons.md)
  returns), 2 (A, U000).
- `LndForm` into `landform`, only the forms that say something of the
  origin of the material: depression (LD), low-gradient footslope (LF)
  and valley floor (LV). The general relief classes (level, sloping and
  steep land, plain, plateau, dissected plain, hill, mountain,
  escarpment zone, valley) are not read: 295 of the 2739 profiles with a
  WRB 2006 group and a landform recorded.

Two regular expressions that read the parent material are fixed:

- **KA5, the P horizon** (`R/diagnostics-ka5-horizons.R`): “ton” matched
  inside limestone, sandstone, siltstone, ironstone and plutonic rocks.
  The clay and clay-marl stone is now read by whole words (Ton,
  Tonstein, Tonschiefer, Geschiebemergel, clay, claystone, marl, shale,
  pelite). On the AfSP profiles below it no longer matches 42 parent
  materials (plutonic rocks, sandstone, limestone, ironstone) and
  changes no KA5 name.
- **SCSJ and NZSC, volcanic ejecta and tephra** (`R/diagnostics-scsj.R`,
  `R/diagnostics-nzsc-groups.R`, `R/diagnostics-nzsc-subgroups-zlme.R`):
  a pyroclastic breccia or another consolidated pyroclastic rock is
  rock, not ejecta or tephra. On AfSP this changes 2 SCSJ names
  (Allophanic Andosols to Calcareous Eutrosols), the same 2 CSCJ names
  (which share the SCSJ reader) and 1 NZSC name (Typic Tephric Recent to
  Weathered Orthic Recent Soils).

The 926 example and canonical profiles of the package (the 31 canonical
WRB profiles, the examples of every national key and the 503 FAO
examples) keep their names under KA5, SCSJ and NZSC.

Measured on AfSP (offline; the 1149 profiles of 0.9.397: all 649 South

## soilKey 0.9.398 (2026-11-10)

### soilKey Pro: the national systems added since 0.9.337 in the app

The systems added since the last published app (Germany KA5, South
Africa 1991, China CST 2001, the FAO-Unesco legends of 1988 and 1974)
were already offered on the Classify and Pedon tabs; four gaps are
closed.

- **The FAO phases and map symbol on the card.** The card of a
  FAO-Unesco result now lists the phases present or undecided and the
  texture and slope classes of the map symbol, as the report’s section
  “Phases and map symbol” does (the same helper, `.fao_phase_lines()`),
  in the session’s language.
- **The FAO edition line and the CST equivalents in Portuguese.** In a
  Portuguese report, and on a card of the app in Portuguese, the words
  around the codes and class names are translated: “Legenda de 1974”,
  “Legenda Revisada (1988)”, the kind of change (“renomeada”, “definição
  alterada” …), “Ap. 4 p.”, “na maior parte”, “em parte”,
  “inteiramente”, “Tabela 4.2”. The conditions of the crosswalk
  (`also_when` of `inst/rules/fao1988/crosswalk.yaml`) are translated in
  a new file, `inst/i18n/fao_crosswalk_pt.yaml`. Class names stay as the
  books print them. In English every line is the one of before, byte for
  byte; the words now come from `inst/i18n/report_translations.yaml` (22
  new keys in each language).
- **The Thanks tab credits every national system.** A new card,
  “National classification systems”, lists each national system of the
  registry by its short reference, with what soilKey reads from it and
  the experimental pill while the registry marks it so; a system added
  to the registry is credited without a change to the app. Every
  `system.yaml` gains a field `citation_short` (authors, year, title,
  publisher, no editorial notes); the Thanks card falls back to the full
  `citation`, then to the name, and the report keeps the full citation.
- **No repeated correlation in the report.** The report’s warnings no
  longer repeat the CST correlation (“Correlation (a note, never a
  class): …”) when the national section shows it; in a Portuguese report
  the repeat was in English. The warnings stored in the result are
  unchanged.
- **Wording (Hugo).** “Textura arenosa” for the coarse texture class of
  the FAO map symbol (`name_pt` of `phases.yaml`, both editions) and of
  the crosswalk conditions; “\[parte dos …\]” for the 1974 classes that
  only partly go to a 1988 class; no “chaveado” in the Portuguese texts
  of the crosswalk.
- **The app test covers every national system.**
  `test-app-national-systems.R` now checks that every national system of
  the registry has its examples on the Pedon tab and that a sample of
  them (first, middle, last) loads and keys to its class with the
  registry’s classifier; new tests cover the FAO phases on the card, the
  Portuguese notes, and the Thanks card in both languages.

Every classification is unchanged.

## soilKey 0.9.397 (2026-11-10)

### South African classification 1991: the vertic A without a plasticity index, and the AfSP loader reads mottles, clay mineralogy and stickiness

Three confusions of the AfSP benchmark of 0.9.394 were examined and
decided by Hugo (2026-11-10). The decisions are recorded in
`inst/rules/za1991/readings.yaml`.

- **B1s: Q17 revised for the vertic A.** AfSP records neither
  slickensides nor a plasticity index, so Q17 (without the plasticity
  index the slickensides decide) refused the vertic A on every profile,
  and Arcadia and Rensburg (0 of 29) were not even among the forms left
  undecided. A measurement not recorded is undecided, so now, with no
  plasticity index and no diagnostic slickensides, criterion (ii) of the
  vertic A, and with it (ii)-(iii) of the melanic A, is undecided when
  the layer has a strong structure (or none recorded) and 30 % clay or
  more (or none recorded). The 30 % is `vertic_pi_clay` in
  `thresholds.yaml`, flagged as a stand-in (all 71 vertic A of the land
  type survey have 30 % clay or more; van Huyssteen 2020). Elsewhere Q17
  stands, and a plasticity index recorded decides as before. Without the
  structure gate the melanic A of the 35 melanic-form examples became
  undecided; with it the examples are unchanged.
- **A-i: D8 kept for the neocutanic B.** A uniform red or yellow-brown
  layer with a weak blocky structure stays an apedal B. Reading it as a
  neocutanic B cost 19 Huttons for 6 Oakleafs on AfSP; reading it so
  only when the layer is not red gained 4 Oakleafs, lost a Kranskop and
  moved Avalon profiles to Oakleaf. AfSP records no variegation, cutans
  or origin that could evidence the neocutanic B, so Oakleaf read as
  Hutton (6) stays.
- **MP1: mottles recorded only as present.** The soft plinthic B needs
  more than 10 % mottles; AfSP records mottles only as present or absent
  (field `Mottling`, 99 South African layers, none in the 5 Bainsvlei
  profiles), and the loader did not read it. A new horizon attribute,
  `mottles_present` (logical), holds it: `TRUE` with no amount or colour
  leaves the soft plinthic B, the low-chroma mottles of the signs of
  wetness and the signs of wetness of a soft carbonate horizon (FC 15)
  undecided, and then only the amount of the mottles
  (`redoximorphic_features_pct`) decides: plinthite or ferric nodules
  recorded, even as 0, do not stand in for it. `FALSE` or not recorded,
  no mottles. The key is not changed; Bainsvlei stays unreached from the
  AfSP data.

[`load_afsp_pedons()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/load_afsp_pedons.md)
now reads: `Mottling` into `mottles_present`; `ClyMinera` into
`clay_mineralogy` (montmorillonitic and SM as smectite, kaolinitic,
illitic, vermiculitic, interstratified; chloritic, sesquioxidic,
allophane, KA/IL and gibbsite have no `clay_mineralogy` word and are
read as not recorded, with a provenance note); and `Sticknss` into
`stickiness` (sticky as moderately sticky). Each code read goes to the
provenance. ClyMinera is an estimate (a dominant clay mineral given to
the layer), not a measurement: it is recorded with the provenance
`inferred_prior` (confidence 0.5), so the evidence grade of a result on
such a profile drops to C, as for the other estimated values; the names
are not changed by it (383 of the 1149 profiles below carry it). The
site fields `Drain`, `ParMat` and `LndForm` are not read in this
version. `inst/schemas/horizon-attributes.yaml`,
`inst/schemas/pedon-schema.json` and `inst/ATTRIBUTES.md` carry the new
attribute.

Measured on AfSP (offline; 1149 profiles: all 649 South African profiles
with a WRB 2006 group and 500 others from 31 countries, sampled with
seed 397), classified with the 17 keys before and after: names change
only in three keys.

| Key | Names changed | Of them South African | Cause |
|----|---:|---:|----|
| FAO 1974 | 9 | 8 | clay mineralogy (Chromic Cambisols and Orthic Solonchaks to Orthic Luvisols 2 each, Haplic to Luvic Phaeozems 2, Chromic to Eutric Cambisols 1, Eutric Cambisols to Orthic Luvisols 1, an undecided profile to Eutric Nitosols 1) |
| RP 2008 | 12 | 7 | clay mineralogy (fersialsol insature to non rattache 8, to brunisol dystrique or eutrique 3; non rattache to brunisol dystrique 1) |
| ZA 1991 | 13 | 6 | B1s 9, mottles present 4 |

WRB 2022, SiBCS, USDA, FAO 1988, CPCS, CSSC, ASC, NZSC, SCSJ, CSCJ, CST,
the Russian, KA5 and HSCS keys give the same names. Recorded as an
estimate, the clay mineralogy changes the same names (the FAO 1974
Luvisols included): the provenance lowers the evidence grade, it does
not change a test. The soft carbonate horizon and the rule on plinthite
with mottles present change no name on these profiles. The AfSP
benchmark row of the suite
([`benchmark_afsp()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/benchmark_afsp.md)
on
[`load_afsp_sample()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/load_afsp_sample.md))
reads a snapshot built by the loader of v0.9.77, so the loader change
does not reach it.

The AfSP run of the South African benchmark (641 scored) with the
profiles of the new loader:

- Main figure: 138 of 641 agree, 21.5 % (0.9.394: 139, 21.7 %). soilKey
  names a form for 210 (was 216), and among those the form agrees for
  65.7 % (was 64.4 %). 429 stop with forms undecided and the label’s
  form is among them for 340 (was 315 of 423): Arcadia now for 15 of 19
  and Rensburg for 8 of 10 (both 0 before). Two Arcadia keyed as Inhoek
  and one Milkwood keyed right now stop with the vertic A undecided.
  Mottles recorded as present change no South African form.
- Second figure, the humic A of 1977: 151 of 641 agree (was 154).
- The 73 form examples, the 404 family examples and the special cases
  (555 runs) keep their names and provisional status.

## soilKey 0.9.395 (2026-11-10)

### The declared notation decides how the older designations are read

Since 0.9.240, 0.9.250 and 0.9.256 the WRB, SiBCS, FAO-Unesco and
Chinese diagnostics read the older notation of the horizon designations
(in use until about 1990: the A2 is the eluvial horizon, the E of today;
the B3 the transition to the C, the BC of today; the “(B)” the B
incipiente, the Bi of today) when a profile shows a mark of it (a B
followed by a number, an A or a C followed by two figures, a “(B)”, “ir”
in a B, “pl” in a B or C). The reading took no account of a notation
declared in `site$designation_system`, so a profile declared in the FAO
notation of 2006, which writes “B1, B2, B3” for three parts of a B, had
its A2 read as E and its B3 as BC, and “(Bw)R” read as “BiwR”. Found
while building the FAO-Unesco module.

As Hugo decided (Q1 to Q9, 2026-11-10), a declared notation now decides
before the marks (`.desg_declared_notation()`,
`R/utils-wrb-ch3-v09220.R`):

- a declared older notation has its A2, B3 and “(B)” read, marks or not:
  the Australian Field Handbook of the ASC (`asc` with or without an
  edition, as `asc4` or `asc2021`, and its aliases: A1, A2, A3, B1, B21,
  B3), the French CPCS of 1967 (`cpcs`, `cpcs1967`, `french`, `fr`), the
  FAO-Unesco Legend of 1974 and the FAO Guidelines of 1977 (`fao1974`,
  `fao1977`, the only older ones among the FAO values), the USDA Soil
  Survey Manual of 1951 and its supplement of 1962 (`usda1951`,
  `ssm1951`, `usda1962`, `ssm1962`, `soilsurveymanual1951`,
  `soilsurveymanual1962`) and the Brazilian notation in use until 1988
  (`br_pre1988`). The USDA of 1975 and the Soviet notation of 1977 are
  not old here;
- a declared present notation has none of them read, whatever the marks:
  `fao`, `fao2006`, `wrb` and its editions, `usda`, `kst`, `sibcs` (the
  notation of Santos et al., 2015), the CSSC, NZSC, SCSJ and CSCJ
  values, and the South African, German, Russian and French notations as
  their own readers recognise them (so “zambia”, “satellite” or
  “dbg-wrb” are not taken for a notation). In a present notation a “(B)”
  loses its parentheses and keeps its letters (“(Bw)R” is read “BwR”,
  “(B)km” “Bkm”), where the older or undeclared notation reads it “Bi”
  as before;
- with no declaration, a value that declares nothing (`NA`, `none`, `SA`
  …), `nz_legacy` or a value soilKey does not know, the marks decide as
  before; `PedonRecord$validate()` notes a value it does not know.
  Declared values are compared lower-cased, accents folded and all but
  letters and digits dropped, a value that is not UTF-8 read as CP1252.

The site reaches every reader as an explicit argument: `.desg_master()`,
`.desg_old_notation()` and `.h_master()` take `site`, and so do the
helpers that received only the horizons (the FAO readers of the master,
the solum, the buried horizons, the rock structure and the texture, the
WRB plough, subsurface, cemented and secondary carbonate and gypsum
readers, the SiBCS readers of the B in the first 100 cm, the abrupt
textural change, the histic and organic layers and the textural ratio,
the Chinese horizon kind). The readers that read one designation at a
time now read it with the notation of its whole profile: the cemented
layers of the WRB qualifiers (each part of “Bt/Cr” read with the parts
of the profile) and the plough designation of the Brunic qualifier.

The NSD reader
([`read_nsd_pedons()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/read_nsd_pedons.md))
now declares `designation_system = "nz_legacy"` (it declared `"nzsc"`):
the National Soils Database surveys are written in the New Zealand
notation, many of them in its older form (A11, A12, B21, B22, B3 beside
Bw). Every reader that compares the notation reads `nz_legacy` (or “NZ
legacy”, compared as a key) as it read `nzsc`: the NZSC, SCSJ, CSSC, ASC
and FAO 1988 notation tests, the frozen-layer pattern and the CPCS,
which reads the f of a New Zealand B as iron, not frozen. The
older-notation reading is judged from each profile’s own marks. The ASC
key also reads `asc` with an edition (`asc3`, `asc2021`) as its
notation. The ISIS reader keeps `fao2006` (Q6).
`inst/schemas/site-attributes.yaml` lists the values the code compares
(`fao`, `fao2006`, `wrb` and its editions, `usda`, `sibcs`, `fao1977`,
`usda1951`, `ssm1951`, `usda1962`, `br_pre1988`, `nz_legacy`) and
`inst/ATTRIBUTES.md` is regenerated.

Measured on 2026-11-10, before and after:

- Every example and fixture keeps its names: 1,302 profiles (the
  canonical WRB and SiBCS fixtures, every `make_*_example()` choice and
  near miss, the FAO 1988 and 1974 examples, the ZA forms and the 225
  KA5 subtypes) under 17 keys, 22,134 names identical.
- BDsolos, FEBR, Redape, AfSP, WoSIS, KSSL and LUCAS: their loaders
  declare no notation, so nothing changes.
- ISIS (974 profiles, `fao2006`): readings change in 8 profiles
  (present-notation designations such as “Ah, B1, B2, B3, B4”, “A1, A2,
  BA, Bt1, Bt2, B3” no longer read as the older notation, “(Bw)R” read
  “BwR”); names change for 3: SiBCS on 2 (CL006 Argissolos
  Bruno-Acinzentados to Neossolos Fluvicos, GH008 Cambissolos Haplicos
  to Neossolos Regoliticos) and the candidates of 1 undecided FAO 1988
  profile. WRB, USDA and FAO 1974 unchanged, so the ISIS benchmarks of
  0.9.392 are unchanged.
- NatSoil (9,703 profiles, `asc`): readings change in 437 (an Australian
  A2 read as E, a B3 as BC, where the profile has no other mark); names
  change on 306 profiles: the FAO 1988 candidates of 300 undecided
  profiles (299 stay undecided with another list, 1 becomes not
  classified), SiBCS on 10 (mostly Neossolos Regoliticos to Argissolos,
  2 to Espodossolos) and WRB on 4. The ASC key does not read these
  designations, so the NatSoil benchmark is unchanged.
- SALI, Queensland (5,716 profiles, `asc`): readings change in 34; names
  change on 20 profiles (22 names): the FAO 1988 candidates of 18
  undecided profiles, WRB on 2 (a Cambic qualifier gained) and SiBCS
  on 2. The SALI benchmark (ASC key) is unchanged.
- NSD (1,330 profiles, now `nz_legacy`): no reading changes, and all
  1,330 profiles give the same names under the 17 keys as before (22,610
  names; the 183 profiles with no horizons stop with the same error
  before and after).

## soilKey 0.9.394 (2026-11-10)

### South African classification 1991: four readings after the AfSP benchmark

Four readings examined on the AfSP benchmark of 0.9.393 and decided by
Hugo (2026-11-10). They are recorded in
`inst/rules/za1991/readings.yaml`; the 73 form examples, the 404 family
examples and the special cases (555 runs) keep their names and
provisional status.

- **B1: a B at the surface needs more than 100 mm.** The reading D7 (a
  red or yellow-brown apedal or neocarbonate surface layer with under
  0.3 % organic carbon directly over hard rock, a lithocutanic B or a
  dorbank is that B, the profile truncated) now holds only when the
  layer is more than 100 mm thick (`surface_b_thick` in
  `thresholds.yaml`, flagged). A thinner layer is not read as a B at the
  surface, so a thin carbon-poor topsoil on hard rock is tested as a
  topsoil and keys to Mispah, as the surveyors wrote it. The limit is
  over 100 mm while the lithosol rule of the general rules takes an
  orthic A under 100 mm, so a topsoil of exactly 100 mm is neither a
  lithosol nor read as a B. A layer whose thickness is not recorded (top
  or bottom missing) leaves the reading undecided, the orthic A or the
  B; no AfSP profile is affected. On AfSP, D7 fired on 6 profiles: the 5
  labelled Mispah (A of 50-100 mm, read as Clovelly) and one labelled
  Hutton (300 mm, red), which keeps its Hutton. Of the 5, one is now
  Mispah and 4 stop with Mispah among the forms left undecided (their A
  stays undecided as organic O or melanic A; examined apart, for Hugo).

- **C1: cutans not recorded leave the pedocutanic B undecided.** When
  clay films are not recorded, soilKey’s argic horizon stood in for the
  cutans both ways; but the pedocutanic B asks for prominent cutans, not
  a clay increase, so argic not holding refused the B. Now, in the
  pedocutanic test only, argic not holding leaves the cutans undecided;
  argic holding still stands in, flagged. The other refusals of the
  cutans reader (no peds, carbonate neoformations, a layer outside the
  zone of the clay maximum of an argic horizon) stand. The shared reader
  of cutans used by the other national systems is unchanged. On AfSP (no
  layer records clay films), the 5 Bonheim keyed as Inhoek now stop with
  Bonheim among the candidates; one Rensburg keyed as Willowbrook stops
  too, and 11 Swartland and Valsrivier profiles that stopped now have
  their label among the candidates.

- **A1: the humic A of 1977 in the benchmark (the key unchanged).** The
  thin humic A came with the second edition; the humic A of 1977 had to
  be thicker than 450 mm. The AfSP report gives a second figure,
  flagged, beside the main one: for labels from a survey before 1991 or
  written as a 1977 binomial (a label with neither is not read so),
  soilKey’s humic form with a humic A of 450 mm or less is scored as its
  orthic counterpart (Inanda as Hutton, Magwa as Clovelly, Kranskop as
  Griffin, Sweetwater as Oakleaf, Nomanci as Glenrosa; internal
  `.za_humic_1977()` in `R/za-benchmark.R`). Lusiki is left out: it has
  no single orthic counterpart (Valsrivier or Swartland by what lies
  below the pedocutanic B). The organic carbon is not corrected: AfSP
  gives no method for the South African SOTER profiles, their values
  read as reported by the laboratory, and the same institute’s WISE
  profiles are coded Walkley-Black.

- **M1: no dry colour and a moist value over 3 is not melanic.** The
  melanic A needs a dry value and chroma of 3 or less. A layer with no
  dry colour was left undecided for the melanic colour (default 9), even
  with a light moist colour; but the dry value is never darker than the
  moist, so a moist value over 3 now refuses the colour, flagged
  (`dry_value_from_moist`). A moist value of 3 or less stays undecided,
  as before. The 200 mm window of the organic O below a description that
  ends in rock is not changed (O1 not adopted). Two older tests that
  exercised default 9 on a layer of moist value 4 or 5 now give that
  layer a moist value of 3. On AfSP, 30 profiles that stopped are now
  decided: 16 agree (Clovelly 8, Mispah 5, Griffin, Hutton and Katspruit
  1 each) and 14 do not, where the B or the material below is not
  recognised from the data (Avalon as Clovelly 5 and as Pinedene 1,
  Kroonstad as Klapmuts 2, Westleigh 2, Clovelly as Hutton, Glenrosa as
  Hutton, Longlands as Pinedene and Valsrivier as Katspruit 1 each).

The AfSP run of 2026-11-10 (641 scored), with all four readings:

- Main figure: 139 of 641 agree, 21.7 % (Wilson 95 % 18.7-25.0; 0.9.393:
  122, 19.0 %). soilKey names a form for 216 (coverage 33.7 %,
  30.1-37.4; was 196, 30.6 %), and among those the form agrees for 64.4
  % (57.8-70.4; was 62.2 %). 423 stop with forms undecided and the
  label’s form is among them for 315 (74.5 %; was 316 of 442, 71.5 %).
  The confusions Mispah to Clovelly (5) and Bonheim to Inhoek (5) are
  gone; Mispah now agrees for 8 of 18 (was 2).
- Without M1 (B1, C1 and A1 only) the main figure was 123 of 641 (19.2
  %), 186 decided (29.0 %), 66.1 % of them.
- Second figure, the humic A of 1977 (surveys before 1991 or 1977
  binomials): 154 of 641 agree, 24.0 % (20.9-27.5); 71.3 % of the
  decided (64.9-76.9). 25 profiles are read so; 19 agreements gained
  (Hutton read as Inanda 8, Clovelly as Magwa 6, Griffin as Kranskop 5)
  and 4 lost: binomials of surveys of 1999-2000 whose surveyors wrote a
  thin humic A as humic (Kranskop 3, Inanda 1). Left: a Griffin of 1982
  whose humic A is 500 mm.

## soilKey 0.9.393 (2026-11-10)

### South African classification 1991: the AfSP benchmark

A new script, `inst/benchmarks/za1991_afsp.R`, compares
[`classify_za1991()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_za1991.md)
with the local classification of the South African profiles of the
Africa Soil Profiles database (AfSP 1.2, ISRIC; field `LocalCls` of
`AfSP012Qry_Profiles.dbf`). The script is offline: it reads the AfSP DBF
files from the directory given as its first argument, the option
`soilKey.afsp_dir` or the environment variable `SOILKEY_AFSP_DIR`, stops
(from R) or exits cleanly (as a script) when there is none, and
downloads nothing. AfSP is CC BY-NC; no profile or label of it is
shipped with soilKey, and the tests use synthetic labels and profiles
only. Every classification is unchanged.

The labels are read by a new internal reader, `.za_match_label()` in
`R/za-benchmark.R`, as Hugo decided (2026-11-10):

- **The era from the shape of the label, not the survey year.** A
  binomial `"<Form> <Series>"` (with or without a comma after the form)
  is a label of 1977 and is scored at the form level as its 1991
  namesake; `"<Form> Form, <Family> Family"` is a label of 1991; a form
  named alone is reported apart. The report gives the agreement overall
  and by era, and notes that some forms were redefined in 1991.
- **Exact names only.** The form word is matched to a form name of
  `inst/rules/za1991/key.yaml` and the family to a family name of that
  form in `families.yaml` (case ignored). The script’s explicit list of
  misspellings (Avanlon, Houhoek, Houwbroek and Kraanskop, with or
  without a comma) is tried only when a label is not read as it stands,
  and such matches are flagged; anything else is unmatched, never
  guessed.
- **No form counts as a disagreement** in the main figure, as in the
  other benchmarks. The report also gives the agreement among the
  profiles soilKey decides, the coverage, the provisional share among
  them, and how often the label’s form is among the forms left undecided
  (the `forms:<code>` entries of `provisional_because`).
- **Families** are scored only where a 1991 label names a family of its
  form and soilKey reaches a family; the series of 1977 are not scored.

The run of 2026-11-10 on AfSP 1.2: 659 South African profiles, 646
labelled, all 646 read (4 by the listed misspellings), 641 scored (5
labelled profiles have no WRB 2006 group and are not built by
[`load_afsp_pedons()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/load_afsp_pedons.md)).
624 are binomials of 1977, 13 labels of 1991 and 4 forms named alone;
108 of the binomials were surveyed in 1991 or later, and all 13 labels
in the 1991 shape come from surveys before 1991 (converted to the 1991
system later, by the compilers).

- Form: 122 of 641 agree, 19.0 % (Wilson 95 % 16.2-22.3); 1977 binomials
  19.6 % (16.6-22.8, n 624), 1991 labels 0 of 13, forms named alone 0 of
  4.
- soilKey names a form for 196 profiles (coverage 30.6 %, 27.1-34.3),
  and among those the form agrees for 62.2 % (55.3-68.7); 121 of the 196
  are provisional (104 at the form level). 442 stop with forms
  undecided, and the label’s form is among them for 316 (71.5 %); 3 get
  no form at all (nothing undecided).
- Candidates: the lists of forms left undecided hold a median of 8.5
  forms. With the labels shuffled across the 442 profiles that stop
  (1000 permutations, fixed seed) the hit rate is 40.9 % (95 % range
  38.0-44.1); by size of the list, 56 of 103 with 1-5 forms (54.4 %),
  116 of 158 with 6-20 (73.4 %), none with 21-40, 144 of 181 with over
  40 (79.6 %). Not in the rate: 8 of the 74 decided disagreements have
  the label’s form among the forms left undecided before the one
  assigned.
- Hutton, the largest class, agrees for 84 of 185 labels (84 of the 93
  soilKey decides).
- Family: 10 of the 13 labels of 1991 name a family of their form;
  soilKey reaches a family for 2 of them, and neither agrees (in both
  the form differs). Of the 3 family names not read, 2 (Glengazi,
  Cleveland) are 1977 series names and 1 (Greendal) looks like a
  misspelling of Greendale (Rg1000); it is not read (no family
  misspelling list, Hugo’s decision).

The main loss is the profiles that stop: most AfSP descriptions do not
record what the key needs to separate the forms (the matrix colour of
the lower B, cutans, slickensides, signs of wetness). Among the decided
disagreements, the most frequent are a humic A where the label has an
orthic A (Hutton to Inanda 8, Clovelly to Magwa 6, Griffin to Kranskop
6), Oakleaf read as Hutton (6), Bonheim keyed as Inhoek (5; in 4 of them
Bonheim, tested before, was left undecided), and a thin, carbon-poor A
on hard rock read as a truncated profile, Mispah to Clovelly (5).

## soilKey 0.9.392 (2026-11-09)

### FAO-Unesco legend: the ISIS benchmark

Twelfth and last part of the FAO-Unesco soil legend. A new script,
`inst/benchmarks/fao_isis.R`, compares both editions with the FAO-Unesco
names ISRIC gave its reference profiles (ISIS, field
`faoClassifications`): the label of 1974 with
`classify_fao(edition = "1974")`, the label of the Revised Legend
(stored under the year of the ISRIC reprint, 1997) with
[`classify_fao()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_fao.md).
As Hugo decided (Q27), it is offline and does not change the ISIS
reader: it reads a saved cache of ISIS profiles from its first argument,
the option `soilKey.isis_cache`, `SOILKEY_ISIS_CACHE` or the user cache
folder, downloads nothing, and run as a script with no cache found says
so and exits cleanly. ISIS data are not shipped. WoSIS is left for
later, with Hugo’s go.

The labels are read by a new internal reader, `.fao_match_label()` in
`R/fao-benchmark.R`: the edition from the publication year (1974 to
fao1974; 1988, 1990 and 1997 to fao1988), the group word singular or
plural, the 1974 Nitosols and the 1988 Nitisols read in the other
edition too (flagged), ISRIC’s third-level subunit (“Ferri-”, “Orthi-”)
cut off and reported apart (the legend defines no third level, so it is
never scored), the words after the group matched to the phases of the
edition, exact names only; a variants list, empty today, is tried only
on a label that is not read. Every one of the 1,515 labels of the cache
of 2026-10-29 (803 of 1974, 712 revised, on 814 profiles) is read as it
stands, with its grouping and unit; 593 revised labels carry a subunit,
212 labels a phase.

The run of 2026-11-09 on that cache, before Hugo’s decisions below (13
labels on 7 profiles with no horizons in the record are not scored):

- Legend of 1974, 796 labels: grouping 250 agree, 31.4 % (Wilson 95 %
  28.3-34.7); unit 120, 15.1 % (12.8-17.7), 48.0 % (41.9-54.2) where the
  grouping agrees. soilKey names a group for 529 labels, and among those
  the group agrees for 47.3 % (43.0-51.5); 260 stop with candidates
  undecided and 7 are not classified (no residual group, Q5). Of the
  529, 267 are provisional (a group tested before it left undecided) and
  134 rest on a stand-in; among the 207 firm labels (classified, neither
  provisional nor on a stand-in) the group agrees for 43.0 %
  (36.4-49.8).
- Revised Legend, 706 labels: grouping 155 agree, 22.0 % (19.1-25.2);
  unit 102, 14.4 % (12.0-17.2), 65.8 % (58.0-72.8) where the grouping
  agrees. soilKey names a grouping for 353 labels, and among those it
  agrees for 43.9 % (38.8-49.1); the other 353 stop with candidates
  undecided. Of the 353, 288 are provisional and 3 rest on a stand-in;
  among the 62 firm labels the grouping agrees for 32.3 % (22.0-44.6).
- Phases: of the labelled phases soilKey finds present the sodic phase
  25 of 29 (1974) and 8 of 11 (1988), the duripan 6 of 7 and 3 of 3, the
  fragipan 5 of 6 and 2 of 2, the petric 9 of 14, the skeletic 8 of 15,
  the gilgai 9 of 9 and the phreatic 6 of 11 in 1988; the field-only
  phases ISIS does not record in the profile data (cerrado, stony,
  rudic, anthraquic, gelundic, takyric) are absent, and the inundic
  phase undecided, as Hugo’s rule for a field observation not recorded
  asks. soilKey finds the sodic phase on far more profiles than the
  labels name (113 and 106), which suggests the labels do not list every
  phase.

The fall-throughs are the main loss: most profiles that stop do so
because a measurement the key needs is not in the record, most often the
gypsum content (the Gypsisols are a candidate in 271 of the 353 revised
fall-throughs; the gypsiric and gypsic tests of the Regosols, Fluvisols
and Arenosols of 1974 likewise), the pyrophosphate and oxalate Al and Fe
of the spodic B, the clay skins and the electrical conductivity.
Following Hugo’s rule, a measurement not recorded leaves its test
undecided and the soil names its candidates instead of a guess. The weak
spots the plan expected show in the confusion tables: Vertisols keyed as
Cambisols (13 of the 1974 labels, 17 of the revised ones), Andosols as
Cambisols (20 and 15), and Ferralsols as Acrisols or Cambisols (24 and
20). The report gives the agreement by edition and level with Wilson
intervals, the provisional, stand-in and fall-through counts, the
candidates left undecided, the phases and the confusion of the
groupings. soilKey’s readings of this part (the edition from the
publication year, the reading of labels, what counts in the benchmark,
and that a phase soilKey finds but a label omits is reported, not
counted as an error) are in `inst/rules/fao1988/readings.yaml` and
`data-raw/fao_readings.yaml`, confirmed by Hugo (2026-11-10); the
vignette on cross-system classification gains a section on the two
editions. Every classification is unchanged (the fixtures of the other
systems byte-identical).

Fixed on the review (2026-11-10). The firm agreement counts only the
labels soilKey classifies (it counted the fall-throughs as firm), and
the provisional and stand-in columns of the agreement table say so; a
profile that could not be run no longer drops an element of the results
list. The crosswalk of 0.9.391: the Lithosols, Rendzinas and Rankers as
units are renamed (p. 117 prints “formerly”), the Vertisols and
Histosols groups the same (no group comment on pp. 118 and 126), the
Calcic Cambisols split, the Dystric Podzoluvisols amended (the gleyic
comment runs onto their row, p. 123), the Rhodic Nitisols new with no
comment printed (bracketed, and an alternative of the Eutric and Dystric
Nitosols), the Luvic Calcisols an alternative of the Calcic Luvisols
(keyed before the Luvisols, p. 119); a condition may be given per
target, so a Eutric Fluvisol of 1988 shows only the fluvic clause of the
Gleysols of 1974, and a 1988 unit shows the alternatives that name its
unit, else those of the group rows (a Calcaric Cambisol no longer shows
the Haplic Xerosols). Hugo confirmed these readings (2026-11-10). The
tests read the benchmark script from the installed package (so they run
under R CMD check), run it end to end on a small synthetic cache, and
check the edition line on constructed results instead of classifying
every example.

Decided by Hugo (2026-11-10), on the causes the benchmark showed. The
ISIS reader reads the profile’s large cracking and, without a cracking
record, gilgai as cracks of 1 cm or more (the lower limit of the medium
surface cracks, 1-2 cm, of the FAO field guidelines’ classes that ISIS’s
own cracksSurface uses); small cracking stays 0.5 cm, since a small
crack may be a fine one. With neither gypsum nor an ECe recorded, an
upper bound of the ECe below 2 dS/m (the reader derives it from the EC
1:2.5) reads as no gypsum, flagged, the rule already used for an ECe
below 2; this serves the gypsic horizon of both editions. Andic
properties with Alox + 1/2 Feox of 2 % or more and a bulk density of 0.9
or less and no P retention measured are undecided, not absent; the rule
that undecided andic properties are absent unless volcanic material is
recorded applies only when fewer criteria are met (the amorphous complex
of 1974 has no such rule and was not changed). The oxic B of 1974 keeps
Q13: clay films recorded as few still count as evidence of illuviation,
a known cause of Ferralsols keyed as Acrisols or Luvisols in the
benchmark. The other consumers of the ISIS reader are unchanged: the CST
2001 and KA5 ISIS benchmarks give the same scores before and after, and
on the 38 ISIS profiles whose cracks change, the WRB and USDA results of
[`benchmark_isis()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/benchmark_isis.md)
are the same (both ask 0.5 cm). No result of
[`make_fao_example()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/make_fao_example.md)
changes, and every other classification is unchanged (the fixtures of
the other systems byte-identical).

The benchmark after these decisions, same cache:

- Legend of 1974, 796 labels: grouping 276 agree, 34.7 % (31.4-38.0);
  unit 143, 18.0 % (15.5-20.8), 51.8 % (45.9-57.6) where the grouping
  agrees. soilKey names a group for 563 labels (529 before), and among
  those it agrees for 49.0 % (44.9-53.1); 226 stop with candidates
  undecided (260 before), 7 are not classified. Among the 254 firm
  labels the group agrees for 46.9 % (40.8-53.0). The Vertisols now
  agree on 22 labels (none before).
- Revised Legend, 706 labels: grouping 186 agree, 26.3 % (23.2-29.7);
  unit 123, 17.4 % (14.8-20.4), 66.1 % (59.1-72.5) where the grouping
  agrees. soilKey names a grouping for 383 labels (353 before), and
  among those it agrees for 48.6 % (43.6-53.6); 323 stop with candidates
  undecided. Among the 195 firm labels the grouping agrees for 51.3 %
  (44.3-58.2). The Vertisols agree on 21 labels (none before), and the
  Gypsisols are a candidate in 166 fall-throughs (271 before).

## soilKey 0.9.391 (2026-11-09)

### FAO-Unesco legend: the crosswalk between the 1974 and 1988 editions

Eleventh part of the FAO-Unesco soil legend.
`inst/rules/fao1988/crosswalk.yaml` holds the correspondence of Appendix
4 of the Revised Legend (“Main changes in the revised legend”,
pp. 113-126) between the 26 major soil groups and 106 soil units of the
Legend of 1974 and the 28 major soil groupings and 153 soil units of
1988. Every 1974 group and unit has one row: the 1988 class or classes
it goes to, or none where it is deleted, with its relation (same name,
renamed, amended, renamed and amended, merged, split, deleted), the
printed page and the comment of the appendix in soilKey’s words. The
1988 classes with no 1974 class are listed as new: the 6 new groupings
beside the Leptosols, which take the Lithosols, Rendzinas and Rankers,
and 59 units. Appendix 4 prints only the 1988 names; the 1974 class of
each row is read from the 1974 list by its name or by the “formerly” the
appendix prints. Codes only: the names are read from the rule files of
each edition.

As Hugo decided (Q8), the three changes the appendix does not flag are
added in brackets: Calcaric Gleysols (Gc) to Calcic Gleysols (GLk) is a
change of definition, the Plinthic Luvisols (Lp) are deleted with no
1988 row, and the Thionic Histosols (HSt) are new. Where a group comment
of the appendix sends part of a 1974 group elsewhere, soilKey adds
bracketed alternatives with their condition: the Luvisol units to the
Lixisols and the Acrisol units to the Alisols by the CEC of the argic B,
the Calcic Cambisols to the Calcisols or Gypsisols, the Calcic
Kastanozems to the Gypsic Kastanozems, the plinthic units to the
Plinthosols, and the units of the deleted Xerosols and Yermosols by
their names. One-to-many rows stay one-to-many (Pellic and Chromic
Vertisols to the four Vertisol units, Eutric and Dystric Histosols to
the Folic, Terric and Fibric ones).

[`fao_crosswalk()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/fao_crosswalk.md)
(exported) returns the table, one row per 1974 class, or with
`from = "1988"` the 1974 classes behind a 1988 code.
[`print()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/print.html) of a result of either
edition, the HTML and PDF reports and the Pro app add one line with the
other edition: a Lixisol of 1988 is new in 1988, some Orthic, Chromic,
Calcic and Vertic Luvisols of 1974 when their argic B has a CEC below 24
cmol(+)/kg clay; an Orthic Luvisol of 1974 is a Haplic Luvisol of 1988
(renamed and amended, p. 122), or a Haplic Lixisol. The line is a note:
the table never classifies, each edition is keyed by its own text, and
every classification is unchanged (the fixtures of the other systems
byte-identical; no FAO result changes, the line is computed when
printed). soilKey’s readings of this part (the 1974 side of each row,
two comments printed between rows, the alternatives read from the group
comments, the targets of the Xerosol and Yermosol units, two slips of
the layout on pp. 115 and 124) are in `inst/rules/fao1988/readings.yaml`
and `data-raw/fao_readings.yaml`. Decided by Hugo (2026-11-10): all of
them are confirmed as proposed.

## soilKey 0.9.390 (2026-11-09)

### FAO-Unesco legend: the phases of 1974

Tenth part of the FAO-Unesco soil legend, the fourth of the Legend of
1974. `classify_fao(edition = "1974")` now gives the 12 phases of
pp. 5-7 in `$phases`, beside the soil unit: stony, lithic, petric,
petrocalcic, petrogypsic, petroferric, phreatic, fragipan, duripan,
saline, sodic and cerrado (the list of p. 5 prints “stony lithic”
without a comma: two phases). Phases subdivide the units by what matters
for the use of the land and are not diagnostic for the units (p. 5), so
the unit, the group and the key trace are exactly those of 0.9.389. Each
phase is three-valued, in the same form as the phases of 1988: `status`
is present, absent, undecided, or not shown where the text excludes the
unit, with `criterion`, the page, the criterion in soilKey’s words, the
fallbacks used and what would decide an undecided phase. Two more rows
give the classes of the map symbol (pp. 4-5): the texture class of the
upper 30 cm with the classes of 1974 (1 coarse, below 18 % clay and
above 65 % sand; 2 medium; 3 fine, above 35 % clay) and the slope class
(a up to 8 %, b to 30 %, c above 30 %). The phases, their pages,
criteria, numbers and Portuguese names are in
`inst/rules/fao1974/phases.yaml`, read by `R/fao-phases.R`.

The numbers are the printed ones. Lithic: continuous coherent hard rock
within 50 cm. Petric: 40 % or more coarse fragments by volume, oxidic
concretions, hardened plinthite or ironstone included, 25 cm thick, the
top within 100 cm, not continuously cemented. Petrocalcic and
petrogypsic: the cemented calcic or gypsic horizon of Soil Taxonomy, or
a pan recorded as calcrete or gypcrete, the top within 100 cm.
Petroferric, fragipan and duripan: the upper level within 100 cm, read
by the readers of the same phases of 1988. Phreatic: a water table
between 3 and 5 m. Saline: an ECe above 4 mmhos/cm in some horizon
within 100 cm. Sodic: more than 6 % exchangeable sodium within 100 cm.
Stony: the record of fragments or outcrops that make mechanised
equipment impracticable (`rudic_recorded`, the same condition as the
rudic phase of 1988). Cerrado: the vegetation recorded at the site. The
“not shown for” rules are applied as printed: no lithic phase for the
Lithosols, no saline phase for the Solonchaks, no sodic phase for the
Solonetz; when such a group is only a candidate, a phase whose criterion
is met is undecided.

Hugo’s decisions of 2026-11-08 are applied: the phases are a separate
list per edition, three-valued, with the “not shown for” rules, and the
cerrado phase is read from the recorded vegetation (Q25); the texture
and slope classes of the map symbol are given when the data allow (Q3);
the field-only phases (stony, cerrado) are absent when not recorded,
with no substitute threshold (default 16); the pans of Soil Taxonomy
read soilKey’s USDA predicates, the WRB horizons only as stand-ins,
flagged (default 17). soilKey’s readings of this part (the stony phase
on the rudic record, the petric phase as the skeletic reader at 100 cm,
the petrocalcic and petrogypsic horizons of the shared reader, the 3 to
5 m of the phreatic phase with both ends included and no morphology
test, no unit-level exclusion) are in `inst/rules/fao1974/readings.yaml`
and `data-raw/fao_readings.yaml` for his word.
[`print()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/print.html) and the HTML and PDF
reports show the phases of 1974 as they show those of 1988. The reader
of the “not shown for” rules takes the length of the group code (two
letters in 1988, one in 1974); every result of 1988, its phases
included, is unchanged, and every other classification is unchanged (the
fixtures of the other systems byte-identical).

Decided by Hugo on the review (2026-11-10). The stony phase is read on
the rudic record (`rudic_recorded`), as proposed.

## soilKey 0.9.389 (2026-11-09)

### FAO-Unesco legend: the 26 major soil groups and 106 units of 1974

Ninth part of the FAO-Unesco soil legend, the third of the Legend of
1974 (Soil Map of the World, Vol. I, Unesco Paris). The legend of 1974
is now registered as `fao1974` (aliases `fao74`, `fao_unesco_1974`;
experimental and opt-in; order 17 in the registry, namespace `fao74`).
`classify_fao(pedon, edition = "1974")` keys it, and
[`classify_fao1974()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_fao1974.md)
is its thin wrapper in the registry, as Hugo decided (Q1); `fao` stays
the Revised Legend (Q2). The key of pp. 43-53 is read in its own order,
not that of the list of pp. 12-13: Histosols, Lithosols, Vertisols,
Fluvisols, Solonchaks, Gleysols, Andosols, Arenosols, Regosols, Rankers,
Rendzinas, Podzols, Ferralsols, Planosols, Solonetz, Greyzems,
Chernozems, Kastanozems, Phaeozems, Podzoluvisols, Xerosols, Yermosols,
Nitosols, Acrisols, Luvisols and Cambisols. Under its group a soil keys
to the first of the 106 soil units whose gate passes, the last unit of
each group being the key’s “Other …” residual (Orthic, Eutric, Haplic,
Chromic, Vitric or Cambic as printed); the Lithosols, Rankers and
Rendzinas are single units, so their result has one level. The groups
are in `inst/rules/fao1974/key.yaml`, the units in
`inst/rules/fao1974/units/`, each with its code and name as printed,
soilKey’s Portuguese gloss, its page and its gate in soilKey’s words.

The gates read the diagnostic horizons (0.9.387) and properties
(0.9.388) of 1974. A new file, `R/key-fao74.R`, holds the predicates
that combine them where a gate reads more than one in one place, or
reads a window, a B or a record the diagnostics do not read: the H
horizon of the Histosols, the rock within 10 cm of the Lithosols, the
clay mixed over 20 cm, cracks and gilgai of the Vertisols, “no
diagnostic horizons other than”, the material of the Andosols to 35 cm,
the coarse texture, albic material and B features of the Arenosols, the
thickness of the umbric A of the Rankers and Humic Cambisols, the
calcareous material under the mollic A of the Rendzinas, the uppermost
diagnostic B, the albic E over a slowly permeable horizon of the
Planosols, the chroma of the mollic A to 15 cm, the 125, 90 or 75 cm of
the calcic and gypsic horizons by texture, the shallower of a calcic and
a gypsic horizon of the Xerosols and Yermosols, the tongues or nodules
of the Podzoluvisols, the clay distribution of the Nitosols, and the
unit gates of the windows, the B horizons, the Podzols, the Ferralsols
and the Planosols. No predicate of 1988 is redefined; the shared readers
run on the 1974 context.

Hugo’s decisions of 2026-11-08 are applied: the key governs where the
definitions differ (Q6: a mollic A with bleached coatings and
hydromorphic properties keys as a Mollic Gleysol, the Acrisols read the
base saturation in some part of the B, the Mollic and Humic Andosols ask
no smeary consistence, the Nitosols do not exclude an albic E); there is
no residual group after the Cambisols (Q5): a soil that no gate takes is
`[Not classified in the FAO-Unesco Legend (1974)]`, and one with gates
undecided names them as candidates; a diagnostic with no depth in the
key is read within 125 cm (Q10); the regime of the Xerosols and
Yermosols is the one recorded, and the shallower of a calcic and a
gypsic horizon decides (Q26); calcareous between 20 and 50 cm is an
alternative of the Calcic Cambisols (default 15). Where the 1974 text
repeats a rule Hugo decided for 1988 (the uppermost diagnostic B decides
at the key, the Kastanozems as the exact complement of the Chernozems,
the thin H horizon over rock, the Rendzic calcareous rock, volcanic
glass not recorded as none, the B of the unit gates, the colours of a
red, yellow or brown B, the slowly permeable horizon), the same reading
is used and recorded for his word. soilKey’s readings of this part
(among them: “coarse texture” as the coarse class of p. 5 to 100 cm,
albic material from the surface to 50 cm, the B characteristics of the
Arenosols as the features their units name, the single-unit groups with
one level) are in `inst/rules/fao1974/readings.yaml` and
`data-raw/fao_readings.yaml`.

`make_fao_example(code, edition = "1974")` gives one synthetic profile
per group (26, each keying to its own group without an undecided gate)
and per unit (106, each keying to its own unit), with near misses that
cross one printed number: 26 at group level (a rock at 11 cm, a calcic
horizon at 91 cm in a medium texture, a base saturation of 45 % in the
lower B) and 52 for the unit gates with a printed number (permafrost at
201 cm, a pH of 5.5 between 20 and 50 cm, 1.64 me per 100 g clay for the
Acric Ferralsols, a base saturation of 50 % in the B to 100 cm for the
Humic Ferralsols, a sandy loam to 100 cm for the Ochric Andosols). The
edition pairs of plan section 11 are tested: a Lixisol of 1988 is an
Orthic Luvisol of 1974, a Calcisol a Calcic Cambisol or, in an aridic
regime, a Calcic Xerosol, gleyic properties at 70 cm make a Gleyic
Luvisol of 1988 and an Orthic Luvisol of 1974, and a Nitisol of 1988
with a mollic A is a Luvic Phaeozem of 1974. The app lists the Legend of
1974 among the national systems with the 26 examples; the i18n
catalogues name the system and its edition in English and Portuguese.
The thresholds table is shipped as `inst/rules/fao1974/thresholds.yaml`
with a new `unit_key` block, and the list of the 26 groups and 106 units
as `data-raw/fao1974_units.csv`. Every result of 1988 is unchanged (the
296 examples of
[`make_fao_example()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/make_fao_example.md),
with their phases and traces), and every other classification is
unchanged (the fixtures of the other systems byte-identical).

The review (2026-11-09) fixed these defects: the lime waiver of the
mollic A of 1974 (more than 40 % finely divided lime waives the limits
of the dry value, 74 p. 24) now waives its dry contrast with the C too,
so a light calcareous A over a chalky C is a Rendzina; the Humic
Ferralsols and Ochric Andosols have near misses; and the tests build a
cambic B over an argillic B (a Cambisol, not a Luvisol) and a Vertisol
whose clay mixed over 20 cm passes where 18 cm would fail.

Decided by Hugo on the review (2026-11-10). The albic E and albic
material of 1974 ask a chroma below 2.5 at the middle values (a moist
value of 4 or 5, a dry value of 5 or 6; 3 over a red parent material),
the limit the 5YR clause of p. 27 presupposes, flagged; the reading “as
printed” of 0.9.387 and 0.9.388 is superseded. In 1974 an E with none of
the kinds p. 27 names below it (a spodic, argillic or natric B, a
fragipan, an impervious layer) is albic material, not an albic E, so a
white sand keys to the Albic Arenosols and a wet A / Eg / Cg to the
Gleysols whatever the letter of the E; 1988 is unchanged. The coarse
texture of the Arenosols is read to 100 cm or to the rock where it is
shallower. The Nitosols lack the ferric properties as printed, the CEC
by NH4Cl below 24 me per 100 g clay included, flagged. “At less than” is
strict for the Thionic Fluvisols (125 cm) and for the Gypsic and Calcic
Xerosols and Yermosols (125, 90 or 75 cm); their examples sit at 124 and
89 cm, the near misses at 125 and 90. An aridic regime not recorded
stays undecided, so a soil keyed after the Xerosols and Yermosols is
provisional until the regime is recorded. The uppermost B decides at the
key only, as in 1988: the Luvic units accept any argillic B. soilKey’s
other readings of this part are accepted (the single-unit groups with
one level, albic material from the surface to 50 cm, the Kastanozems as
the complement of the Chernozems, the uppermost B at the key, the slowly
permeable horizon of the Planosols, the vitric material of the
Andosols). The lime waiver of the mollic A, which waives the limits of
the dry value, now waives the dry contrast with the C in 1988 too (the
same words, p. 26): a correction to 0.9.382, which applies to the umbric
A as well; none of the 296 examples of 1988 changes.

## soilKey 0.9.388 (2026-11-09)

### FAO-Unesco legend: the diagnostic properties of 1974

Eighth part of the FAO-Unesco soil legend, the second of the Legend of
1974. `R/diagnostics-fao74.R` now also reads the diagnostic properties
of pp. 27-32 and the terms the 1974 key uses without a definition
section, as 28 internal predicates returning a `DiagnosticResult` that
passes, fails or stays undecided, with the layers, the per-layer
answers, what would decide it, the fallbacks used and any stand-in:
`abrupt_textural_change_fao74()`, `albic_material_fao74()`,
`aridic_regime_fao74()`, `amorphous_complex_fao74()`,
`ferralic_properties_fao74()`, `ferric_properties_fao74()`,
`gilgai_fao74()`, `high_om_b_fao74()` (with `kind = "acrisol"`),
`high_salinity_fao74()`, `hydromorphic_properties_fao74()`,
`interfingering_fao74()`, `permafrost_fao74()`, `plinthite_fao74()`,
`slickensides_fao74()`, `smeary_fao74()`, `soft_powdery_lime_fao74()`,
`sulfidic_materials_fao74()`, `takyric_features_fao74()`,
`thin_iron_pan_fao74()`, `tonguing_fao74()`,
`vertic_properties_fao74()`, `weatherable_minerals_fao74()`,
`recent_alluvial_deposits_fao74()`, `calcareous_fao74()`,
`bleached_coatings_fao74()`, `heavy_clay_fao74()`,
`exchangeable_sodium_fao74()` and `acric_cec_fao74()`. A property with
no printed depth is read within 125 cm (Q10). Nothing is registered or
classified yet.

The numbers are the printed ones. The abrupt textural change sits at the
base of an A or E and asks the clay to double within 8 cm, or, from 20 %
clay, 20 points more with double the clay somewhere in the horizon
below. The exchange complex dominated by amorphous material asks a bulk
density below 0.85 and one of its other marks (Q20). The ferralic and
ferric properties read a CEC by NH4Cl below 24 me per 100 g clay in the
cambic B, right below the A or in the argillic B. The B of high organic
matter asks 1.35 % organic matter over 100 cm (1.5 % in the upper B of
the Acrisols). High salinity is an ECe above 15 within 125, 90 or 75 cm
by the texture of the upper 30 cm, or above 4 within 25 cm at a pH above
8.5. The hydromorphic properties are the test of the text (Q22):
groundwater reaching the surface with its capillary fringe, a histic H,
neutral or bluish hues, or the colours of reduction in five branches for
soils with a spodic B, a mollic A, an argillic B under the plough layer,
an oxic B, and other soils, within 50 cm or the depth the caller gives.
The recent alluvial deposits ask 0.35 % organic matter to 125 cm, an
irregular decrease, stratification or sulfidic materials. Sulfidic
materials ask 0.75 % sulfur and no jarosite; vertic properties ask
cracks of 1 cm within 50 cm of the top of the B. The Acric CEC is 1.5 me
per 100 g clay or less, the sodium of the Solodic Planosols more than 6
%, and the heavy clay 60 % clay (soilKey’s number, flagged).

Where Appendix 4 of 1988 calls a property unchanged (interfingering,
permafrost, plinthite, slickensides, smeary consistence, soft powdery
lime, tonguing, weatherable minerals), the reader of 1988 runs on the
1974 context, where the argillic and cambic B are those of 1974;
calcareous and soft powdery lime read the numbers of 1988, flagged
(Q23). Those 1988 readers were moved into named functions with no
change: every `_fao88` result is the same. Where the 1974 answer stays
undecided, a USDA reader of soilKey stands in, then a WRB one, marked as
a stand-in (the amorphous complex, high salinity, the hydromorphic
properties, sulfidic materials, takyric features). soilKey’s readings of
this part (among them: the 8 cm of the abrupt change as an abrupt or
clear boundary, the albic colours as printed, the branches of the
hydromorphic test, sulfidic materials absent where sulfur is measured
nowhere and no marine setting is recorded) are in
`data-raw/fao_readings.yaml` for his word. Every classification is
unchanged (the fixtures of the other systems and the 1988 examples
byte-identical).

Decided by Hugo on the review (2026-11-09). soilKey’s readings of this
part are accepted. The ferralic properties read “respectively”:
`kind = "cambisol"` the cambic B, `kind = "arenosol"` the horizon right
below the A. In the hydromorphic properties an undecided spodic,
argillic or oxic B is read both ways, as the mollic A already was: a
layer is decided where the readings agree, else it stays undecided (the
designation fallback is dropped). The sulfidic criterion of the recent
alluvial deposits stays absent, flagged, where sulfur is measured
nowhere and no marine, tidal or brackish setting is recorded. The review
also fixed these defects: in 4.2 the shift to 75 cm when a calcic
horizon intervenes belongs to the chroma 1 branch only; a hue nearest to
2.5Y starts at 1.25Y; an iron pan not named thin or placic asks the 40
mm limit; and the 8 cm of the abrupt textural change cites the boundary
classes of the 1967 Guidelines.

## soilKey 0.9.387 (2026-11-09)

### FAO-Unesco legend: the diagnostic horizons of 1974

Seventh part of the FAO-Unesco soil legend, the first of the Legend of
1974 (Soil Map of the World, Vol. I, Unesco Paris). A new file,
`R/diagnostics-fao74.R`, reads the H horizon of the master horizons
(p. 21) and the 13 diagnostic horizons of pp. 24-27 as internal
predicates, each returning a `DiagnosticResult` that passes, fails or
stays undecided, with the layers, what would decide it, the fallbacks
used and any stand-in: `h_horizon_fao74()`, `histic_h_fao74()` (with
`base = "eutric"` or `"dystric"`), `mollic_a_fao74()`,
`umbric_a_fao74()`, `ochric_a_fao74()` (with `grade = "very_weak"` or
`"weak"`) and `ochric_grade_fao74()`, `argillic_b_fao74()`,
`natric_b_fao74()`, `cambic_b_fao74()`, `spodic_b_fao74()`,
`oxic_b_fao74()`, `calcic_fao74()`, `gypsic_fao74()`, `sulfuric_fao74()`
and `albic_e_fao74()`. Depths are read from the soil surface, horizons
buried under 50 cm of new material are not diagnostic (p. 32), and a
horizon with no printed depth is read within 125 cm (Q10). Nothing is
registered or classified yet.

The 1974 text writes organic matter, read as organic carbon x 1.724,
flagged (Q11). The H horizon has 20 % organic matter without clay to 30
% at 60 % clay and is saturated; the histic H is more than 20 cm of it,
or a thin surface or plough layer that, mixed to 25 cm, holds 14 to 28 %
organic matter. The mollic and umbric A ask 1 % organic matter (4 % with
the lime waiver) and have no strongly humic waiver of the colour
contrast; the umbric A drops the consistence rule where the A never
dries and excludes plaggen layers. The ochric A has two grades for the
Yermosols and Xerosols: very weak below a line of organic matter in the
upper 40 cm that falls from 1 % at a sand/clay ratio of 1 to 0.5 % at 13
(1.2 and 0.6 % in 18 cm over a shallow pan), and weak otherwise. The
argillic B asks the clay increase of 3 points, a ratio of 1.2 or 8
points within 30 cm and, unlike the 1988 argic B, evidence of
illuviation (clay skins, oriented clay or clay bridges; a Bt designation
counts, flagged, Q13), with one tenth of the overlying horizons, 7.5 cm
(15 cm in sand) or 15 cm of lamellae, and no texture limit. The natric B
adds columnar structure and more than 15 % sodium. The cambic B asks a
CEC above 16 me per 100 g clay or weatherable minerals, an alteration
(colour, clay, carbonates or the colours of reduction) and a base at 25
cm, with no minimum thickness. The oxic B asks 30 cm, an NH4Cl retention
of 10 or an ECEC below 10 and a CEC of 16 me per 100 g clay or less,
more than 15 % clay, only traces of primary minerals and rock structure
below 5 %. The sulfuric horizon asks jarosite mottles beside a pH below
3.5 (Q18).

Where Appendix 4 of 1988 calls a horizon unchanged (the albic E it calls
amended), the readers of 1988 are shared through the edition of the
profile context and branch only where the printed text differs (histic
H, mollic, umbric and ochric A, spodic B below 12.5 cm and below an Ap,
gypsic more than 15 cm, albic E without a chroma limit at the middle
values); every `_fao88` result is unchanged. Where a 1974 horizon stays
undecided, the USDA reader of soilKey stands in, then the WRB one,
marked as a stand-in. soilKey’s readings of this part (among them: the
saturation of the H horizon, the weak ochric A as every other ochric A,
fine clay compared only when recorded, sand and loamy sand as coarser
than very fine sand, “traces” of primary minerals as 3 % or less, no
thickness for the sulfuric horizon, and the stand-ins) are in
`data-raw/fao_readings.yaml` for his word. Every classification is
unchanged (the fixtures of the other systems and the 1988 examples
byte-identical).

Decided by Hugo on the review (2026-11-09). soilKey’s readings of this
part are accepted. The weak ochric A is every ochric A that is not very
weak, and a rock or pan shallower than 18 cm reads the 18 cm limits,
flagged. The spodic B is read below the deeper of 12.5 cm and the base
of an Ap, and a layer reaching below that depth counts by its part
below. The review also fixed these defects: the histic H of 1974 is
built from the saturated H horizon (a well-drained O no longer passes),
with its thin surface and plough layer paths kept; the swelling 2:1
clays of the argillic B take the evidence of pressure, a third more fine
clay or 8 points more fine clay as alternatives; where only the natric
exclusion of the argillic B is undecided, the USDA and then the WRB
natric horizon decide that exclusion alone, keeping the 1974 layers; a
stand-in that passes keeps only its layers within the upper limit and
not buried; and a cambic B with a CEC by NH4Cl of 16 or less leaves that
criterion undecided.

## soilKey 0.9.386 (2026-11-09)

### FAO-Unesco legend: the phases of 1988

Sixth part of the FAO-Unesco soil legend (the Revised Legend of 1988,
read in the ISRIC reprint of 1997).
[`classify_fao()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_fao.md)
now gives the 16 phases of chapter VIII (pp. 67-71) in `$phases`, beside
the soil unit: anthraquic, duripan, fragipan, gelundic, gilgai, inundic,
lithic, petroferric, phreatic, placic, rudic, salic, skeletic, sodic,
takyric and yermic. Phases are features of the land that may limit its
use; they cut across the units and never define one (p. 67), so the
unit, the grouping and the key trace are exactly those of 0.9.385. Each
phase is three-valued: `status` is present, absent, undecided, or not
shown where the text excludes the unit, with `criterion` (the test
alone), the page, the criterion in soilKey’s words, the fallbacks used
and, for an undecided phase, the attributes that would decide it. Two
more rows give the classes of the map symbol (Appendix 2, p. 107): the
texture class of the upper 30 cm (1 coarse, 2 medium, 3 fine, read by
the reader of 0.9.381) and the slope class (a up to 8 %, b to 30 %, c
above 30 %, from `slope_pct`). The phases, their pages, criteria,
numbers and Portuguese names are in `inst/rules/fao1988/phases.yaml`,
read by a new file, `R/fao-phases.R`; the numbers are those of the
`phases` block of the thresholds table.

The numbers are the printed ones. Lithic: continuous hard rock within 50
cm (`continuous_hard_rock_fao88()`). Salic: an ECe above 4 dS/m in a
layer within 100 cm. Sodic: more than 6 % exchangeable sodium within 100
cm. Skeletic: 40 % or more coarse fragments by volume, 25 cm thick, the
top within 50 cm, not continuously cemented. Inundic: more than 10 days
of surface water in the growing period. Phreatic: a water table within
500 cm with no gleyic properties. Anthraquic: stagnic properties within
50 cm under long continued irrigation, read from the site’s flood
irrigation, years under rice or a land use naming rice or paddy. Yermic:
less than 0.6 % organic carbon in the surface 18 cm mixed (0.20 % when
coarser than sandy loam, waived when the salic criterion is met) and one
of the six desert features. The duripan, fragipan, petroferric and
placic phases are a layer within 100 cm read by soilKey’s USDA
predicates (Soil Taxonomy 1975, p. 67), by the kind of pan recorded in
the field, or by the designations qm and x in the FAO notation, flagged;
the WRB petroduric, fragic and petroplinthic horizons stand in only
where the attributes of the USDA predicate are not recorded, flagged.
The “not shown for” rules are applied: no salic phase for the Solonchaks
and the Salic Fluvisols, no sodic phase for the Solonetz and the Sodic
Solonchaks, no phreatic phase for the Fluvisols and Gleysols; when such
a unit is only a candidate, a phase whose criterion is met is undecided.

Hugo’s decisions of 2026-11-08 are applied: the phases are a separate
list per edition, three-valued, with the “not shown for” rules, and the
phreatic phase is a water table within 500 cm without gleyic properties
outside the Fluvisols and Gleysols (Q25); the texture and slope classes
of the map symbol are given when the data allow (Q3); field-only phases
(gelundic, gilgai, rudic, takyric, the desert features) are absent when
not recorded, with no substitute threshold (default 16); the four pans
of Soil Taxonomy read the USDA predicates, the WRB horizons only as
stand-ins, flagged (default 17). The readings of this part are in
`inst/rules/fao1988/readings.yaml` and `data-raw/fao_readings.yaml`.
[`print()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/print.html) shows the phases present,
those undecided, those not shown and the map symbol; the HTML and PDF
reports add a section “Phases and map symbol” (English and Portuguese).
Every other classification is unchanged (the fixtures of the other
systems byte-identical), and the unit and grouping of every example of
[`make_fao_example()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/make_fao_example.md)
(296 profiles, near misses included) are those of 0.9.385.

Decided by Hugo on the review (2026-11-09). soilKey’s readings of this
part are accepted, with these changes. A moist rupture resistance of
firm or more (the layers of `fragipan_usda()`) is a sign of a fragipan
only, flagged and undecided, unless a second sign holds in the layer:
very or extremely firm with a massive structure, or a bulk density of
1.65 g/cm3 or more (the number of soilKey’s WRB fragic horizon; the text
has none); a designation with x (E/Bx too) or a recorded fragipan is one
by itself. The petroferric phase needs iron: 50 % plinthite or more, a
recorded ironstone or ferricrete, or a designation with m and v, c or s;
a layer cemented by carbonates, gypsum or silica is not petroferric. The
salic phase is not shown for the Salic Fluvisols either (the printed
reason of p. 69). Heavy textured, for the takyric phase, is the fine
class of the upper 30 cm (p. 107). A layer whose coarse fragments are
not recorded is not skeletic, flagged. A rice land use alone makes the
irrigation of the anthraquic phase, flagged, unless the site records no
irrigation. The lithic phase stays shown for the Leptosols. The review
also fixed these defects: the USDA pan layers count only when the
predicate passes (a firm layer too thin for a fragipan is none); a NASIS
fragipan without its depth is undecided; a recorded “not irrigated”
decides before the land use; the yermic carbon that fails is undecided
while the salic criterion is, and its blown sand is a sand sheet or
cover sand, not a dune, shifting sand or a negation;
`classify_fao(gapfill = TRUE)` gap-fills once, so the key and the phases
read the same pedon; a phase left open by a candidate unit names it
(`major_groups:SC`) in `missing`, with a note; a pan undecided by a
short description carries no “absent” flag; the slope class is given for
a pedon without horizons; and a phase that fails to read records the
error as a flag.

## soilKey 0.9.385 (2026-11-09)

### FAO-Unesco legend: the 153 soil units of 1988

Fifth part of the FAO-Unesco soil legend (the Revised Legend of 1988,
read in the ISRIC reprint of 1997). `fao1988` now has its second level,
the 153 soil units of the key (chapter X, pp. 75-89), registered as
`units` after the major soil groupings.
[`classify_fao()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_fao.md)
keys a soil to its grouping and then, under it, to the first unit whose
gate passes, in the key’s order, not the order of the lists (which start
with the Eutric or Haplic unit): `name` is the unit as printed (“Chromic
Luvisols”), `rsg_or_order` the grouping, and `levels` has one row per
level with its code, name, page and soilKey’s Portuguese gloss. The last
unit of each grouping is the key’s “Other …” residual: Haplic in 17
groupings, Eutric in 9, and the Terric Histosols and Urbic Anthrosols,
whose descriptions are shown as information and not tested (default 9).
A unit the data leave undecided before the one assigned makes the unit
provisional, listed as `units:<code>` in `provisional_because` with the
grouping still decided. The units are in `inst/rules/fao1988/units/`,
one file per grouping, each with its code, name, gloss, page, gate and a
summary of the gate in soilKey’s words; their numbers are in the
`unit_key` block of the thresholds table.

Most unit gates read the diagnostics of 0.9.382 and 0.9.383 directly:
permafrost within 200 cm, gleyic properties within 100 cm, stagnic
properties within 50 cm, plinthite, calcic and gypsic horizons within
125 cm, a sulfuric horizon or sulfidic material, the mollic, umbric and
ochric A, the eutric and dystric histic H, the argic B, calcareous or
gypsiferous from 20 to 50 cm, sodic, salic, andic, vertic and ferric
properties, tonguing, strongly humic, the petrocalcic and petrogypsic
horizons within 100 cm. A new file, `R/key-fao-units.R`, holds the
predicates of the gates that read more than one diagnostic in one place
or a record the diagnostics do not read: the drainage and fibres of the
Folic and Fibric Histosols, deep cultivation and man-made sediments of
the Aric and Cumulic Anthrosols, the rock within 10 cm and the
calcareous material under the mollic A of the Lithic and Rendzic
Leptosols, the base saturation of a window or of a B, the smeary
consistence and texture of the Vitric Andosols, the thick albic E, clay
increase, colour below the A and cambic alteration of the Arenosols, the
ignition, Fe/C ratio and thin albic E of the Podzols, the plinthite
horizon of the Dystric Plinthosols, the geric and ferralic properties
inside a B, the rubbed colours of the Rhodic, Xanthic and Chromic units,
and the slowly permeable horizon of the Dystric Planosols.

Hugo’s decisions of 2026-11-08 are applied: the key governs where
chapter VI differs (Q6), the two passages in italics of this part are
applied as printed (soft powdery lime in the Calcic Solonetz, p. 83; “in
at least some part of the B” in the Humic Cambisols, p. 89; Q4), and the
Gypsiric Regosols keep the key’s name with Gypsic Regosols, the name of
the lists, as an alias (Q7). Every name of the final list resolves to
exactly one unit. `make_fao_example(code)` now takes a unit code too:
153 synthetic profiles, each keying to its own unit without an undecided
grouping or unit before it, and 87 near misses, one for each unit gate
with a printed number, each crossing that number (a rock at 11 cm, a
calcic horizon at 126 cm, a base saturation of 50 % from 20 to 50 cm, a
rubbed chroma of 4 at 7.5YR) and keying to another unit. The i18n
catalogues name the level in English and Portuguese (“Soil unit”,
“Unidade de solo”); the app keeps its 28 examples, one per grouping. The
grouping of the 56 examples of 0.9.384 is unchanged, and every other
classification is unchanged (the fixtures of the other systems
byte-identical).

Decided by Hugo on the review (2026-11-09). soilKey’s readings of this
part are accepted, with these changes. The fimic A itself
(`fimic_a_fao88()`) now needs a sign of manuring: citric P2O5 above 250
mg/kg, a manuring term (plaggen, hortic, manure, compost, midden,
kitchen garden) in the layer origin, anthropic material, designation or
the site’s land use, or the WRB plaggic or hortic horizon, always tried;
artefacts neither make nor exclude it, so fills, wastes and man-made
sediments stay Anthrosols and key to the Cumulic or Urbic units, and the
unit-level guard of the first draft is gone. A Rhodic B whose dry value
is not recorded is undecided. A smeary consistence not recorded leaves
the Vitric Andosols undecided unless the texture is coarser than silt
loam. A calcareous rock under the mollic A (CaCO3 measured, or
limestone, chalk, marble or dolomite recorded) makes a Rendzic Leptosol.
The colour of a red, yellow or brown B is read in every layer of it. The
Fibric Histosols are very poorly drained or recorded undrained, not
artificially drained; a drainage range that spans the limit, or no
drainage record, leaves the Folic and Fibric units undecided. The other
readings are accepted as proposed: a depth missing from a unit gate is
read within 125 cm, “fibre content dominant” is the fibric material of
Soil Taxonomy, the Cumulic sediments are sandy loam or finer, silt loam
or finer excludes loam, the Luvic Arenosols compare a layer with any
layer above it, the carbon enrichment of a Podzol B is the h of its
designation, the plinthite horizon is the upper run of the gate, “the B”
is the upper diagnostic B of the grouping’s kind, and the slowly
permeable horizon is the layer below the E with the adjoining layers of
its master horizon. The review also fixed these defects: one vocabulary
of the anthropic record now serves the Anthrosols gate, the fimic A and
the Cumulic unit (plain “irrigation sediment”, “irragric”, “terric”, a
raised surface or a positive silting test alone were not read; “mine” is
read as a word, not inside “mineral”); a drainage range is read by both
ends, with the codes VP, P, W and Portuguese terms; an undecided B above
a sure one decides where their answers differ; free iron and carbon both
0 fail the Ferric Podzols; and the Gelic Leptosols have a near miss at
201 cm on a deep Leptosol with less than 20 % fine earth (87 near
misses).

## soilKey 0.9.384 (2026-11-09)

### FAO-Unesco legend: the 28 major soil groupings of 1988

Fourth part of the FAO-Unesco soil legend (the Revised Legend of 1988,
read in the ISRIC reprint of 1997). The legend is now registered as
`fao1988` (aliases `fao`, `fao88`, `revised_legend`; experimental and
opt-in; order 16 in the registry, namespace `fao88`), with one level for
now, the major soil groupings. `classify_fao(pedon, edition = "1988")`
is the user function of the module and
[`classify_fao1988()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_fao1988.md)
its thin wrapper in the registry, as Hugo decided (Q1);
`edition = "1974"` stops with a message until the Legend of 1974 is
keyed in a later part. The key of chapter X (pp. 75-89) is read in its
own order, not that of the lists: Histosols, Anthrosols, Leptosols,
Vertisols, Fluvisols, Solonchaks, Gleysols, Andosols, Arenosols,
Regosols, Podzols, Plinthosols, Ferralsols, Planosols, Solonetz,
Greyzems, Chernozems, Kastanozems, Phaeozems, Podzoluvisols, Gypsisols,
Calcisols, Nitisols, Alisols, Acrisols, Luvisols, Lixisols and
Cambisols. The gates read the 16 diagnostic horizons (0.9.382) and the
27 diagnostic properties (0.9.383); `R/key-fao.R` adds the predicates
that combine them where a gate reads more than one in one place: the
organic layers of the Histosols, the record of a profound human
modification, the rock, highly calcareous or cemented layer or the fine
earth of the Leptosols, the clay, cracks and slickensides of the
Vertisols, “no diagnostic horizons other than”, the coarse texture and
coarse fragments of the Arenosols, the plinthite under an albic E or a
stagnic horizon, the E over a slowly permeable horizon, the chroma of
the mollic A to 15 cm, the uncoated grains of the Greyzems, the base
saturation to 125 cm, the tongues or nodules of the Podzoluvisols, the
clay distribution and boundaries of the Nitisols, and the CEC and base
saturation of the argic B.

The tests are three-valued: an undecided gate before the one that passes
makes the result provisional. The key governs where the descriptions of
chapter VI differ (Q6), and the passage in italics of the Regosols gate
in the 1997 text (lacking soft powdery lime) is applied as printed (Q4).
There is no residual grouping after the Cambisols (Q5): a soil that no
gate takes is
`[Not classified in the FAO-Unesco Revised Legend (1988)]`, with the 28
failed gates in the warnings, and one that no gate takes while some stay
undecided names them as the candidates, in brackets. The names are as
printed, with soilKey’s Portuguese gloss in `levels$name_pt` and the
page of the key in `levels$page`. `make_fao_example(code)` gives one
synthetic profile per grouping (28, each keying to its own grouping
without an undecided gate) and, with `near_miss = TRUE`, the same
profile with one printed number of its gate crossed (28, each keying
elsewhere). The app lists the Revised Legend among the national systems
with the 28 examples; the i18n catalogues name the system, its edition
and the level in English and Portuguese. The thresholds table is shipped
as `inst/rules/fao1988/thresholds.yaml`, the readings of the 1988
edition as `inst/rules/fao1988/readings.yaml`, and the list of the 28
groupings and 153 units as `data-raw/fao1988_units.csv`. Every other
classification is unchanged (the fixtures of the other systems
byte-identical).

Decided by Hugo on the review (2026-11-09). soilKey’s readings of this
part are accepted, with these changes. The uppermost diagnostic B within
125 cm decides at the key (p. 42): the gate of a grouping defined by an
argic, natric, cambic, spodic or ferralic B passes only when its B is
the uppermost one, undecided when an undecided B lies above it
(`upper_b_fao88()`), so an argic B over a ferralic B is no Ferralsol and
a cambic B over an argic B no Luvisol. The CEC of the argic B is read
per layer (ch. VI p. 52): 24 cmol(+)/kg clay or more in every layer for
the Alisols and Luvisols, below 24 in at least one for the Acrisols and
Lixisols. An organic layer on rock or fragmental material makes a
Histosol when more than 20 cm thick (the histic H minimum), and a bulk
density not measured is read as 0.1 or more, flagged. The deep path of
the Plinthosols needs gleyic or stagnic properties in a horizon above
the plinthite within 100 cm (ch. VI p. 60), not in the plinthite itself.
The 35 cm of andic properties are measured from the mineral soil
surface, flagged when an O or H is skipped. The Kastanozems are the
exact complement of the Chernozems: a chroma above 2 in any layer of the
upper 15 cm of the A. The boundaries of the Nitisols are tested at the
A-to-B transition only. A crack with its depth but not its width leaves
the Vertisols undecided. The review also fixed the plinthite runs (read
layer by layer), the cracks (width and depth of the same record), the
missing attributes of the Planosols trace, the NT example (pressure
faces, which the nitic properties read) and the near-miss tests (every
gate evaluated directly).

## soilKey 0.9.383 (2026-11-09)

### FAO-Unesco legend: the diagnostic properties of 1988

Third part of the FAO-Unesco soil legend (the Revised Legend of 1988,
read in the ISRIC reprint of 1997). A new file,
`R/diagnostics-fao88-properties.R`, reads the 27 diagnostic properties
of chapter V (pp. 34-41) as internal predicates, each returning a
`DiagnosticResult` that passes, fails or stays undecided, with the
