- **Undecided key questions (Q4):** an undecided question follows every
  branch; one outcome gives the horizon, several leave it undecided with
  the candidates.
- **The surface horizon (Q11):** the agro horizon, else the thickest
  natural organic or humus horizon starting at the surface or under a
  deposit under 40 cm; the others are read as features.
- **Templates (Q13):** a type’s formula is closed on the vocabulary of
  its division: a horizon that appears in any scheme of the division
  must be matched when present; a horizon foreign to the division is
  ignored. The most specific scheme is tried first, agro before natural;
  when two match, the more specific wins and the other is an intergrade
  in the trace.
- **Formulas (Q14):** a horizon in parentheses is optional; terminal
  symbols are tested only where they name the type; “directly under”
  skips transitional rows and sub-horizons, with an allowed gap (up to
  15 cm between AU and BCA).
- **No type (Q15):** when no scheme matches, the name stops at the
  division and the trace lists the nearest schemes.
- **Subtypes (Q16):** every listed feature that passes is named, in list
  order; typical when every one is FALSE; provisional when some are
  undecided, which are listed; a feature already written in the type’s
  formula is not named again.
- **Also accepted:** sub-horizons are merged (BT1, BT2 = BT);
  transitions are not diagnostic; small horizons are marked rows, not
  diagnostic horizons; one layer may hold a horizon and an overlay (S,
  X, V).

## soilKey 0.9.333 (2026-11-01)

### France: the 276 subgroups of the CPCS 1967

[`classify_cpcs1967()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_cpcs1967.md)
now keys a pedon to its subgroup, the fourth and last registry level,
`subgroups`. A subgroup the text names in full stands alone (“Podzols
humo-ferrugineux”, “Chernozem modal”); one it names by an adjective
follows its group (“Rankers, à mor”, “Sols ferrallitiques moyennement
désaturés en (B) typiques, Faiblement appauvri”). `name` is now the
deepest level.

- **Subgroups.** The text names most subgroups by a secondary process or
  by one side of a measure; soilKey’s readings are listed in
  `readings.yaml`.
  - A subgroup the data cannot decide leaves the name provisional.
  - When no listed subgroup of a group fits (27 groups have no modal),
    the name stops at the group and the trace says why; 22 groups have
    no subgroups.
  - The other subgroups whose tests pass are noted in the trace as
    “intergrade vers …”, and a brown soil with hydromorphic signs only
    below its (B) as a “faciès hydromorphe”.
- **Five new fields:** `humus_form` (site: mull, moder, mor, hydromull,
  hydromoder, hydromor, anmoor, tourbe), `caco3_active_pct`,
  `coarse_sand_pct`, `fine_sand_pct` and `gibbsite_pct` (horizon).

#### Hugo’s decisions (2026-11-01)

- **Inventory:** the main text of the AFES edition, 276 subgroups; I/16
  has no common subgroups; the two peat subgroups under each peat group
  (XI/111 to XI/132); “Sans horizon B” is XI/221; VII/115 and VII/413
  included; IV/22 takes the subgroups of IV/21. Codes: the class and the
  text’s three digits (I/111 under I/11).
- **Order:** the printed order, modal last; a subgroup that splits the
  group by a measure after those of a secondary process, and a composite
  subgroup before its parts.
- **Hydromorphy:** signs (redox features above 0 %, mottle colours, a
  reduced matrix, or a g or G where no mottles are recorded) in a layer
  starting within 100 cm; also a water table within 1 m for “à nappe”;
  pronounced signs or concretions within 50 cm for the vertisols; signs
  from 50 cm and none above for II/142.
- **Shallow profiles:** by the profile type: hard rock directly under
  the A for the lithosols, C or R within 45 cm for IV x13 and 50 cm for
  VII/411, a (B) on hard non-calcareous rock within 50 cm for VII/115.
- **Vertisols:** “vertiques” with slickensides common at most;
  self-mulching with fine structure to 10 or 20 cm.
- **Salt and sodium:** EC 4 dS/m or more, exchangeable Na 6 % of the CEC
  or more, within 100 cm.
- **Rendzinas:** a very strong effervescence or 10 % active carbonate
  (V/112), under 10 % carbonate with 15 % coarse fragments (V/114), a
  dry climate (V/115).
- **Crusts:** an encroûtement is a recorded accumulation (5 % secondary
  carbonates, 5 % more carbonate than the layer below, or a Ca of the
  notation); a croûte is a cemented layer.
- **Isohumic soils:** vertique = protovertic or a coarse prismatic (B);
  à B textural = the textural B of VII/12; rubéfié = the reddened B of
  class IX.
- **Brunified soils:** the measures decide (allophane, clay index, pH of
  the B); the colour words of the A2 and the humus are descriptions,
  except the ashy A2 over an ochre B of VII/124.
- **Podzolised soils:** Bh and Bfe by the notation, then the colour;
  deep hydromorphy below the base of the B with none above it.
- **Classes IX and X:** the accepted IX/X table; “faiblement rajeuni” at
  3 % weatherable minerals; “faiblement remanié” by the evidence of the
  reworked groups; X/322 by a dark brown B, pH under 4.5 and gibbsite
  (or Ki under 1.0).
- **Class XI:** the peats by their pH (5.5), else the moor type; anmoor
  by a C/N under 20, hydromor by the humus form, else a C/N of 20 or
  more; XI/321, 322, 341 and 342 by the morphology.
- **Class XII:** XII/21 by the surface structure, then the EC route;
  XII/23 by the Na of the first B; XII/114 by a thionic horizon, or pH
  under 4 with jarosite or sulfidic S.
- **After the review** (Hugo, 2026-11-01):
  - the sub-class IX-1 takes the nearly saturated tropical sands of
    IX/114 (8 % clay or less to 100 cm, under 1 % OM in the A) whatever
    their base saturation, and IX/114 reads V 80 % or more in the larger
    part of the B;
  - an encroûtement needs a recorded accumulation, not soilKey’s calcic
    horizon alone;
  - the yellow and brown subgroups of classes IX and X come after the
    subgroups of a process, and the thick calcic brown soils (V/213)
    before the brunified rendzinas;
  - IX/213 and IX/222 take any hydromorphic sign;
  - a subgroup left undecided before the assigned one makes it
    provisional, as at the other levels;
  - the detailed readings soilKey made where the plan was silent are
    kept, marked as soilKey’s in readings.yaml.

## soilKey 0.9.332 (2026-11-01)

### France: the 101 groups of the CPCS 1967

[`classify_cpcs1967()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_cpcs1967.md)
now keys a pedon to its group, a third registry level, `groups`, for
example “Podzols”, “Sols lessivés” or “Sols ferrallitiques fortement
désaturés en (B) typiques”. The subgroups follow.

- **Groups.** The text defines most groups by a profile type, a colour
  word or a property with no number; soilKey’s readings are listed in
  `readings.yaml`.
  - A group the data cannot decide leaves the name provisional.
  - When no group of a sub-class fits (VIII-1, VIII-2, XI-1 have no
    default), the name stops at the sub-class and the trace says why.
- **Two new fields:** `patterned_ground` (site: polygons, circles,
  stripes, mud boils, hummocks, palsas) and `ice_form` (horizon: ice
  lenses, wedges). They decide the groups of the cold-desert and
  permafrost soils; not recorded, those groups are undecided.
- The FAO and USDA suffixes i, e and a of an O horizon give the fibre
  class of a peat when no fibre content is recorded.

#### Hugo’s decisions (2026-11-01)

- **Deposits and erosion (I-1, II-4):** the origin recorded for the
  material under the A within 50 cm, else the parent material;
  anthropic, volcanic, alluvial, colluvial, aeolian, in that order; no
  origin recorded, the erosion group.
- **Classes I to IV:**
  - the lithosols of the deserts: hard rock within 10 cm;
  - II/23 allophanic first (pH NaF 9.5 or more, or Alo + 1/2 Feo 2 % or
    more), II/22 only on a calcareous rock;
  - II/31: under 1 % OM and an arid climate;
  - the vertisol groups by the structure of the top 15 cm (self-mulching
    is angular, massive undecided);
  - IV/21: base saturation of 50 % or more in the (B), pH 6 or more
    without it.
- **Classes V and VI:**
  - V/13 cryptorendzinas first (dolomite), then V/11 rendzinas (no (B)),
    V/12 the others;
  - V/22 (OM above 20 % on hard carbonate rock), V/23 (fine polyhedral
    A, CEC of the clay 50 or more), V/21 the others;
  - the isohumic groups by the mean OM of the top 20 cm (chernozems
    above 5 %, chestnut soils 3 % or more, marron soils 1 % or more).
- **Classes VII and VIII:**
  - the leached soils: the clay index (largest clay of the B over
    smallest of the A) above 1.4 with 5 % clay more; films recorded as
    none or few rule it out;
  - the sod-podzolic soils: an A1 of 25 cm or more and tongues;
  - one colour table for the podzolised soils (ashy = albic, pale = one
    Munsell value above the A1 and the B, ochre = 10YR to 5YR with
    chroma 6, brown = chroma 4 or less);
  - boreal podzols (Köppen Dc or Dd, or latitude 50 or more) before
    alpine ones (ET or EF below 60 degrees, or 1,500 m).
- **Classes IX and X:**
  - IX/12 leached, IX/13 impoverished, IX/11 the others, by the clay
    index, the thickness of the A, the C and the clay films;
  - IX/21: a calcium reserve within 100 cm, or a (B) with V 95 % or more
    and pH 7 to 7.5;
  - class X in the order humic, leached, impoverished, reworked,
    rejuvenated, typical (X/24 read as reworked).
- **Classes XI and XII:**
  - the peat groups by the fibre class over the greatest thickness;
  - XI-3 in the order 35, 36, 34, 31, 33, 32 (the specific groups
    first);
  - XII-2 in the order solodised, Solonetz, Solonchak-Solonetz.
- **After the review** (Hugo, 2026-11-01):
  - the deep gley of the amphigley starts at 80 cm; in a declared FAO
    notation, g is a pseudogley and l the fringe of a gley;
  - a water table recorded as none, or not recorded, makes a stagnogley
    of a profile with its morphology (undecided when not recorded);
  - VIII/13 allows an A2 under 5 cm and no Bh over 3 cm; a site at 1,500
    m or more below 60 degrees is alpine;
  - V/31 is the AR or ACR profile, its thinness a description; a plain B
    of the CPCS notation is a textural B when clay is not recorded;
  - ice-wedge polygons are a strong ice segregation; XII/23 without a pH
    is undecided; a columnar B is compact;
  - names carry soilKey’s insertions in brackets: “\[possible\]” for
    III/21-22 (the text prints “nul”), “\[remaniés\]” for X/24.

## soilKey 0.9.331 (2026-11-01)

### France: the 35 sub-classes of the CPCS 1967

[`classify_cpcs1967()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_cpcs1967.md)
now keys a pedon to its sub-class, a second registry level,
`subclasses`, for example “Sols ferrallitiques fortement désaturés en
(B)” or “Sols brunifiés des climats tempérés humides”. The groups and
subgroups follow.

- **The climate.** The sub-classes rest on the pedoclimate where they
  can. A climatic sub-class needs its climate and the morphology of one
  of its groups.
  - The climate is read from a new site field, `koppen_climate` (the
    Köppen code), else from the USDA soil temperature and moisture
    regimes, else from the latitude.
  - With no climate recorded, the soil falls to the class’s non-climatic
    or temperate sub-class, and the trace says so.
  - A second new field, `mean_annual_precip_mm`, is recorded but decides
    nothing yet.
- **The other sub-classes** read the profile:
  - the external drainage of the vertisols, from the slope or the
    landform;
  - the organic matter of the andosols;
  - gypsum and carbonate in the A for the calcimagnesic soils;
  - hydromorphy reaching the A2 or the top of the B for the podzolised
    soils;
  - the base saturation of the B for the sesquioxide and ferrallitic
    soils;
  - the peat and the anmoor for the hydromorphic soils;
  - the structure for the sodic soils.
- The app and the report label the new level “Subclass”.

#### Hugo’s decisions (2026-11-01)

- **Climate:** Köppen first, then the USDA regimes, then the latitude.
  With no climate, the default sub-class. The isohumic soils, whose four
  sub-classes are all climatic, stay undecided unless the property test
  of VI-1 holds.
- **Classes I and II:**
  - I-2 cold deserts and I-3 hot deserts;
  - II-2 humic: 5 % OM or more in the A, pH under 6.8, not arid;
  - II-3 xeric: a dry climate, under 2 % OM, no calcareous accumulation.
- **Classes III and IV:**
  - III-1: a slope under 2 % or a flat landform; nothing recorded leaves
    it undecided;
  - IV-1: OM above 10 % in the A over 25 cm.
- **Classes V, VII and VIII:**
  - V-3 gypseous first, then V-1 carbonated, then V-2;
  - VII-4 tropical, VII-3 boreal and VII-2 continental, each with the
    morphology of its groups;
  - VIII-3 hydromorphic, then VIII-2 cold.
- **After the review:**
  - every Köppen climate falls in one isohumic sub-class (VI-1 Cf, Dfa,
    Af, Am; VI-2 the other D, BSk, BWk, E; VI-3 Cs; VI-4 BSh, BWh, Aw,
    As, Cw);
  - VII-1 and VIII-1 hold under a temperate climate or none recorded;
    under another recorded climate, a soil without the morphology of the
    climatic sub-class is undecided rather than named temperate.
- **Classes IX to XII:**
  - IX-1 when base saturation is under 65 %;
  - X by the thickness-weighted base saturation of the (B), at 40 % and
    20 %;
  - XI-1 peat, XI-2 anmoor;
  - XII-2 by the sodium route.

## soilKey 0.9.330 (2026-11-01)

### France: the twelve classes of the French soil classification (CPCS 1967)

[`classify_cpcs1967()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_cpcs1967.md)
keys a pedon to the twelve classes of the French soil classification of
1967 (Commission de Pédologie et de Cartographie des Sols,
*Classification des sols*), a system of its own beside the other
national systems.
[`make_cpcs1967_example()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/make_cpcs1967_example.md)
gives one profile per class. The names are French, as the text writes
them, in `name` and `levels$name_native`. The sub-classes, groups and
subgroups follow.

- **An order of classes.** The CPCS gives no key. soilKey keys the
  classes in an order built from the text’s statements of precedence: I
  sols minéraux bruts, III vertisols, XII sols sodiques, IV andosols,
  VIII sols podzolisés, X sols ferrallitiques, IX sols à sesquioxydes de
  fer et manganèse, XI sols hydromorphes, II sols peu évolués, VI sols
  isohumiques, V sols calcimagnésiques, VII sols brunifiés.
- **The old French notation** (Aoo, Ao, A1, A2, A3, (B), B, Bh, Bfe, Bt,
  Cca, Can, Cs, Cn, Sa, g, G, R, a Roman numeral for a change of parent
  material), declared with `site$designation_system = "cpcs"` or
  recognised by its own symbols, beside the FAO letters. In a profile
  without designations, soilKey’s diagnostic horizons stand in for the
  profile type.
- **The class tests** read organic matter as 1.72 × organic carbon, with
  depths from the top of the first mineral horizon:
  - the intensity of hydromorphy and halomorphy that makes classes XI
    and XII;
  - Ki (or the CEC of the clay) for the ferrallitic soils, read in the
    larger part of the B;
  - the podzolic B by its C/N;
  - the andic properties with a (B);
  - the sharp or gradual fall of organic matter that separates the
    calcimagnesic soils from the isohumic soils.
- In the Pro app, the CPCS is a national system of its own; the level is
  labelled “Class”.

#### Hugo’s decisions (2026-11-01)

- The order of the classes above. Class XI excludes permafrost soils
  (they stay in class II); the sesquioxide soils exclude the isohumic
  soils.
- **Class XI:** peat (30 % OM, 20 % in sandy material) over 40 cm of the
  top 80 cm; 8 to 30 % OM over 20 cm on a gley; or hydromorphic layers
  over most of the profile from the base of the A1 to 100 cm. A deep
  gley alone does not count, and a mottle that is not recorded is
  absent.
- **Class XII:** EC above 7 dS/m in every horizon to 100 cm, or Na above
  10 % of the CEC with a massive or columnar, compact structure. Na
  only; clean sands and gypsum alone excluded.
- **Conventions:** OM = 1.72 × C; depth zero at the top of the A1;
  ranges read as in the SiBCS; data first, the notation where the data
  do not decide.
- **Names:** French in both name fields.
- **After the canonical profiles** (the 44 WRB, SiBCS and USDA examples
  keyed under the CPCS):
  - class IX’s individualised iron is a reddened B (5YR or redder,
    chroma 4) or iron concretions, a yellower B only under a tropical
    climate;
  - the gradual fall of OM of class VI is read at a third, and class V
    drops its own fall test (the isohumic soils are keyed before it);
  - the EC of class XII is read in the solum;
  - the cracks of class III are 0.5 cm, as soilKey reads the WRB.
- **Classes I, II and IV:**
  - class I has traces of OM, 0.5 % (1.5 % in the top 3 cm);
  - class II has permafrost, or an AC profile with more than traces;
  - an AC soil with the chemistry of class V and a source of Ca or Mg is
    calcimagnesic unless a recent deposit or recent erosion is recorded;
  - class IV needs the andic properties over 30 cm, a CEC above 25 (the
    thickness-weighted mean of the andic A and (B)) and a (B).
- **Classes III and VIII:** the CPCS’s own vertisol reading
  (slickensides to 150 cm, 30 % clay in the (B)); the podzolic B by
  criterion 2 (OM above 0.5 %, C/N above 14), or an ashy A2 without a B.
- **Classes X, IX, V, VI and VII:**
  - X: Ki of 2.0 or less, else a CEC of the clay of 16 or less;
  - IX: Ki above 2, base saturation above 50 % and individualised iron;
  - V: no B, pH above 6.8 and Ca + Mg above 90 %;
  - VI: a gradual fall over half the solum, OM minima by texture, S/T of
    50 % or more in the upper horizons and 80 % in the B (p. 39);
  - VII: the remaining soils with a B or (B).
- **Supporting readings:** the ashy A2 is albic material; in an
  undesignated profile, the B is read from soilKey’s diagnostics.
- **After the reviews:**
  - the notation gives the profile type (B, (B), A2), and the recorded
    data the properties: a g with 0 % mottles recorded is not a
    hydromorphic layer;
  - class VII takes the soils with an A2 and no B;
  - a peat excludes the mineral classes keyed before class XI, and class
    I takes no organic layer (an organic layer counts as more than
    traces for class II);
  - the Canadian, New Zealand and Australian letters keep their own
    meanings (f iron, v vertic, z frozen), and the recorded data come
    before the Ca, Cs and Cn of the notation.

The other systems do not change.

## soilKey 0.9.329 (2026-11-01)

### Japan: the soil phases of the Comprehensive Soil Classification System of Japan (the CSCJ now complete)

[`classify_cscj2011()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_cscj2011.md)
now gives the soil phases of chapter VIII in
`ClassificationResult$phases`, beside the class name, as
[`classify_scsj2017()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_scsj2017.md)
does. With them, the CSCJ 2011 is complete in soilKey: 10 great groups,
27 groups, 116 subgroups, 381 soil series groups and the phases.

- **Temperature phase:** from the soil temperature, else the USDA
  regime, else estimated from the mean annual air temperature plus 2 C,
  as the CSCJ says.
- **Man-made phases**, with the CSCJ’s names:
  - a fill is named by its texture or, for a kuroboku fill, its humus
    class, and by its kind of soil or material
    (多腐植質黒ボク土盛土造成相, 粗粒質浚渫土砂盛土造成相, as the text’s
    examples);
  - the Reformed soils: the fill over the original soil’s group
    (細粒質低地土／粘土集積赤黄色土造成相).
  - a fill in the plough layer alone takes no phase (chapter IX, step
    A);
  - a fill with none of the five kinds that the materials name is keyed
    on its own and named by its great group when 25 cm or more, by its
    texture alone when thinner;
  - a kuroboku fill on other material is a natural combination (chapter
    IX, step D; also on
    [\#133](https://github.com/HugoMachadoRodrigues/soilKey/issues/133)):
    the text’s example keys as 腐植質下層低地アロフェン質黒ボク土 with
    the phase 腐植質黒ボク土盛土造成相.
- No forest phases: the CSCJ has none.

#### Hugo’s decisions (2026-11-01)

- The air temperature plus 2 C for the CSCJ temperature phase, marked as
  estimated.
- A fill’s name puts the texture word, or the humus class of a kuroboku
  fill, before the soil kind; for the Reformed soils, the fill’s texture
  and great group over the original soil’s group.
- A kuroboku fill is a natural combination in the CSCJ only: it does not
  make the soil Man-made (on
  [\#133](https://github.com/HugoMachadoRodrigues/soilKey/issues/133)
  and merged up the stack).
- A fill with none of the five kinds: 25 cm or more is classified on its
  own and named by its great group; a thinner one is named by its
  texture word, when decided.

The SCSJ 2017 and the other systems do not change.

## soilKey 0.9.328 (2026-11-01)

### Japan: the 381 soil series groups of the Comprehensive Soil Classification System of Japan

[`classify_cscj2011()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_cscj2011.md)
now keys a pedon down to its soil series group (土壌統群), the CSCJ’s
lowest category, for example “fine-textured Reddish Argic Red-Yellow
soils” / 細粒質赤色粘土集積赤黄色土.

- **Lists.** Each subgroup has its own ordered list, drawn from the
  text’s vocabulary:
  - bedrock, a gravel layer or a pan layer within 60 cm;
  - the texture of the subsurface;
  - peat, alluvial or kuroboku layers in the subsoil, and the
    non-allophanic feature;
  - the humus classes;
  - the mineral layers and fibre of the peat soils;
  - the base-rich dark surface horizon;
  - wetness.
- **New horizon attributes:** `texture_class_jp` (the Japanese texture
  classes, codes or words) and `hardness_yamanaka_mm` (soil hardness,
  for the pan layer).
- **App and report** label the new level “Soil series group”.

#### Hugo’s decisions (2026-11-01)

- Series groups are named by their term, in lower case, before the
  subgroup’s name.
- **Bedrock, gravel and pan layers:**
  - bedrock and the gravel layer are measured from the soil surface;
  - a gravel layer is 20 % or more in either record; with no record,
    there is no gravel layer;
  - hardness not recorded means no pan layer.
- **Texture:**
  - it is read from `texture_class_jp`;
  - without it, clay of 15 % or more is fine, and medium vs coarse stays
    undecided;
  - it is read on the horizon of 15 cm or more with the largest overlap
    of 20 to 40 cm; a tie goes to the larger part of the section, then
    to the thicker horizon;
  - with no subsurface, no texture class is met.
- **The base-rich dark surface horizon** is undecided where liming is
  recorded.

The SCSJ 2017 and the other systems do not change.

## soilKey 0.9.327 (2026-11-01)

### Japan: the 116 subgroups of the Comprehensive Soil Classification System of Japan

[`classify_cscj2011()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_cscj2011.md)
now keys a pedon to its subgroup (chapter VI), named by its word before
the group’s name, for example “Argic Calcaric Dark Red soils” and
粘土集積石灰性暗赤色土.

- **Subgroups shared with the SCSJ** are its generic gates, read by the
  CSCJ edition under CSCJ names with the same depths and features.
  Within them, the Andic subgroups have P retention as their only
  substitute, and the Endoaeric Lowland Paddy soils read the CSCJ’s
  yellowish brown.
- **New or different:**
  - the Cumulic Fulvic Andosols, by the brown polyhumic surface horizon
    over 50 cm within 60 cm;
  - the Low-humic Allophanic Andosols;
  - the Dark Red groups’ Argic and Haplic subgroups;
  - the Brown Forest soils in the CSCJ’s order, with Aquic by either
    wetness, Eutric on every subhorizon at pH 6.5 and the new Terrace
    subgroup.

#### Hugo’s decisions (2026-11-01)

- Terrace by recorded words for Pleistocene deposits, negations taken
  out, a Holocene or alluvial terrace and a rock not counting; nothing
  recorded means not.
- Eutric as written, with no liming clause.

The SCSJ 2017 and the other systems do not change.

## soilKey 0.9.326 (2026-11-01)

### Japan: the 27 groups of the Comprehensive Soil Classification System of Japan

[`classify_cscj2011()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_cscj2011.md)
now keys a pedon to its group (chapter VI): for example the Fulvic
Andosols, the Calcaric, Dystric and Eutric Dark Red soils, and the Brown
Lowland soils.

- **Groups shared with the SCSJ** are its gates, read by the CSCJ
  edition under CSCJ names.
- **New groups and readings:**
  - the Fulvic Andosols, by the brown polyhumic kuroboku surface
    horizon: layers with the kuroboku feature, a moist value and chroma
    of 3 or more and 4 % carbon or more each, 30 cm in 40 cm, with a
    weighted mean of 6 % or more;
  - the Calcaric and Dystric Dark Red soils;
  - the Brown Lowland soils, by the CSCJ’s own yellowish-brown colour,
    which leaves out 5YR.

#### Hugo’s decisions (2026-11-01)

- The brown polyhumic horizon adds up the layers that meet it, with no
  allowance for layers that fail between them.
- The Brown Lowland soils use the CSCJ’s yellowish brown.
- Where liming is recorded, the Dystric and Calcaric Dark Red groups are
  undecided (the soil keys to the Eutric group, provisional).
- The Non-allophanic Andosols by the key alone.
- The Volcanogenous Regosols’ undeveloped horizons leave buried horizons
  out, in both Japanese systems (the SCSJ change is on
  [\#130](https://github.com/HugoMachadoRodrigues/soilKey/issues/130)
  and merged up).
- With no subsurface section, a criterion on its subhorizons is not met,
  in both systems (on
  [\#129](https://github.com/HugoMachadoRodrigues/soilKey/issues/129)
  and merged up).

The appendix’s typos “Fuluvic” and “Volcangenous” are written Fulvic and
Volcanogenous. The other systems do not change.

## soilKey 0.9.325 (2026-11-01)

### Japan: the Comprehensive Soil Classification System of Japan, the ten great groups

[`classify_cscj2011()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_cscj2011.md)
keys a pedon to the ten great groups of the Comprehensive Soil
Classification System of Japan, First Approximation (Obara et al. 2011,
NIAES), a system of its own beside the SCSJ 2017.
[`make_cscj2011_example()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/make_cscj2011_example.md)
gives one profile per great group. Names are the English names of the
text’s appendix 2, with the Japanese ones in `levels$name_native`. The
27 groups, 116 subgroups, 381 soil series groups and the phases follow.

- **Shared code, the CSCJ’s own limits.** The diagnostics the two
  Japanese systems share are read with the SCSJ code, by the CSCJ
  edition:
  - the argic horizon by the CSCJ’s clay increase (the WRB 2006 values);
  - the immature kuroboku feature with P retention as its only
    substitute;
  - the heterogeneous fill of the Man-made soils by the CSCJ great
    groups, without the SCSJ’s Regosol-group rule;
  - a fill that keys as Andosols is a combination that occurs in nature
    (chapter IX, step D), so it does not make the soil Man-made.
- **Podzols before Andosols**, as the CSCJ keys them.
- **New great group:** the Dark Red soils, by a dark red subsurface (the
  new colour word) or an origin from limestone or calcareous deposits
  with a base-rich subsurface.
- **The CSCJ’s Red-Yellow soils**, without the SCSJ’s base-status
  criterion.
- In the Pro app, the CSCJ is a national system of its own.

#### Hugo’s decisions (2026-11-01)

- The soil surface, which the CSCJ does not define, is read as in the
  SCSJ.
- The CSCJ’s own argic limits.
- The subsurface section excludes the plough layer, as in the SCSJ.
- The Dark Red colour is that of the thickest B horizon in the
  subsurface section (a buried B included), else the first B below it,
  else the thickest layer of the section.
- Limestone or calcareous deposits come from recorded words or 40 %
  CaCO3 or more; nothing recorded means not. Liming leaves a high base
  status undecided.
- The Podzols: one horizon may meet both the analysis and the morphology
  criteria; the single parent material is read on the bleached and
  accumulation horizons.
- The Red-Yellow soils’ 25 cm are those of one horizon, in the CSCJ and
  in the SCSJ alike.
- A kuroboku fill is a natural combination in the CSCJ only: the text’s
  example of a humic kuroboku fill on alluvium keys as an Andosol, not
  as a Man-made soil. The SCSJ still reads every recorded fill as not
  natural.
- Decided for the later parts:
  - a Japanese texture-class attribute;
  - the series-group names with their term first;
  - the air temperature plus 2 C for the CSCJ temperature phase;
  - the texture layer in 20 to 40 cm and the non-allophanic test by the
    key.

The other systems do not change; the SCSJ changes only in its Red-Yellow
soils’ count (also on
[\#129](https://github.com/HugoMachadoRodrigues/soilKey/issues/129)).

## soilKey 0.9.324 (2026-10-31)

### Japan: the soil phases of the Soil Classification System of Japan

[`classify_scsj2017()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_scsj2017.md)
now gives the soil phases of chapter V in `ClassificationResult$phases`,
a new field (kind, code, English and Japanese name, basis), which
[`print()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/print.html) lists. The class name is
left as it is.

- **Temperature phase:** frigid, mesic, thermic, hyperthermic, from the
  mean annual soil temperature or the USDA soil temperature regime.
- **Man-made phases:** mixed-layer, cut and fill phases for the other
  great groups, the fill named by its materials; the gley, wet, gravelly
  or plain phase of the Artifactual soils, named by the artificial
  material; the fill over the original soil, with the same endings, for
  the Reformed soils.
- **Forest phases**, on forest or grazing land: the 1975 forest soil
  type when recorded (new site field `forest_soil_type`, read in any
  spelling and for the other 1975 groups by their moisture letter);
  otherwise the three development phases of the Podzols on the key’s own
  pairings (new horizon attribute `leached_spots`), and the seven
  moisture phases of the other forest soils from soilKey’s reading of
  their descriptions.
- A phase is given only when it is decided: a test earlier in its order
  that the data leave undecided gives none.

#### Hugo’s decisions (2026-10-31 and 2026-11-01)

- The phases sit beside the class name, not in it.
- The temperature phase reads the soil temperature or the USDA regime,
  with no estimate from the air.
- One man-made phase for the Man-made soils: gley before wet before
  gravelly; the Reformed soils take it too, as the supplement’s example.
- The forest moisture phases: the recorded type, else rules from the
  structures, undecided when ambiguous. Slightly wet: no O, a crumb A of
  25 cm or more, a B without blocky, nutty or granular structure.
  Moderately dry: nutty structure in the lower A and the upper B.
  Moderately moist, drier type: granular upper A or nutty lower A, no
  crumb required. Angular blocky is nutty.
- The 1975 types of the other groups are read by their moisture letter.
- A thin fill is named by its materials; mixing counts only below the
  plough layer; land consolidation alone is not a cut.
- Undecided data give no phase.

Other systems do not change.

## soilKey 0.9.323 (2026-10-31)

### Japan: the 120 subgroups of the Soil Classification System of Japan

[`classify_scsj2017()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_scsj2017.md)
now keys a pedon to the subgroups of chapter III: 120 under the 26
groups (Haplic, Humic, Cumulic, Brown-humic, Thapto-humic,
Thapto-upland, Endofluvic, Aquic, Peaty, Anthraquic, Albic, Epi-gleyed,
Thionic, Strong and Mottled, Reddish, Andic, Podzolic, Eutric, Calcaric,
Granitic, Para-lithic …). Each is named by its word before the group’s
name, in English and in Japanese (`levels$name_native`; the generic
classifier now fills `{parent}` in the native name too).

- New horizon attributes: `ph_h2o2` (potential sulfuric material),
  `peat_moor_type` (high-moor, transitional or low-moor peat) and
  `artefacts_organic` (mainly organic artificial material).
- The subgroups also read the humic and polyhumic surface horizons, the
  buried humic layer, the buried non-kuroboku upland soil, the paddy
  reverse gley layer, jarosite, carbonates, the site’s landform and
  groundwater depth, and the parent rock.
- Hugo’s decision (2026-10-31): the mottle class ‘contains’ of the
  Strong Gley Fluvic soils, for which the text gives no figure, is 5 %
  or more.
- On paddy land the Aquic subgroups do not read the paddy horizons’
  mottles as groundwater wetness, as the groups do; the groundwater gley
  layers are adjacent gley horizons reaching 75 cm.
- Hugo’s decisions (2026-10-31): the Brown-humic colour is a moist value
  and chroma both 3 or more (chapter VI); a paddy greyed horizon within
  30 cm rules the Aeric Pseudogley soils out; the Endoaeric brown layer
  is below the plough layer and the surface horizons; the Podzolic Brown
  Forest soils read the podzolic accumulation horizon as the text gives
  it (its colour suffices).
- Corrections to the shared definitions: “at A to B cm” windows no
  longer pass a layer that may start above A; the humic surface horizon
  starts at the soil surface and reads gaps and the end of the
  description as possible; a buried humic layer may be several horizons;
  an H horizon with carbon but no kuroboku data is peat material; a
  buried plough layer is not the plough layer; Japanese drainage classes
  are read.

The readings are in `inst/rules/scsj2017/readings.yaml`. Other systems
do not change.

## soilKey 0.9.322 (2026-10-31)

### Japan: the 26 groups of the Soil Classification System of Japan

[`classify_scsj2017()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_scsj2017.md)
now keys a pedon past its great group to the 26 groups of chapter III,
among them Podzolic, Regosolic, Gleyed, Wet, Non-allophanic and
Allophanic Andosols, Fluvic Paddy, Gley, Gray, Brown and Regosolic
Fluvic soils, Argic and Cambic Red-Yellow soils, Stagnogley and
Pseudogley soils, Magnesian and Calcareous Eutrosols, and Volcanogenous
and Sandy Regosols, Lithosols and Terrestrial Regosols. Each has its
English and Japanese name.

- New horizon attribute `exchange_acidity_y1` (the exchange acidity y1
  of the non-allophanic kuroboku feature, not read on farmland). The
  groups also read Sio (`si_ox_pct`), Alp/Alo (`al_pyro_pct`,
  `al_ox_pct`) and exchangeable Ca and Mg.
- The gley layers are subdivided as the text does (groundwater gley
  layers reach 75 cm or deeper, taken together).
- Man-made soils: a fill and the soil under it that both key to Regosols
  are compared by their groups; a part of a profile keyed on its own is
  read as complete.
- Corrections to 0.9.321: a layer with the kuroboku feature no longer
  also has the immature one (an ash layer that is certainly one of the
  two still counts for the Andosols); a fill keeps the material it
  records, so a fill of the same material is read as part of an ordinary
  profile (chapter VI, the fill phase); colour words decided by value or
  chroma alone; a run’s certain depth and the end of the description
  read in the depth tests.

#### Hugo’s decisions (2026-10-31)

- The podzolic accumulation horizon’s criterion (2) is read for the
  soil, as its verb says (as in 0.9.321).
- “Several gley layers” are adjacent gley horizons taken together; an
  oxidised layer separates two gley layers.
- On paddy land the paddy horizons’ mottles are not the groundwater
  wetness feature of the Wet Andosols and Gray Fluvic soils.
- The mottle class “contains” (the Strong Gley Fluvic soils, next
  release) is 5 % or more.
- Later (2026-11-01): the Volcanogenous Regosols’ undeveloped horizons
  leave buried horizons out.

The readings are in `inst/rules/scsj2017/readings.yaml`. Other systems
do not change.

## soilKey 0.9.321 (2026-10-31)

### Japan: the great groups of the Soil Classification System of Japan (2017)

A new, experimental and opt-in system: the Soil Classification System of
Japan (SCSJ 2017) of the Japanese Society of Pedology, Fifth Committee
for Soil Classification and Nomenclature. This release keys the ten
great groups of chapter II with the definitions of chapter IV; groups,
subgroups and the soil phases follow, then the Comprehensive Soil
Classification System of Japan (2011) as a system of its own.

- **[`classify_scsj2017()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_scsj2017.md)**
  keys a pedon to Man-made soils, Organic Soils, Andosols, Podzols,
  Fluvic soils, Red-Yellow soils, Stagnic soils, Eutrosols, Brown Forest
  soils or Regosols. Each level gives the official English name of the
  SCSJ table and, in `levels$name_native`, the Japanese one (a new
  column that the generic classifier fills for any system whose classes
  carry `name_native`).
- **[`make_scsj2017_example()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/make_scsj2017_example.md)**
  gives one made-up profile per great group.
- The key reads the Japanese horizon notation of the Soil Survey
  Handbook (H, O, A, E, B, C, G with Go and Gr, R; p, g, t, w, s, h, ir,
  mn; a 2 or II prefix; a trailing b), colours by the colour words of
  the text, the subsurface control section (20 to 60 cm), paddy land
  from `site$land_use` or `site$flood_irrigated`, and the recorded
  origin of the layers (fill, volcanic ejecta, alluvial deposits).
- New horizon attributes: `phosphate_absorption_coef` (mg P2O5/100 g;
  the kuroboku feature needs 1500 or more), `active_al_test` (the
  Japanese field active-aluminium test, -, +-, +, 2+, 3+) and `n_value`
  (physical immaturity). The dipyridyl test is the existing
  `childs_test`.

#### Hugo’s decisions (2026-10-31)

- The SCSJ 2017 complete (great groups, groups, subgroups and phases),
  then the CSCJ 2011 as a system of its own.
- English names with the Japanese ones beside them.
- The phosphate absorption coefficient is a new attribute; P retention
  (85 %) or Alo + 1/2 Feo (2.0 %) replace it when it is not measured, as
  the text allows, and the field active-aluminium test after them.
- Paddy land is read from the land use; with none recorded the paddy
  horizons are undecided, not absent.
- Podzols: the bleached horizon must lie above the podzolic accumulation
  horizon, the sequence of the great group’s concept.
- The subsurface section (20 to 60 cm) counts the horizons with 5 cm or
  more inside it.
- An undesignated layer of 20 % carbon or more is peat on a poorly or
  very poorly drained site and a forest floor on any other; undecided
  without a drainage class.
- In the forest-floor notation (L, F, H), an H under L or F is the humus
  layer of the floor, not peat.
- Later (2026-11-01): the Red-Yellow soils’ 25 cm are those of one
  horizon, not added up over separate horizons; with no subsurface
  section, neither base-status criterion is met; a gravel layer (in
  either record) that reaches into the subsurface section cuts it at its
  top.

The choices where the text is silent are in
`inst/rules/scsj2017/readings.yaml`. Other systems do not change: the 44
canonical profiles key as before under WRB, SiBCS and USDA, and the
Canadian, Australian, New Zealand and Hungarian examples as before.

## soilKey 0.9.320 (2026-10-30)

### Australia: Queensland’s SALI read from its site reports and its soil chemistry API

Queensland’s Soil and Land Information system (SALI) publishes about
21,000 sites with the surveyors’ ASC label and laboratory data,
anonymously and under CC BY 4.0 (State of Queensland). Its morphology
exists only in a per-site report (a PDF), so the reader reads the PDF.
The data are not shipped with soilKey.

- **[`fetch_sali()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/fetch_sali.md)**
  downloads the site layer (Queensland Spatial, MapServer layer 101: the
  sites with an ASC label and laboratory data), then per site the report
  (SALI4320) and the samples with their results from the SALI soil
  chemistry API (OData). It is resumable, waits between requests,
  retries with a backoff, stops on any login, key, terms or firewall
  page, and talks only to the layer and, per site, to the report host
  and the API.
- **[`read_sali_pedons()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/read_sali_pedons.md)**
  reads the folder into pedons. The report is read from the coordinates
  of its words (pdftools, in Suggests), and each row of its morphology
  table is translated into the coded horizon of the NatSoil API and read
  by the NatSoil reader’s own code, the laboratory samples too, so the
  two Australian panels are read alike. The provenance has a row per
  horizon for the morphology and one per laboratory value, naming its
  source and method. The site fields it adds (`sali_*`) are listed in
  [`site_attribute_spec()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/site_attribute_spec.md)
  and `inst/ATTRIBUTES.md`.
- **[`benchmark_sali()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/benchmark_sali.md)**
  gives the metrics of
  [`benchmark_natsoil()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/benchmark_natsoil.md)
  (which it calls), with a table by surveyed order and one by the ASC
  edition the report cites.
  **[`sali_citation()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/sali_citation.md)**
  gives the CC BY 4.0 attribution.

#### Hugo’s decisions

- **Reports over 150 KB are not downloaded** (`cap_bytes = 150e3`):
  those with embedded site photographs are aborted at the cap, marked
  and not tried again.
- **MIR predictions** (method codes ending in \_MC2, \_MC91, \_MQ01,
  \_MQ02 and the like) are used only where nothing was measured for that
  attribute in that horizon. The provenance marks them as predictions
  (source `predicted_spectra`, a note naming the MIR codes), and the
  evidence grade of such a pedon is B. The pilot left them out. MIR
  methods the NatSoil reader has no code for are read by the property
  their name gives: 15C2_CEC (“Cation exchange capacity - MIR QLD
  Calibration 1”) as the CEC, 6B4 (total organic carbon) as organic
  carbon and 15J2 as the effective CEC.
- **The lab table printed in the report** is used only when the API
  holds no samples for the site’s observation; the provenance says which
  of the two each value came from.

#### The readings (the pilot’s, kept)

- Sites labelled “Unclassified” are left out; observation 1 of a site is
  read.
- The label is read by position (order, suborder, great group,
  subgroup), each name matched, case-insensitive, to the 3rd edition. A
  name the 3rd edition does not have stays NA; “No Available Class” is
  ZZ and “Class Undetermined” YY. The edition the report cites is kept
  in `site$sali_asc_edition`, without changing the codes. The report’s
  confidence phrases are 1 to 4; conversions from another classification
  and rapid checks of key attributes are “C”.
- An empty cell is not recorded; “No mottles”, “No segregations” and “No
  coarse fragments” are recorded absent. A colour without its moisture
  status is moist. Mottles of biological mixing, mechanical mixing and
  substrate influence are not mottles; jarosite mottles are.
- Textures: “Loam, fine sandy” is a loam, sandy and silty clays are
  clays of unspecified grade, and heavy or light before a grade lighter
  than a clay is the + or - qualifier. The first structure listed is
  read; “Blocky” alone names no type; “Not recorded (historical)” is NA.
  A strength without its moisture is not read.
- Field pH by depth: Raupach and Tucker first, then an electrode in
  situ, then a 1:5 suspension by probe; the pH after peroxide and the
  field EC are not used. The effervescence field test gives the
  horizon’s effervescence.
- Laboratory samples go to the horizon holding their middle, then
  NatSoil’s overlap rule applies; bulked samples count; results flagged
  invalid are dropped; “\<x” is x/2 with NatSoil’s limit rule. A
  trailing letter of a method variant is dropped (6B2b is 6B2), and
  2Z2_Clay is 2Z2_C.
- Tidal landform spellings are NatSoil’s; no tidal flooding is inferred,
  nor the soil water status. The depth to free water and the substrate
  are kept in the site but not used.

#### The run (6,911 sites, 5,600 pedons)

Of the layer’s sites with an ASC order, 18,557 are not in NatSoil
already (same project and site, or a NatSoil site within 100 m). They
were taken in a fixed random order, in stages of 2,000. The run stopped
in the fourth stage, when the report server began refusing requests
(after some 14,000, from 2 processes pausing 1 s): 6,911 sites were
fetched. Reports over 150 KB (those with embedded site photos) were not
downloaded: 1,286 sites (18.6%), unevenly by order (Organosols 82%,
Calcarosols 41%, Dermosols 29%, Tenosols 27%; Vertosols 11%, Hydrosols
15%). 25 reports have no morphology table, which leaves 5,600 pedons.
Against the surveyors’ labels:

| ASC level | Profiles compared | Agreement | Where the key decides |
|----|----|----|----|
| order | 5,600 | 34.8% (36.6% counting a keyed Arenosol for a surveyed Tenosol or Rudosol) | 83.3% of 1,017 |
| suborder, where the order agrees | 1,854 | 82.6% | 91.8% of 571 |
| great group, where the suborder agrees | 1,106 | 42.8% | 73.5% of 340 |
| subgroup, where the great group agrees | 446 | 40.1% |  |

The order agreement stayed within 34% to 35% from the first stage (1,588
pedons) to the last. The Hydrosols (1,377 pedons) agree in 4.9%, mostly
keyed as Kandosols: the key confirms a Hydrosol by its drainage, which
the reports seldom record (the depth to free water, observed once, is
kept but not used). The Ferrosols (156) agree in 11.5%; most of the rest
are keyed as Dermosols, as free iron was measured in only 30 of them.
The laboratory data come from the API for 5,008 pedons and from the
report’s table for 562; 30 have none. The MIR predictions fill 243
values in 30 pedons. A MIR water pH never stands beside a measured CaCl2
pH; two MIR calibrations behind one value occur in 4 pedons (16 values).

A pilot of 200 sites stratified by order (186 pedons) gave 37.6% at the
order and 83.3% of 36 where the key decides. For comparison, the
Queensland profiles of NatSoil (agencies 301, 302, 304 and 399; 4,412
profiles) give 54.3% at the order, 82.6% of 783 where the key decides.
The 44 canonical fixtures are byte-identical under WRB, SiBCS and USDA.

#### Ferrosols: vertic properties that are not recorded

- The Ferrosol test keeps a soil out when at least 0.3 m of its B2 has
  vertic properties. A B2 horizon whose vertic properties are not
  recorded now counts as without them; only recorded slickensides or
  lenticular peds keep a soil out. Slickensides are seldom recorded
  (Queensland’s site reports have no column for them; NatSoil reads them
  as absent only when other cutans are recorded), so a measured free
  iron above 5% in the major part of the B2 had decided the order in 1
  of 30 SALI Ferrosols and 2 of 35 NatSoil Queensland ones. The trace
  gives the thickness read this way (`vertic_unrecorded_b2_cm`), and the
  test names slickensides as missing only when recorded vertic
  properties leave the answer open.
- SALI: 18 pedons change to Ferrosols, 17 of them surveyed Ferrosols and
  1 a Kandosol (order 34.5% to 34.8%). NatSoil: 19 change, 16 surveyed
  Ferrosols and 3 Kandosols (all 9,700 profiles 43.9% to 44.0%;
  Queensland 54.0% to 54.3%).
- Gley colours and mottles were looked at for the Hydrosols and left out
  of the key. The ASC says they may or may not be present and are not
  universally indicative of saturation. A reading by low chroma, gley
  colours or mottles in most of the upper metre would raise SALI (where
  a quarter of the pedons are Hydrosols) to 52.9% but lower NatSoil
  Queensland (where 2% are) from 54.0% to 52.1%.

## soilKey 0.9.319 (2026-10-30)

### New Zealand: the fluvial features read river deposits and the spelling aluvium

- **NZSC fluvial features** (Fluvial Recent and Fluvial Raw Soils): a
  recorded origin naming a river deposit (river, rivers, riverine,
  riverbed) is fluvial, and alluvium is also read in the spelling
  aluvium, both as NSD parent-rock notes write them (Hugo). A place name
  such as Riversdale is not read as a river.
- **WRB Raptic** reads riverine and riverbed like river.
- On the NSD (94 surveys) the NZSC group agreement goes from 26.7% to
  27.0% (303 to 306 of 1,134). Of the 73 profiles the surveyors call
  Fluvial Recent Soils, 37 are keyed as such (34 in 0.9.318). Order
  (43.6%) and subgroup (14.7%) are unchanged, as are WRB and USDA on the
  NSD and the 44 canonical fixtures.

### Australia: the agreement on NatSoil, measured again

The Australian key has been measured since 0.9.278 on CSIRO’s NatSoil
([`benchmark_natsoil()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/benchmark_natsoil.md),
profiles with the surveyor’s ASC label, CC BY 4.0, not shipped). On
9,700 profiles with the current code no prediction has changed since the
last measurement (2026-10-27), at any level:

| ASC level | Profiles compared | Agreement | Where the key decides |
|----|----|----|----|
| order | 9,700 | 43.9% (45.8% counting the Arenosols, absent from the older labels, as Tenosols or Rudosols) | 74.5% of 1,305 |
| suborder, where the order agrees | 3,694 | 75.9% | 95.5% of 694 |
| great group, where the suborder agrees | 2,669 | 32.8% | 77.5% of 413 |
| subgroup, where the great group agrees | 852 | 33.3% | 25.0% of 20 |

## soilKey 0.9.318 (2026-10-30)

### The New Zealand National Soils Database read by Hugo’s readings

#### NSD reader (`read_nsd_pedons()`)

- **The older ped term nut** (and nutty) is granular or polyhedral, one
  of the two, not known which (NZ Soil Description Handbook 2024, Note
  12.1; Milne et al. 1995 has no nut). It goes to a new horizon
  attribute, `structure_type_one_of` (“granular or polyhedral”), and
  `structure_type` stays empty.
  - [`classify_nzsc4()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_nzsc4.md)
    reads a criterion under each shape: it holds when it holds for both,
    fails when it fails for both, and is undecided otherwise. A
    criterion that needs polyhedral peds is undecided for a nut horizon.
  - The other keys read the shape as not recorded.
- **The older strength words** moderately weak, moderately firm and
  moderately strong belong to the Taylor and Pohlen (1962) scale, which
  has no class in Milne et al. (1995). They stay unread (undecided).
- **The older notation**, for designations the NSD has not converted
  itself:
  - A2 is E, with its subdivisions and suffixes (A21 E1, A2g Eg, A22x
    Ex2).
  - The old master G (a gley horizon) is Bg when a B horizon lies below
    it in the profile, otherwise Cg (GC: BCg or Cg).
  - The old master D (the substratum) is C, its prefixes and suffixes
    kept (BD BC, DG Cg, Dh Ch), except its old suffixes r and n. The
    NSD’s own conversions give Dr as Cu or C and Dn as Bt, 2Btb, Cm or
    Cu, so neither is the r (reduced) or n (sodium) of the current
    notations: Dr and Dn are C.
  - The provenance keeps the recorded designation and says what it was
    read as.
- **The soil note PARENT ROCK** goes down to the layers whose origin is
  not recorded (`layer_origin`, read by the NZSC fluvial features); a
  layer with its own origin keeps it.
  - A note of one material goes to every such layer.
  - A note naming a sequence (“loess over outwash gravels”; over,
    overlying or on, or under and underlain by read from the bottom) is
    split by the profile’s lithologic groups (2C, IIC) when its parts
    are as many: the first part to the unnumbered layers, the next to
    the next group. Otherwise it stays the site’s `parent_material` and
    goes to no layer. A slash is not read as a sequence: the NSD also
    writes it in mixtures and abbreviations.
- A survey whose soil table has no `classifier_usda` (or
  `classifier_nzsc`) column is read.

#### WRB 2022

- **Raptic:** the recorded origin of the layers on each side of a lithic
  discontinuity also reads loess (and wind-blown material) as aeolic,
  volcanic ash, pumice, lapilli and scoria as tephric, and river and
  estuarine deposits (and alluvium spelt aluvium) as fluvic (Hugo). Such
  a discontinuity is not Raptic.

#### soilKey Pro

- A loaded example without coordinates no longer keeps the previous
  profile’s. The coordinates, country and parent material are the loaded
  profile’s, and blank where it has none, as the moisture and
  temperature regimes already were. Coordinates feed the inferred
  temperature regime. The 44 WRB and SiBCS examples carry all four; the
  national examples carry no coordinates.

#### Agreement on the NSD (94 surveys)

| NZSC level | 0.9.317           | 0.9.318               |
|------------|-------------------|-----------------------|
| order      | 43.2% (492/1,139) | **43.6% (497/1,139)** |
| group      | 24.3% (276/1,134) | **26.7% (303/1,134)** |
| subgroup   | 13.8% (154/1,114) | **14.7% (164/1,114)** |

Of the 73 profiles the surveyors call Fluvial Recent Soils, 34 are now
keyed as such (9 in 0.9.317). The 44 canonical fixtures are
byte-identical under WRB, SiBCS and USDA.

## soilKey 0.9.317 (2026-10-30)

### The national systems in soilKey Pro, and their agreement measured

#### soilKey Pro

- **The Classify tab offers the four national systems:** Canada (CSSC,
  3rd ed.), Australia (ASC, 3rd ed.), New Zealand (NZSC, 4th ed.) and
  Hungary (HSCS 2024). They sit under WRB, SiBCS and USDA, each with its
  edition and an “experimental” label, and run only when ticked.
  - Each ticked system gets a card with the class at each level and its
    code (and the English gloss for Hungary).
  - A collapsed note lists the classes the key could not decide before
    the assigned one, with the attributes each needs.
  - For Hungary, a table lists the subtype and variety properties in the
    name and those undecided, with what would decide them.
  - The key trace and the Missing data panel include the national
    systems.
- **The Pedon tab’s canonical profiles include one example per order (or
  type) of each national system:** 10 Canadian, 15 Australian, 15 New
  Zealand and 15 Hungarian, each keying to the class it is labelled
  with. Loading one ticks its system and keeps the site details its key
  reads (the horizon notation, the drainage).
- **The report and the session file:**
  - [`report()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/report.md),
    [`report_html()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/report_html.md)
    and
    [`report_pdf()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/report_pdf.md)
    take `systems`. The default runs WRB, SiBCS and USDA as before
    (byte-identical reports); a registry id or alias adds that system.
  - A saved session keeps the ticked systems, and reopening it ticks
    them again.
- The WoSIS data-source line is shown only for WoSIS data, not for the
  site details a session or an example carries.

#### Canada: designations in the FAO notation (CSSC)

- A profile that declares the FAO notation (`site$designation_system`
  “fao2006”, “fao”, “wrb”) is read by the Canadian key through a
  translation of its designations where the letters mean the same. The
  source is the book’s Table 6 (p. 154), checked against the definitions
  of Ch 2 and WRB 2022 Annex 3.
  - Masters: E = Ae, AE = Ahe, EB = AB.
  - B suffixes: Bw = Bm, Bs = Bf, Bhs = Bhf, Btn = Bnt.
  - Other suffixes: f (permafrost) = z, y and z (salts) = s, i = ss, m
    after a cementing agent = c, a 2 prefix = II.
  - The letters with no Canadian equivalent are not read, and what the
    FAO notation cannot write (the h of a plain A, the m of a plain B,
    the vertic v) stays undecided.
  - The designations are kept, and the evidence lists what each one was
    read as.
- A bare m (Bm, Cm) is not a cementation, as in WRB since 0.9.315.
- A fragipan (Bx) is no Bm: the m “lacks a brittle consistence when
  moist” (Ch 2, p. 14).
- [`isis_profile_to_pedon()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/isis_profile_to_pedon.md)
  declares the FAO notation, so the Canadian key no longer reads an FAO
  z (salts) as frozen.

#### Hungary (HSCS 2024)

- **The clay ratio of the clay accumulation horizon (8.2)** passes over
  a transitional AB, BA, EB or BE horizon with no clay recorded (Hugo),
  and reads the row against the horizon above it.

#### New Zealand: the National Soils Database

- **[`read_nsd_pedons()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/read_nsd_pedons.md)**
  reads the survey exports of Manaaki Whenua’s National Soils Database
  (NSDR; zips or folders of CSV tables) in memory into pedon records. It
  reads:
  - the field description, decoded through each survey’s code lists;
  - the laboratory samples, given to their horizons;
  - the provenance of every value;
  - the surveyor’s NZSC class, NZ Genetic class and Soil Taxonomy name.
    The 3rd-edition codes are recoded to the 4th: MIW becomes MIC, and
    BLAM (withdrawn) is read at no level.
- The older notation is translated: (B) = Bw, and fe, ca, cs = s, k, y.
- **[`benchmark_nsd()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/benchmark_nsd.md)**
  compares
  [`classify_nzsc4()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_nzsc4.md)
  with the surveyor’s code at order, group and subgroup level.
- **[`nsd_citation()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/nsd_citation.md)**
  gives the acknowledgement. The NSD is licensed CC BY-ND 4.0 and is not
  shipped.

#### WRB and USDA

- **The frozen suffix follows the declared notation**
  ([`cryic_conditions()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/cryic_conditions.md)
  and the mollic criterion 6a):
  - FAO and USDA write a frozen layer f.
  - The Canadian notation writes it z (CSSC Ch 2, p. 16); its f is the
    Fe and Al of a podzolic B.
  - The New Zealand and Australian notations have no frozen suffix
    (their f is fibric peat and faunal accumulation).

  On the NSD, 12 New Zealand profiles with fibric peat had keyed to the
  Gelisols; 7 are now Histosols, as the surveyors named them.

#### Agreement measured

| System | Profiles | Level | 0.9.316 | 0.9.317 |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| CSSC | ISIS Canada, 20 | order | 8 | **13** |
|  |  | great group | 5 | **9** |
|  |  | subgroup | 3 | **4** |
| HSCS | ISIS Hungary, 20 | type (genetic name via the guide’s section 9) | 6 (8 lenient) | **7 (9 lenient)** |
| NZSC | NSD, 1,139 with a class | order | (no reader) | **43.2%** |
|  | 1,134 | group |  | **24.3%** |
|  | 1,114 | subgroup |  | **13.8%** |
| USDA | NSD, 600 with a class | order |  | **38.5%** |

- On the NSD, 77% of the NZSC results are provisional at order level.
  Where every earlier order was decided (265 profiles), the order agrees
  on 72.8%.
- Most disagreements come from data the NSD does not hold: glass in sand
  (Pumice Soils), carbonates (Semiarid), bulk density (Allophanic) and
  moist strength (Pallic). Others come from old descriptions (agreement
  26% in the 1960s surveys, 61% in the 1980s) and from 4th-edition
  criteria that older classes do not meet.
- WRB, SiBCS and USDA are unchanged on every panel, and the 44 fixtures
  keep their names. The new readings concern declared national notations
  and the national keys.

## soilKey 0.9.316 (2026-10-30)

### The Hungarian system (HSCS 2024) names its subtypes and varieties

- [`classify_hscs2024()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_hscs2024.md)
  now names, besides the 15 types, the subtype properties (altípus
  tulajdonságok, 8.5, p. 29-33) and the variety properties (változati
  tulajdonságok, 8.6, p. 34-36) of each type’s table (section 7,
  p. 8-22), with the modifiers of 8.7 (p. 37). As the guide writes it
  (p. 7), the subtypes come before the type, the first with a capital
  letter, and the varieties after it, in parentheses, in the table’s
  order. The guide’s own example, “Savanyú, humuszszegény
  Agyagbemosódásos talaj (sekélyen kőzettörmelékes)”, is a test.
- The tables are in `inst/rules/hscs2024/properties.yaml`. Each of the
  74 properties is a three-valued function, and the result carries every
  property with its verdict, depth and label (`$qualifiers$status`) and
  one `levels` row per property named.
- **Readings decided by Hugo (2026-10-30):**
  - Every listed property whose definition holds is named. A row of
    degrees of one property (carbonate degrees, humus classes, base
    status, peat decomposition, sekély/mély, művelt/rigolozott) names
    only the strongest, and none when a stronger one is undecided.
  - A property defined by a layer takes the depth modifier of 8.7
    (felszíntől, sekélyen, középmélyen, mélyben) from where its layer
    starts. The intensity words are used only where the text defines
    them.
  - The humus classes are read layer by layer. The surface horizon of
    humuszszegény, lápföldes and nyers is the weighted A horizon.
  - Rozsdabarna needs hue 10YR or redder and chroma 5 or more. Fakó is
    read in an eluvial horizon only. A g suffix shows the reductive
    conditions of pangóvizes.
  - In a Láptalaj every organic horizon is peat.
  - The measured CaCO3 decides the carbonate degree, and 15 % or more
    without secondary carbonates is közepesen.
  - Karbonát-szulfátos and -kloridos need carbonate making 20 % of the
    salts.
- The other readings where the text is silent are listed in
  `inst/rules/hscs2024/readings.yaml` (five new entries).
- **New attributes**, undecided when not recorded:
  - horizon: `soluble_salts_sulfate_pct`, `soluble_salts_chloride_pct`,
    `soluble_salts_carbonate_pct`, `p2o5_al_mg_kg`, `digo_pct`,
    `coarse_fragments_shape`, `secondary_carbonates_form`,
    `mottle_size_class`;
  - site: `contaminated`, `terraced`, `flood_irrigated`,
    `wind_deflation`.
- The Antropogén key reads the hortic route of the anthropogenic horizon
  (8.1, criterion 1) from `p2o5_al_mg_kg`. The ISIS reader reads the
  mottle size (`mottlesSizeclass`).
- **On ISRIC’s ISIS profiles from Hungary, Slovakia and Romania** the
  names are what the data show. For example:
  - “Középmélyen erősen karbonátos, telített, sekélyen magnéziumos,
    kérges Szolonyec talaj (iszapos agyag)” for HU014, a Columnic
    Solonetz in WRB terms;
  - “Telítetlen, sekélyen podzolos, sekélyen fakó Agyagbemosódásos talaj
    (középmélyen duzzadó, sekélyen vörös, iszapos vályog)” for RO008.

  No property errs on the 974 ISIS profiles. The type of every profile
  is unchanged.

## soilKey 0.9.315 (2026-10-30)

### The last WRB 2022 and USDA readings of the ISIS triage

#### WRB 2022

- **Gleysols, item 2 (Ch 4, p. 103):** a mollic or umbric horizon more
  than 40 cm thick, with reducing conditions from 40 cm below the
  mineral soil surface, over a gleyic layer 10 cm or more thick whose
  lower limit is at 65 cm or deeper.
- **Retisols (Ch 4, p. 118):** the argic horizon starts within 100 cm of
  the mineral soil surface and has retic properties at its upper
  boundary. A natric horizon no longer counts, since the text names the
  argic one only.
- **The limiting layer (Ch 2.1, rule 8, p. 23)** includes the other
  cemented layers. A recorded cementation class of moderately cemented
  or stronger counts, or the suffix m after a cementing agent (Bsm, Bkm,
  Bqm). Continuity is read as met, as for the petric horizons. A
  limiting layer has no texture class, so a shallow soil over rock no
  longer leaves Arenic, Clayic and Siltic undecided.
- **Mollic and umbric horizons:** criterion 6a, 10 cm or more when
  directly over continuous rock, technic hard material or the horizons
  the text names. Rock, technic hard material and petric layers end the
  run of mollic layers.
- **Qualifiers (Ch 5):**
  - Rendzic (p. 145): a mollic horizon that contains or directly
    overlies material or rock with 40% CaCO3 equivalent or more. Any
    layer of the mollic horizon counts. Rock recorded as limestone,
    chalk, dolomite or marble counts without a measured CCE (Hugo).
  - Calcaric material and Endocalcaric read the HCl reaction where CaCO3
    is not measured. Endocalcaric and Endodolomitic count from the
    mineral soil surface.
  - Arenic and Clayic are read as Loamic and Siltic are: from the
    mineral soil surface, with the limiting-layer alternative and the
    sand limit of \> 45% of Table 8.39.
  - Hypercalcic: 50% CCE or more in every layer of the calcic horizon
    (Ch 2.1, p. 23).
  - The texture group without specifiers gives its first applicable
    member. When an earlier member is undecided, which one is first is
    not known, so the group gives none (Hugo).
  - With `specifiers = TRUE`, the texture qualifiers of one group that
    apply at different depths are all given, each with its specifier (Ch
    2.1, p. 24-26). The depth specifiers follow Ch 2.3.1 rules 1 and 2
    (p. 27).
- **The Technosols lists** of Ch 4 (p. 97) are read as printed, in two
  columns.
- **ISIS reader, surface cracks:**
  - Medium cracks are cracks of 1 cm.
  - “No cracks observed” means no cracks only in a profile described dry
    at the surface (cracks “may be evident only when the soil is dry”,
    3.2.12, p. 80); described moist, they stay unknown (Hugo).

#### USDA Soil Taxonomy

- **Aridisols (KST 13, item G, p. 69):**
  - No aridic moisture regime is inferred when none is recorded. soilKey
    had read low surface carbon as aridic, which KST does not give. With
    no regime recorded, the order is undecided and the key goes on.
  - The order follows item G point by point: an ochric or anthropic
    epipedon, the diagnostic horizons KST lists within 100 cm, the
    cambic horizon’s 25 cm, and item G.2, the salic path.
  - The canonical Calcisol, Gypsisol, Solonchak and Durisol fixtures
    record an aridic moisture regime (Hugo).
- **The kandic horizon:** a layer with no recorded lower boundary is
  undecided, not an error (KSSL 2523).
- **[`texture_class_from_pct()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/texture_class_from_pct.md)**
  follows the texture triangle (WRB 2022 Annex 1, Table 8.39, after Soil
  Science Division Staff 2017) at four boundaries it had wrong:
  - sandy clay needs more than 45% sand;
  - clay 35 to \< 40% with more than 45% sand is sandy clay;
  - silt 50 to \< 80% with \< 12% clay is silt loam;
  - clay \< 7% with \< 50% silt and more than 43% sand is sandy loam.

  It now matches
  [`aqp::ssc_to_texcl()`](https://ncss-tech.github.io/aqp/reference/texture.html)
  on the whole grid. 707 horizons of the panels change class, and no
  name changes.

#### Results against 0.9.314

| panel | 0.9.314 | 0.9.315 |
|----|----|----|
| FEBR USDA (886) | 44.5 | 50.9 |
| KSSL USDA (497) | 38.4 | 38.8 |
| ISIS USDA (748) | 47.5 | 47.9 |
| ISIS WRB 2022 (481) | 61.1 | 61.3 |
| FEBR WRB (218), WoSIS (130), AfSP (120) | 22.0, 16.2, 28.3 | unchanged (qualifiers change) |
| BDsolos, FEBR and Redape SiBCS | 57.5, 37.6, 87.1 | unchanged |

- In FEBR and KSSL no profile records a moisture regime, so no profile
  there is an Aridisol now. The 127 FEBR profiles move to the Ultisols,
  Alfisols and others. KSSL loses 34 reference Aridisols and gains 36
  other profiles.
- ISIS KE069 (an indurated Ckm at 30 cm) is now a Phaeozem, as ISRIC
  names it.
- **Fixtures:** the WRB and SiBCS names of the 44 canonical fixtures do
  not change. In USDA, the Durisol is now a Typic Torriorthents (its
  duripan is not cemented) and the Luvissolo a Typic Hapludalfs (no
  moisture regime).

## soilKey 0.9.314 (2026-10-29)

### WRB 2022 mollic and umbric horizons: criteria 1-3 in every layer

- WRB 2022 Ch 2.1 (p. 23): when a diagnostic horizon consists of several
  subhorizons, every criterion except the thickness must be met in each
  subhorizon, unless the text says otherwise. For the mollic (3.1.20)
  and umbric (3.1.39) horizons, only the base saturation is “on a
  weighted average”. The horizon is now the run of layers from the
  mineral soil surface that each meet:
  - criterion 1, the structure (not recorded still does not block it);
  - criterion 2, \>= 0.6% SOC;
  - criterion 3, the colour, items a-c. A plough layer takes the colour
    of the subhorizon below it.

  The thickness and the weighted base saturation are read on that run.
- Before, the carbon test passed when any one layer had 0.6%, and the
  structure was a share of the whole dark stack. An Ah of subangular
  blocky structure over thick massive dark layers therefore had no
  horizon. Bounding the stack by structure alone would have given ISIS
  CN012 a mollic horizon from its massive 6 cm Ah, since the colour and
  carbon tests let its C layers in; reading every criterion in every
  layer gives it none.
- **Colour where it is not wholly recorded:**
  - A moist value with no dry value still reads the dry value as the
    moist value + 1.
  - Of the older proxies, only one stays (Hugo, 2026-10-29): a layer
    with no colour recorded at all and \>= 1.5% SOC is read as dark. The
    FEBR and WoSIS panels record no colour.
  - A dry colour alone now leaves criterion 3 undecided unless its value
    is above 5, and the dry chroma no longer stands in for the moist
    chroma.
  - The colour subtest records, for each layer, where its reading came
    from.
- A criterion that fails now decides the horizon even when another one
  is undecided. Until now, an undecided colour beside a massive surface
  layer left the horizon undecided.
- **Results against 0.9.313:**
  - FEBR WRB (22.0%) and WoSIS (16.2%): no name changes.
  - AfSP: 27.5 to 28.3%. BI wasp_2, an Ah of subangular blocky structure
    over massive dark layers, is an Umbrisol again.
  - ISIS: 61.5 to 61.1% (294 of 481), with 3 gained and 5 lost, each by
    the text:
    - gained: two profiles that record a dry colour only, which the
      dry-only proxy made Umbrisols, and an Arenosol;
    - lost: three that record a dry colour only or lose carbon below the
      first layer, a Kastanozem whose Ap is recorded as massive, and a
      Luvisol whose plough layer now takes the colour of the Ah below it
      (a Phaeozem).
  - The SiBCS and USDA panels and the 44 canonical fixtures are
    unchanged.

## soilKey 0.9.313 (2026-10-29)

### ISIS: slickensides and pressure faces are read as absent only where the cutans field is free

- ISIS has one cutans field per layer. With
  `absent_unless_recorded = TRUE`, slickensides and pressure faces that
  a described horizon does not mention were read as absent. Where that
  field records clay cutans, or cutans of no kind, they could not have
  been recorded there, so they now stay unknown (Hugo, 2026-10-29).
  Where the field is free or records no cutans, they are still read as
  absent.
- The seven ISIS Nitisols that record clay cutans only (KE015, KE016 and
  others) no longer read as having no pressure faces. KE016’s nitic
  horizon becomes undecided instead of absent.
- **Results:** the WRB and USDA names of the ISIS profiles do not change
  (481 and 748, rebuilt with this reader). The other panels do not read
  ISIS.

## soilKey 0.9.312 (2026-10-29)

### The AfSP reader reads its structure codes

- AfSP keeps the structure type, grade and size as class codes of the
  FAO-ISRIC (1990) and FAO (2006) guidelines. The reader passed them on
  unread, and the diagnostic tests look for words. A massive “M” or a
  single-grain “N” read as structure not recorded, so since 0.9.311 it
  did not block the mollic and umbric horizons. In the 120 profiles of
  the AfSP sample, 190 layers in 50 profiles record a structure type and
  59 layers in 23 profiles a massive, single-grain or rock structure.
- The codes are now read by the AfSP dictionary
  (`AfSP012Qry_DictioClassValues`):
  - a range of grades by its lower end, as the ISIS reader does (“weak
    to moderate” is weak);
  - a range of sizes with both ends, since soilKey reads a size range by
    its upper end;
  - a code the dictionary does not define as not recorded (in AfSP 1.2:
    grade V, A and R, in 83 of 74,961 layers, and size S, in 5).
- Each code goes to the provenance. The bundled sample
  ([`load_afsp_sample()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/load_afsp_sample.md),
  built in 0.9.77) and profiles built before are read when they are
  loaded or benchmarked.
- **AfSP WRB:** 33 of 120 profiles agree with the reference, as before,
  with 12 RSGs changed: 2 gained and 2 lost.
  - Gained: a Solonetz whose Btn records columnar structure, and a
    Cambisol.
  - Lost: an Umbrisol whose Ah over 116 cm of massive dark layers falls
    short of the structure criterion; a Regosol whose B records
    subangular blocky structure, a Cambisol now.
  - The other panels do not read AfSP and are unchanged.

## soilKey 0.9.311 (2026-10-29)

### WRB 2022 qualifiers, the argic, nitic, mollic and irragric horizons, and two ISIS reader guards by the text

These are the remaining corrections from the triage of the ISIS profiles
where soilKey and ISRIC disagree.

- **Qualifiers (Ch 5):**
  - Calcaric needs a layer of calcaric material 30 cm thick within 100
    cm, and no calcic horizon. A moderate or stronger HCl reaction
    counts when CaCO3 is not measured.
  - Skeletic needs 40% coarse fragments averaged over 100 cm.
  - Geric no longer reads a missing Al as 0.
  - Aric needs a ploughed layer of 10 cm or more with an abrupt lower
    boundary.
  - Sodic needs a layer of 20 cm and no natric horizon.
  - Loamic and Siltic use the texture classes of the triangle.
  - Brunic needs a layer that fails cambic criterion 1 and meets
    criteria 3 and 4.
  - Pellic is tested in the upper 30 cm.
- **Argic horizon (3.1.3):**
  - Item 2.a.ii: when the coarser layer directly over the argic horizon
    is a plough layer, the clay increase does not count. The argic
    horizon is then shown by illuvial clay (2.b).
  - Item 2.a.i: a lithic discontinuity between the two layers also voids
    the clay increase. Readings decided by Hugo: the discontinuity
    counts when a material number records it or the coarse fragments
    show it (3.2.7, criteria 3-6). The particle-size ratios of criterion
    2 are not read, since its item 2.b (not the original variation of
    the parent material) is not shown by the data.
- **Nitic horizon (3.1.22):** the shiny ped faces are pressure faces,
  not clay films. ISIS cutans of kind pressure are read into the new
  attribute `pressure_faces`, and the second-level structure into
  `structure_type_secondary`.
- **Mollic and umbric horizons:**
  - Criterion 1 needs aggregates of 10 cm or less, or cloddy structure,
    in half of the horizon. A recorded massive or single-grain structure
    fails it; structure or size not recorded does not block it (Hugo).
  - Criterion 5 is the weighted base saturation.
- **Irragric horizon:** follows its criteria (3.1.18). Since none of the
  data record a raised land surface, it is never shown, only ruled out
  or left open.
- **ISIS reader:**
  - An R row inside a described horizon is not read as continuous rock
    (IT017: an “R 0-5” row inside an Apkc 0-35).
  - A particle-size record of zeros only is missing.
- **Results against 0.9.310:**
  - FEBR WRB goes from 20.2 to 22.0%. AfSP goes from 28.3 to 27.5% (1
    profile), and WoSIS is unchanged.
  - ISIS goes from 64.7 to 61.5%, with 4 profiles gained and 19 lost:
    - 7 Nitisols that record clay cutans only;
    - 4 Phaeozems whose Ah is recorded as massive;
    - 8 argic horizons under a plough layer with patchy clay films.
  - The SiBCS and USDA panels are unchanged.
- **Fixtures:** 7 of the 44 change qualifiers only: Skeletic, Calcaric
  and Irragric dropped where the text does not support them, Loamic
  added where it does, and Hypereutric now shown.

## soilKey 0.9.310 (2026-10-29)

### WRB 2022 diagnostics by the text: six groups

Found by running soilKey on ISRIC’s World Soil Reference Collection
(ISIS). Six investigations sorted the profiles where soilKey and ISRIC
disagree. Many came from soilKey readings that did not follow the 2022
text, and those are fixed here, group by group. Each group was measured
on the BDsolos, FEBR, KSSL, Redape, AfSP, WoSIS and ISIS panels. The
SiBCS and USDA keys keep their readings: where they shared a WRB
diagnostic, it now has a separate reading for them.

- **Mollic family:**
  - Phaeozems need base saturation of 50% or more throughout to 100 cm
    or to a limiting layer, and carbonates are allowed (Ch 4, p. 113).
  - Chernozems and Kastanozems need a protocalcic layer or a calcic
    horizon at the depth the key gives, with base saturation of 50% or
    more above it.
  - Protocalcic properties are visible secondary carbonates (3.2.8), not
    laboratory CaCO3.
  - The chernic horizon follows its seven criteria and no longer needs
    worm holes.
  - Umbrisols take an umbric, mollic or hortic horizon, and the umbric
    horizon is the contiguous stack from the mineral surface.
  - Where base saturation is missing, the pH stands in, by Annex 2 Table
    9.2.
- **Argic family:**
  - The argic horizon gains criterion 1 (8% clay or more), the
    transition of 15 cm or less, and criterion 2.b.ii (clay films common
    or more). It is a subsurface horizon.
  - Acrisols, Lixisols, Alisols and Luvisols use the 2022 tests: CEC
    below 24 per kg clay, and exchangeable Al above the bases in half of
    50-100 cm. Where the cations are missing, the pH stands in, by Table
    9.3.
  - The natric horizon gets its structure and ESP criteria, and Solonetz
    need a natric horizon within 100 cm.
  - The ferralic thickness counts adjoining sub-horizons. Ferralsols
    follow the text on the argic horizon above the ferralic.
- **Vertic horizon:**
  - Wedge-shaped aggregates count as well as slickensides.
  - The 25 cm counts adjoining layers, and the COLE path stays in the
    USDA reading only.
  - Vertisols need the vertic horizon within 100 cm, 30% clay above it,
    and cracks; missing crack data is undecided.
- **Redox and plinthite:**
  - Gleyic and stagnic properties are told apart by colour and by the
    site’s groundwater. This replaces a “mottles decreasing with depth”
    test that is not in the text. ISIS groundwater is now read into the
    new site attributes `groundwater_kind` and `groundwater_depth_cm`.
  - Stagnosols need stagnic properties on a third of 0-60 cm, and
    Planosols an abrupt textural difference within 75 cm with a
    transition of 2 cm or less.
  - Plinthosols take a plinthic, pisoplinthic or petroplinthic horizon.
    The pisoplinthic horizon reads nodules, and the petroplinthic
    horizon is at least strongly cemented.
- **Organic material and Andosols:**
  - Organic material is 20% organic carbon, not 12%. Histosols follow
    the key: 40 cm of organic material within 100 cm, or 10 cm over rock
    or ice.
  - Andosols sum the andic layers within 100 cm.
  - Where bulk density is missing, Alox + 1/2 Feox of 2% or more with a
    pH NaF of 9.5 or more counts as andic, as a field test. The new
    attribute `ph_naf` holds the pH NaF, and ISIS phnf is read into it.
  - Cryosols gain item 2: a cryic horizon within 200 cm with
    cryoturbation.
- **Weakly developed and carbonate groups:**
