  - The cambic horizon excludes only the layers of another diagnostic
    horizon. Cambisols, Calcisols, Gypsisols and Fluvisols get their
    depth tests.
  - The calcic horizon follows criterion 2.
  - Arenosols use a weighted average of texture.
  - Fluvic material needs a water origin, and its strata are a texture
    reversal or irregular organic carbon. ISIS deposition origin is now
    read into `rock_origin`.
- **Readings decided by Hugo after the measurement:**
  - A profile described above 100 cm is decided on the part that is
    described (Phaeozems, Arenosols).
  - With no secondary carbonates recorded, a layer with CaCO3 \>= 15%
    meets calcic criterion 2 by the laboratory.
  - Gleyic criterion 1 (\>= 95% reductimorphic features) needs at most
    5% oximorphic features, and criterion 3 needs a layer below that
    meets criterion 1.
- **Results:** on the 481 ISIS profiles with an ISRIC WRB 2022 name, the
  Reference Soil Group agrees for 310 (64.4%), up from 221 (45.9%) in
  0.9.308. Other WRB panels: AfSP 25.0 -\> 28.3%, FEBR 19.3 -\> 20.2%,
  WoSIS 16.9 -\> 16.2% (one profile, a Histosol whose H horizons have
  under 20% organic carbon). BDsolos SiBCS goes from 57.2 to 57.5%;
  Redape and the USDA panels are unchanged against 0.9.309.
- **Fixtures:** 10 of the 44 canonical fixtures change their WRB name,
  each by the text:
  - the Planossolo becomes a Planosol;
  - the Argissolo and the Nitossolo become Lixisols;
  - Cambic is dropped where the cambic layers belong to another horizon;
  - the Phaeozem fixture becomes Chernic.

  The Chernozem, Kastanozem, Acrisol, Fluvisol, Stagnosol, Planosol,
  Retisol and Gleysol fixtures gained or changed recorded properties so
  that they keep showing the soil they were written for (the Gleysol:
  the groundwater its drainage class names).

## soilKey 0.9.309 (2026-10-29)

### ISRIC’s KE009: four WRB qualifiers and the key to the Oxisols by the texts

Jelle Janssen’s profile KE009 (ISRIC, Kenya) is a Rhodic Ferralsol
(Clayic, Epic, Eutric, Humic) and a Rhodic Eutrustox for ISRIC. soilKey
gave Rhodic Ferralsol (Clayic, Epic, Ferric, Ochric) and Typic
Paleustolls. Each difference was a soilKey reading that did not follow
the text. KE009 now gets ISRIC’s names in both systems.

- **Humic** (WRB 2022 Ch 5, p. 136): the weighted average of soil
  organic carbon to 50 cm from the mineral soil surface, with the range
  below a limiting layer counting 0. soilKey counted every layer that
  starts above 50 cm whole, from 0 cm, so a deep layer with little
  carbon pulled the average down (KE009: 0.83% for 1.15%).
- **Ochric** (p. 141) also requires that the Humic criteria are not met.
- **Eutric, Dystric and their subqualifiers** use the pH when the
  exchangeable cations are not recorded. The text allows it (“pH values
  may be used according to Annex 2 (Chapter 9.13)”), by Table 9.3:
  exchangeable bases equal the Al at pH (water) 4.6, 4.9 or 5.4 for
  organic carbon below 2, 2 to 7.5 and 7.5 to 20 %. With the carbon
  unknown, the pH decides only where the three classes agree.
- **The ferric horizon** (Ch 3.1.11, p. 45) is read from its criteria:
  coarse red or black masses, or 5 % or more of nodules over 2 mm
  (`ferric_nodules_pct`), in 15 cm or more, outside a plinthic,
  pisoplinthic or petroplinthic horizon. soilKey had read it from
  Fe-dithionite of 5 % or more, which is not a criterion, so red
  Ferralsols with no nodules became Ferric. The argument
  `min_fe_dith_pct` of
  [`ferric()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/ferric.md)
  becomes `min_nodules_pct`.
- **The kandic horizon** follows Keys to Soil Taxonomy (13th ed.,
  pp. 26-27):
  - the clay increase within 15 cm: 3 % absolute, 20 % relative or 8 %
    absolute, by the clay of the overlying horizon;
  - the depth of its upper boundary;
  - a thickness of 30 cm;
  - a texture of loamy very fine sand or finer;
  - an apparent CEC of 16 cmol(+) per kg clay or less in half of the 100
    cm below the clay increase;
  - no fine stratification.

  soilKey had taken the WRB argic horizon with a low CEC.
- **The key to the Oxisols** (KST 13, Ch 8, item E, pp. 68-69) reads
  both of its items. One is an oxic horizon within 150 cm with no kandic
  horizon within that depth. The other is 40 % or more clay in the upper
  18 cm with a kandic horizon within 100 cm. Since v0.9.17 soilKey had
  used “no argillic horizon above the oxic” instead, which made clayey
  Oxisols with a kandic horizon into Mollisols, Ultisols or Alfisols.
  soilKey records no weatherable minerals, and the kandic horizon of the
  second item is read as its oxic horizon is.
- **Fixtures:** 20 of the 44 canonical fixtures change qualifiers only.
  - Humic for Ochric in seven of them, where the 50 cm average is 1 % or
    more.
  - Eutric added in six of them, from the pH.
  - Ferric removed from four, which have no nodules.
  - The Nitossolo fixture becomes a Rhodic Kandiudox (USDA), since it
    has a kandic horizon.
- Against 0.9.308, no WRB Reference Soil Group changes on any panel
  (qualifiers only). The USDA order agrees with ISRIC for 47.5% of the
  ISIS profiles (from 47.3%); KSSL is unchanged; FEBR goes from 44.8 to
  44.5%, as Latosols with a textural gradient now have a kandic horizon
  by KST 13 (their reference names predate the kandic horizon).

## soilKey 0.9.308 (2026-10-29)

### soilKey reads ISRIC’s World Soil Reference Collection (ISIS)

Asked for by Jelle Janssen (ISRIC), who had matched the ISIS properties
to soilKey’s by hand.

- [`read_isis()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/read_isis.md)
  reads profiles live from ISRIC’s ISIS GraphQL service, by profile code
  (`read_isis(c("KE009", "ZW005"))`) or by country
  (`read_isis(country = "KE")`). It returns soilKey pedons ready for
  [`classify_all()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_all.md),
  and writes nothing to disk.
- [`isis_profile_to_pedon()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/isis_profile_to_pedon.md)
  does the translation:
  - Laboratory values go to soilKey units: organic carbon, nitrogen,
    CaCO3 and gypsum from g/kg; water at 1500 kPa from volume to mass;
    water-dispersible clay as a clay content.
  - FAO field codes go to soilKey’s words: structure, consistence,
    stickiness, plasticity, cutans, mottles, boundaries, effervescence,
    cementation and pans.
  - Base saturation, ECEC, aluminium saturation and silt (100 - sand -
    clay) are calculated from the parts.
  - Every value names its ISIS field in the provenance.
- The site carries the names ISRIC gives the profile: `reference_wrb`,
  the new `reference_wrb_full` and `reference_wrb_edition`,
  `reference_usda` and its subgroup, and the new
  `reference_usda_edition`.
- It also carries the soil moisture and temperature regimes when ISIS
  records them (KE009: ustic, isohyperthermic), gilgai, the licence and
  the citation
  ([`isis_citation()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/isis_citation.md)).
- Readings decided by Hugo:
  - ISIS keeps the field description and the laboratory samples in
    separate rows in more than half its profiles. Each sample goes to
    the described horizon that holds its mid-depth, as a
    thickness-weighted mean that fills only what the horizon lacks. A
    described horizon left with no laboratory value takes the samples
    that overlap it.
  - Clay films are the FAO (1977) cutans of kind clay: patchy, broken
    and continuous become few, common and many. Clay cutans with no
    abundance count as few, and so do cutans of no kind in a horizon
    whose designation has t.
  - Cutans of kind slickensides are the slickensides, counted as common
    when patchy, broken or of no recorded abundance.
  - The profile’s cracking (large or small) or, without it, gilgai gives
    cracks of 0.5 cm or more in the horizons starting above 100 cm.
  - Coarse fragments come from the middle of the FAO class when cfvo is
    not measured.
  - Calcareous inclusions are secondary carbonates. Hard Fe/Mn
    concretions over 2 mm are nodules. In a v horizon or an iron pan,
    mottles and soft Fe/Mn concretions are plinthite.
  - EC 1:2.5 is used only where it decides the salic horizon: 15 dS/m or
    more is a lower bound of the paste EC; below that, EC 1:2.5 x 12.5
    is an upper bound. It goes into the new attribute `ec_max_dS_m`,
    which only the salic test reads, to rule a layer out.
  - With `absent_unless_recorded = TRUE` (the default), mottles,
    slickensides, plinthite, a duripan and artefacts that a horizon’s
    field description does not mention are absent in that horizon.
    Mottles stay unknown in a g, l or r horizon with no mottle field.
- [`benchmark_isis()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/benchmark_isis.md)
  sets soilKey’s WRB and USDA names beside ISRIC’s. On the 481 profiles
  with an ISRIC WRB 2022 name, soilKey now gives the same Reference Soil
  Group for 221 (45.9%); with the first draft of the translation it was
  149 (31.0%). The USDA order agrees for 354 of 748 (47.3%; ISRIC’s USDA
  names are from the 1975 and 1999 editions). The median number of close
  calls per profile fell from 7 to 4.
- The investigation behind these numbers also found deviations of
  soilKey’s WRB 2022 diagnostics from the text, on the mollic, argic,
  redox, vertic, organic and weakly developed groups. They are fixed in
  the PRs that follow.

## soilKey 0.9.307 (2026-10-29)

### A soil temperature regime warmer than gelic rules out permafrost

Found on Jelle Janssen’s profile KE009 (ISRIC, Kenya), which kept the
Cryosols open for want of a permafrost temperature.

- [`cryic_conditions()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/cryic_conditions.md)
  (WRB Cryosols, the cryic horizon and the Cryic qualifier) and the USDA
  permafrost test (Gelisols, the Histosols’ exclusion, the Gelods) now
  read `site$soil_temperature_regime`. A regime warmer than gelic
  (cryic, frigid, mesic, thermic, hyperthermic and their iso forms)
  means no permafrost, so the answer is no instead of undecided. KST 13
  (Ch. 3, p. 50) gives the cryic regime a mean annual soil temperature
  between 0 and 8 C and no permafrost; the others are warmer.
- Gelic, the older pergelic, a missing regime or a word that is not a
  regime leave the question open. A measured `permafrost_temp_C` at or
  below 0 C, or a frozen designation, still wins.
- The Pro app has a field “Soil temperature regime (USDA)” beside the
  moisture regime. It is saved with the session and restored when the
  session is opened again.
- No name changes on the 44 canonical fixtures; profiles whose site
  states a warm regime lose the Cryosols (and Gelisols) from their close
  calls.

## soilKey 0.9.306 (2026-10-29)

### Pro app: the close calls name their classes, and a field for the soil moisture regime

Both reported by Jelle Janssen (ISRIC).

- The Ambiguities tab of the Classify page showed “?” in place of each
  reference soil group that could not be ruled out. The panel read the
  fields `name` and `code`, while the results carry `rsg_name` and
  `rsg_code`. It now shows the group and its code, for example “Cryosols
  (CR): missing permafrost_temp_C”.
- The Pedon page has a “Soil moisture regime (USDA)” field in the site
  section (unknown, aquic, aridic (torric), udic, perudic, ustic,
  xeric). The Soil Taxonomy key reads it: ustic leads to the Ustolls and
  Ustalfs, xeric to the Xerolls. It is saved with the session and
  restored when the session is reopened. A profile loaded from a fixture
  or from WoSIS sets it from its own site data, or back to unknown, so a
  regime is never carried over from the previous profile.

## soilKey 0.9.305 (2026-10-29)

### The Hungarian diagnostic soil classification: the 15 soil types

[`classify_hscs2024()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_hscs2024.md)
keys a profile through the key to the soil types of the Hungarian
diagnostic classification (Michéli et al. 2024, *A diagnosztikus
szemléletű hazai talajosztályozási rendszer*, second approximation),
from the Láptalaj (peat soil) to the Földeskopár (other soils).
Experimental and opt-in, like the other national systems:
`classify_all(p, systems = "hscs")`.

- The key and its gates follow the text’s own order: the types after the
  first are “other soils that …”, so each gate tests only its own
  requirements (`inst/rules/hscs2024/key.yaml`,
  `R/diagnostics-hscs-types.R`).
- The diagnostic horizons, properties and materials of section 8 are in
  `R/diagnostics-hscs.R`: organic, humic, clay accumulation, swelling,
  cambic, solonetz and solonchak horizons; continuous hard rock,
  reductive conditions and the groundwater gley colour pattern;
  carbonate classes, artefacts and stratified material.
- The horizon notation is the FAO (2006) one the text adopts
  (`R/designation-hscs.R`): an l or r suffix shows reductive conditions,
  i slickensides, k carbonates, n sodium, p ploughing, t clay
  accumulation, u artefacts, w a cambic horizon.
- The texture triangle the text prints (p. 36) is the USDA triangle with
  Hungarian names, so Hungarian field textures (homok, vályogos homok,
  homokos vályog …) are read on it, as are English names and lab
  particle sizes.
- Names are the Hungarian singular, as the text’s naming example writes
  them; `levels$name_en` gives an English gloss. The codes (LAP … FOL)
  are soilKey’s. The subtype and variety properties are not keyed yet.
- New horizon attribute `soluble_salts_pct`: total water-soluble salts
  as Hungarian laboratories report them (the solonchak horizon). The EC
  is not converted, as the text advises.
- [`make_hscs2024_example()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/make_hscs2024_example.md)
  gives one example profile per type.
- `classify_hierarchical()` adds a `name_en` column to `levels` when the
  classes of a system carry an English gloss; the other systems keep
  their three columns.

Hugo decided seven readings (2026-10-29):

- reductive conditions (Réti talajok) are shown by a dipyridyl test,
  methane, iron sulfides, or an l or r suffix within 50 cm, and are
  undecided when none is recorded;
- the solonchak horizon reads the new `soluble_salts_pct` only;
- the sodium shares of the solonetz horizon are of the CEC;
- an organic horizon with no bulk density measured counts as 1 g/cm3 or
  less;
- slickensides common, many or continuous meet the 10 % of the swelling
  horizon, and they stand for the cracks when none are recorded;
- names in the Hungarian singular with an English gloss;
- stratified material reads 10 points of USDA sand (2-0.05 mm).

The other choices where the text is silent are in
`inst/rules/hscs2024/readings.yaml` (17 topics).

## soilKey 0.9.304 (2026-10-29)

### New Zealand Soil Classification: rows of unknown role under the A horizon and in the B

Two places where
[`classify_nzsc4()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_nzsc4.md)
read a mineral row with no designation one way only now try every
reading and keep a verdict only when all agree.

- The base of the A horizon. A row with no designation directly under
  the A may be A too, so every test measured from the base of the A is
  read at each base the A may have (its designated base, then the bottom
  of each such row in turn): the sandy groups (GS, RS, BS), part 1 of
  the Ultic Soils, part 2 of the Granular Soils, parts 1 and 2(a) of the
  Pallic Soils, the Rocky Recent Soils and the Perch-gley Typic Ultic
  Soils. Until now such a row was read as below the A.
- Part 2(b) of the Pallic Soils (also read by the Mottled-pallic Orthic
  Recent Soils). Rows with no designation below the topsoil may be part
  of the B or BC, so every choice of them is tried. Until now a B
  thinner than 10 cm over such rows was read as not meeting part 2(b).

On the 6,351 profiles of the NZSC review set, 6 change: one Argillic
Perch-gley Pallic Soil becomes undecided at the Pallic order (its platy
row under the A may be A, and then no fine texture lies between the A
and 60 cm), and five Sandy Recent Soils become undecided at the sandy
group, because a row with no designation runs below 60 cm and an A
reaching 60 cm leaves the sandy window empty, which the sandy groups
already read as undecided. Profiles with every row designated are
unchanged. The readings file `inst/rules/nzsc4/readings.yaml` gains one
topic (81 in all).

## soilKey 0.9.303 (2026-10-29)

### Pro app: uploads and downloads over the websocket, and a notice when the connection is lost

On soilkeypro.com some uploads and downloads failed with “Not Found”.
Shiny moves files by plain HTTP requests to `/session/<token>/upload/`
and `/session/<token>/download/`, which only the R process holding the
session can answer. Cloud Run keeps a visitor on one instance on a
best-effort basis, so while a new instance was starting a request could
reach another one. The websocket stays on the instance of the session,
so the files now travel over it.

- `sk_file_input()` replaces
  [`shiny::fileInput()`](https://rdrr.io/pkg/shiny/man/fileInput.html)
  (7 controls). It draws the same box and button;
  `www/soilkey-transfer.js` sends the file in slices of 512 KB, each one
  acknowledged before the next, and the server rebuilds it. `input$<id>`
  keeps the shape `fileInput()` gave (name, size, type, datapath), so
  the tabs read it as before. The size limit is still
  `shiny.maxRequestSize` (5 MB by default); drag and drop still works.
- `sk_download_button()`, `sk_download_link()` and `sk_download()`
  replace `downloadButton()`, `downloadLink()` and `downloadHandler()`
  (13 downloads). A click runs the same file name and content functions;
  the file comes back in slices and the browser saves it under the same
  name. An error shows its message as a notification.
- When the connection to the server drops (the session ended, a phone
  put the page to sleep, or the network failed), a bar at the top of the
  page says so and offers a Reload button, in English or Portuguese,
  instead of a grey page that no longer responds. A profile saved with
  “Save session” can be reopened after the reload.

## soilKey 0.9.302 (2026-10-29)

### New Zealand Soil Classification: the subgroups of the Brown, Anthropic, Recent and Raw Soils

[`classify_nzsc4()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_nzsc4.md)
now keys the 20 groups of the Brown, Anthropic, Recent and Raw Soils to
their 109 subgroups, following the keys to subgroups of the New Zealand
Soil Classification, 4th edition: from the Mottled Allophanic Brown
Soils to the Typic Sandy Raw Soils. With this release every group of the
15 orders is keyed to its subgroups (336 subgroups of 70 groups); the
Hydrothermal Recent Soils and six groups of Raw Soils have none and keep
the group name.

- The keys live in `inst/rules/nzsc4/subgroups/`, one file per order, in
  the book’s order. The last subgroup of each group is the default (in
  the Allophanic Brown Soils the key gives the Typic subgroup criteria
  and makes the Pedal one the last).
- The gates are in `R/diagnostics-nzsc-subgroups-barw.R`: earthy or
  light B horizons, firm horizons beneath them, pallic colours, magnesic
  Brown criteria, impeded Acid Brown Soils, humose and immature Orthic
  Brown Soils, the Maori, refuse, mixing and fill subgroups of the
  Anthropic Soils, acidic windows, weathered-B horizons reaching 30 cm,
  sulfuric soil material, tephric material, buried soils, and the sandy
  Gley Raw Soils.
- Part 2(b) of the Pallic Soils is now one helper that the order key and
  the Mottled-pallic Orthic Recent Soils share.
- Shared gates gained arguments: fluid and saline horizons within 30 cm,
  scoria to 60 cm, contacts from the soil surface, and cemented horizons
  of a least thickness.
- New site fields: `mechanical_mixing_purpose` and
  `acid_neutralising_amendment`.

Hugo decided seven readings:

- the Maori Anthropic subgroups read the existing fields (artefacts and
  the layer origin);
- the purpose of mechanical mixing is a new site field, absent when not
  recorded;
- a coarse fill layer has 80 % or more coarse fragments and artefacts;
- acid-neutralising amendments are a new site field, absent when not
  recorded;
- the Humose Orthic Brown Soils have 10 % or less clay in every horizon
  to 90 cm;
- a compacted fill has one fill horizon of bulk density 1.5 or more;
- a placic horizon is left to the Placic Firm Brown Soils, not counted
  as the cemented horizon of the Cemented and Mottled-cemented Firm
  Brown Soils, as the Acid Brown key does.

The other readings are in `inst/rules/nzsc4/readings.yaml` (80 topics).

Two independent reviews were made, and their findings are fixed. The
review against the book confirmed every code, position and default, and
found the Maori names without their macron, scoria that need not reach
60 cm in the Scoriaceous Tephric Recent Soils, a coarse fill layer of
natural gravel, and word lists that matched inside other words. The
logic review ran 6,000 random profiles and refilled their missing
values; it found no error and no change against 0.9.301, and verdicts
decided where a horizon of unknown role leaves them open (the firm
horizon and the B above it, the earthy B, the greater part of the B, the
thin weathered-B, the subsurface horizons). The fill of the Compacted
Fill Anthropic Soils is now the anthropic soil material the order key
reads, and only the uppermost buried soil counts. Outside the four
orders, rock (R, CR) with no pH is no longer read as possibly acid in
the acidic subgroups of 0.9.299, which can only decide an open verdict.

## soilKey 0.9.301 (2026-10-29)

### New Zealand Soil Classification: the subgroups of the Semiarid, Oxidic, Granular and Pallic Soils

[`classify_nzsc4()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_nzsc4.md)
now keys the 17 groups of the Semiarid, Oxidic, Granular and Pallic
Soils to their 78 subgroups, following the keys to subgroups of the New
Zealand Soil Classification, 4th edition: from the Mottled Aged-argillic
Semiarid Soils to the Typic Immature Pallic Soils. Eleven of the 15
orders now reach subgroup level (227 subgroups of 50 groups); the Brown,
Anthropic, Recent and Raw Soils follow.

- The keys live in `inst/rules/nzsc4/subgroups/`, one file per order, in
  the book’s order. The last subgroup of each group is the default.
- The gates are in `R/diagnostics-nzsc-subgroups-sxnp.R`: alkaline
  horizons, weathered coarse fragments, lithic and paralithic contacts,
  the clay decrease of the Brown Oxidic subgroups, cutanoxidic horizons
  below 25 cm, allophanic layers apart from the bulk density, sodic
  features or a calcareous horizon within or next to an argillic horizon
  or a fragipan, argillic horizons over the fragipan, acid or reddish
  parts of the argillic horizon, lamellae, cemented horizons and pedal B
  horizons.
- Shared gates gained arguments: the acidic B or BC subgroups read a pH
  limit and the major part (Granular Soils), the argillic subgroups a
  thickness, and the calcareous subgroups any depth.
- New horizon attribute: `weathered_fragments_pct`, the share of the
  coarse rock fragments weathered enough to break easily by hammer or
  spade.

Hugo decided two readings:

- the weathered coarse fragments are recorded in the new attribute, and
  not recorded reads as none;
- sodic features that are not measured are absent from a designated
  horizon without the n suffix, as the z suffix marks saline soil
  material (the group key of the Argillic Pallic Soils keeps its
  reading).

The other readings are in `inst/rules/nzsc4/readings.yaml` (69 topics).

Two independent reviews were made, and their findings are fixed. The
review against the book confirmed every code, name and position. The
logic review ran 6,000 random profiles and refilled their missing
values; it found no error and no change against 0.9.300. The fixes:

- a clay decrease of the Brown Oxidic subgroups is decided when the
  missing clays cannot undo it;
- the pedal B of the Immature Pallic subgroups and the major part of the
  B or BC try each choice of the rows of unknown role (the topsoil
  aside), as now also the B or BC of the acidic, allophanic and magnesic
  subgroups of 0.9.300;
- lamellae with no bottom are weighed both ways (also in the Laminar
  Pallic group key);
- fragipans and densipans recorded as a pan type are not cemented;
- a fragipan or argillic horizon the description ends in leaves
  “immediately beneath” open;
- an undesignated row with no fine-earth record may be rock;
- exchangeable Na below 0.7 with no CEC is not a measure of the ESP;
- recorded coatings with no colour value may be dark, so the cutanic
  horizon they mark stays open.

## soilKey 0.9.300 (2026-10-28)

### New Zealand Soil Classification: the subgroups of the Podzol, Allophanic, Pumice and Melanic Soils

[`classify_nzsc4()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_nzsc4.md)
now keys the 17 groups of the Podzol, Allophanic, Pumice and Melanic
Soils to their 79 subgroups, following the keys to subgroups of the New
Zealand Soil Classification, 4th edition: from the Humus-pan Densipan
Podzol Soils to the Typic Orthic Melanic Soils. With the Organic, Gley
and Ultic Soils of 0.9.299, the subgroups of seven of the 15 orders are
keyed (149 subgroups of 33 groups); the other eight orders follow.

- The keys live in `inst/rules/nzsc4/subgroups/`, one file per order, in
  the book’s order. The last subgroup of each group is the default.
- The gates are in `R/diagnostics-nzsc-subgroups-zlme.R`: Bh horizons
  and their thickness, an argillic horizon beneath a Bh or a pan, fluid
  horizons above the podzolic-B, silt-mantled eluvial horizons, acidic
  and allophanic B or BC horizons, vitric allophanic material, buried
  granular B horizons, compacted ignimbrite, the Orthic Pumice subgroups
  (podzolic, allophanic, buried-allophanic, scoriaceous, immature),
  redox segregations within 60 cm, and pedal weathered-B horizons under
  the A.
- Shared gates gained arguments: pans at any depth (the Podzol subgroups
  name no depth) or with their top less than 90 cm down (the
  ironstone-pans and duripans “within 90 cm”), a calcareous horizon
  within or at 90 cm (Melanic Soils), a peaty topsoil at the surface
  only (where the text names no buried one), and the magnesic criteria
  in the B or BC horizon (Mafic Melanic Soils).
- New horizon attributes: `pore_coatings_hue_moist`,
  `pore_coatings_value_moist` and `pore_coatings_chroma_moist`, the
  colour of coatings on pores or gel-like masses (Acidic and
  Vitric-acidic Orthic Allophanic Soils).

Hugo decided seven readings:

- the colour of coatings on pores is recorded in the three new
  attributes, and not recorded reads as none, so the pH decides alone;
- “hue 7.5YR or more” (Podzolic Orthic Pumice Soils) is 7.5YR or redder;
- a silty layer (Peaty-silt-mantled and Silt-mantled Perch-gley Podzol
  Soils) is one of the silt, silt loam, silty clay loam and silty clay
  classes;
- any ignimbrite counts as the Taupo ignimbrite of the Mottled-compacted
  and Compacted Impeded Pumice Soils;
- the Bh of the Ultic-humose Densipan Podzol Soils tops a B horizon that
  is clayey and prismatic as a whole;
- the layer of the Allophanic Orthic Pumice Soils is itself vitric and
  allophanic;
- a scoria of no named composition is basaltic (Scoriaceous Orthic
  Pumice Soils), and “predominantly” is read by the thickness-weighted
  gravel from the mineral soil surface to 25 cm.

The other readings are in `inst/rules/nzsc4/readings.yaml` (61 topics).
The key gives the last Orthic Pumice subgroup (MOT) no name; the
chapter’s summary table names it Typic Orthic Pumice Soils.

Two independent reviews were made, and their findings are fixed. The
review against the book confirmed every code, name and position, and
found eight defects, among them a Bh read only under an eluvial horizon,
“within 90 cm” read as “at 90 cm or less” for the ironstone-pans and
duripans, and the buried B of the Buried-granular Orthic Allophanic
Soils decided while its allophanic status was open. The logic review ran
6,000 random profiles and filled their missing values 185,000 times: it
found two walks that never ended on a horizon of no thickness (in two
new gates and in the acidic subgroups of 0.9.299), and eleven verdicts
decided where the data leave them open, or open where they decide.

Outside the four orders, four readings change; none of the 6,000 random
profiles changes order, group, or subgroup of the Organic, Gley and
Ultic Soils against 0.9.299:

- the acidic subgroups of the Gley Soils no longer hang on a horizon of
  no thickness under the A;
- recorded coatings of moist value 5 may be cutanic (the Diagnostics
  admit value 5 with chroma 3 or less, and the coatings chroma is not
  recorded), so the Granular Acid Gley Soils leave such a B open;
- the Magnesic Yellow Ultic Soils read a mineral row of unknown role as
  a possible B;
- the vertic criteria of the Vertic Melanic Soils read a recorded grade
  below moderate, or a structure type other than blocky or prismatic, as
  ruling the pedality out on its own (it was undecided).

## soilKey 0.9.299 (2026-10-28)

### New Zealand Soil Classification: the subgroups of the Organic, Gley and Ultic Soils

[`classify_nzsc4()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_nzsc4.md)
now keys the 16 groups of the Organic, Gley and Ultic Soils to their 70
subgroups, following the keys to subgroups of the New Zealand Soil
Classification, 4th edition: from the Buried-podzol Litter Organic Soils
to the Buried-granular and Typic Yellow Ultic Soils. The name of such a
profile is now its subgroup (for example “Peaty Orthic Gley Soils”,
“Mottled Yellow Ultic Soils”); the group and the order stay in `levels`.
The subgroups of the other 12 orders follow.

- The keys live in `inst/rules/nzsc4/subgroups/`, one file per order, in
  the book’s order. The last subgroup of each group is the default,
  except under the Densipan and Perch-gley Ultic Soils, which the text
  gives none.
- The gates are in `R/diagnostics-nzsc-subgroups.R`. Criteria the groups
  share use one gate with arguments: sulfidic, saline, fluid, peaty,
  acidic, concretionary, calcareous, pan, mottled, nodular, argillic,
  and the horizons below a densipan or an eluvial horizon.
- New diagnostics: sulfidic and saline soil material, the mottled
  profile form, buried peaty topsoils, coatings on 10 % or more of the
  ped faces and dark coatings.
- New horizon attributes: `sphagnum_fibres_pct` (the Sphagnic Fibric
  Organic Soils) and `shelly_layer` (the Calcareous Recent Gley Soils).

Hugo decided four readings:

- sulfidic soil material that is not measured is absent when no horizon
  in the window can look sulfidic in the field (a reductimorphic horizon
  with a hue of 5Y or less red, or black), as the text describes it;
  otherwise it is undecided;
- saline soil material that is not measured is absent when the horizons
  are designated and none carries the z suffix; with no designations it
  is undecided;
- the Sphagnum share of the fibres and a shelly layer are recorded when
  met, so not recorded reads as none;
- a Densipan or Perch-gley Ultic Soil that passes no subgroup keeps the
  group name, with a warning.

The other readings are in `inst/rules/nzsc4/readings.yaml`. Two subgroup
names follow their groups’ spelling: Typic Sulfuric Gley Soils (the text
writes “Sulphuric”) and Typic Yellow Ultic Soils (the text writes
“Soil”).

Outside the subgroups, two readings change:

- “in some part” now finds a run of 10 cm that passes when it lies
  directly below a horizon left undecided (it was read as undecided);
- the peaty topsoil reads a horizon with a recorded mineral field
  texture and no measured carbon as not peat (it was undecided), as the
  text defines it by peat or peaty textures.

Both can only turn an undecided order or group into a decided one.

An independent review against the text of the book found six defects,
all fixed: (f) horizons counted in the mottled profile form, which the
4th edition excludes; the window of the organic material measured from
its top rather than from the soil surface; a buried podzol written with
the buried prefix missed under litter; a B horizon ending above 60 cm
left undecided in the Granular Acid Gley Soils; the peat reading above;
and coatings of value 5 left open in the Podzolic Yellow Ultic Soils.
Recorded dark coatings now make a cutanic horizon without the (h)
notation in the Granular Acid Gley Soils.

A second review checked the logic with 12,500 random profiles: no
errors, no row-order effects, and every order or group that changes
against 0.9.298 goes from undecided to decided through “in some part”.
Its findings are fixed: a buried peat under a peaty horizon that is not
a topsoil was missed; an undesignated row under the A, nothing described
under litter, a window the description does not reach (for sulfidic and
saline material), a gap above the clay of the Buried-granular Yellow
Ultic Soils and a densipan with no depths were read as absent rather
than undecided; one decisive lab value did not settle “less silt than
clay”; and a pan could pass as the argillic horizon of the Argillic
Orthic Gley Soils. The readings file now has 50 topics.

## soilKey 0.9.298 (2026-10-28)

### New Zealand Soil Classification: the 77 groups

[`classify_nzsc4()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_nzsc4.md)
now keys each of the 15 orders to its groups, following the keys to
groups of the New Zealand Soil Classification, 4th edition: 77 groups,
from the Litter, Fibric, Mesic and Humic Organic Soils to the Hydric,
Gley, Hydrothermal, Cryic, Rocky, Sandy, Fluvial, Tephric and Orthic Raw
Soils. The name of a classified profile is now its group (for example
“Orthic Brown Soils”, “Fragic Pallic Soils”); the order stays in
`rsg_or_order` and in `levels`. Subgroups follow.

The groups read diagnostics the order key did not need: sulfuric and
tephric soil material, densipans, perch-gley features, redox-mottled
horizons, peaty topsoils, slowly permeable layers, nodular horizons and
fluvial features. They also read new horizon attributes:
`packing_degree`, `ksat_mm_h`, `penetration_resistance_kpa`,
`redox_segregations_location`, `sulfate_s_pct`, `roots_abundance`,
`maori_cultural_layer` and `coatings_value_moist`. On the site they read
`soil_temp_30cm_C`, `mean_annual_air_temp_C`, `surface_water`,
`methane_odour`, `mechanical_mixing_depth_cm` and
`artificially_drained`.

Hugo decided four readings:

- the new attributes are created, as above;
- features that a describer records when met are absent when not
  recorded: stratification, nodules, cracks, refuse and Maori cultural
  layers, permafrost, surface water and mechanical mixing;
- the pans that the text names as often working as slowly permeable
  layers count as such: fragipans, argillic horizons, densipans,
  humus-pans, ortstein-pans, and lithic and paralithic contacts;
- the hydrothermal groups compare the soil temperature at 30 cm with the
  air temperature, in two new site fields.

The other readings are in `inst/rules/nzsc4/readings.yaml`, which now
has 39 topics.

Two independent reviews checked the groups: one against the text of the
book, one for the logic, with 3,600 random profiles. Their findings are
fixed, and they changed the order key in three places:

- clay lamellae make an argillic horizon only when they add up to 15 cm
  within 90 cm;
- outside the New Zealand notation a Cr reads as a paralithic contact;
- site fields are read one value at a time.

Outside the NZSC,
[`ensure_horizon_schema()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/ensure_horizon_schema.md)
now reads “yes” and “no” (and y, n, 1, 0) in logical columns as TRUE and
FALSE; before, they became NA. The other systems do not change: the 44
canonical fixtures are identical.

## soilKey 0.9.297 (2026-10-28)

### The SiBCS family no longer repeats the class, and reads texture from mineral material

Two fixes to the family (5th level) of a SiBCS name, as Hugo decided:

- A class that already states the base saturation takes none in its
  family. The book uses the base saturation “except for the classes that
  already consider it at a higher level” (Cap 18, p 285), and the same
  rule holds for “álico” when the class is already Alumínica. The rule
  used to be set per order, so the Gleissolos Háplicos Ta Eutróficos
  repeated “eutrófico”. It is now read on the class name itself.
  [`classify_sibcs_familia()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_sibcs_familia.md)
  gains `nome_superior` (the name of the higher levels), which
  [`classify_sibcs()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_sibcs.md)
  passes.
- The textural group, the gravel class and the skeletal constitution are
  averaged over the mineral horizons only, in every order: an H or O
  horizon no longer enters them. The Organossolos give their texture
  only through the underlying material (“Organossolos Háplicos, material
  subjacente médio”), no longer through a textural group of the whole
  profile (“textura média”).

Four family labels of the 44 canonical fixtures change (two Gleissolos,
two Organossolos); no class changes, and the fixtures, named without the
family, are identical.

## soilKey 0.9.296 (2026-10-28)

### The SiBCS family label in the words of the book

The family (5th categorical level) of a SiBCS name used to be written
with soilKey’s internal codes, as in “Latossolos Vermelhos Eutróficos
típicos, muito_argilosa, moderado”. It is now written as the SiBCS
(2018, Cap 18) writes it: “…, textura muito argilosa, A moderado”. The
textural group or subgroup follows “textura” (“textura média-arenosa”),
with the gravel class and “esquelética” after it with no comma and the
sand mineralogy in parentheses (“textura argilosa pouco cascalhenta
(micácea)”). The surface horizon follows “A” (“A moderado”, “A húmico”),
and the histic one reads “horizonte hístico”. In the Organossolos, the
underlying material reads “material subjacente argiloso”, and the
woodiness reads “muito lenhoso”. Hugo decided three of these readings:
“horizonte hístico”, “material subjacente”, and writing the gravel class
and “esquelética” together when both apply. The names keep the plural of
the key’s classes. The codes in `FamilyAttribute$value` do not change,
and neither does any class: the 44 canonical fixtures, named without the
family, are identical. Seen in the name of an ISRIC profile sent by
Jelle Janssen.

## soilKey 0.9.295 (2026-10-28)

### Many profiles from one horizon table

[`classify_profiles()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_profiles.md)
classifies every profile of a table that has one row per horizon and a
column saying which profile each horizon belongs to, as a survey or a
database export usually comes. Site properties such as
`soil_moisture_regime` come from a second table (one row per profile) or
a list named by profile id. A `map` renames columns and converts their
units on the way in:
`data.frame(from = "ORGC", to = "oc_pct", factor = 0.1)` reads an
organic carbon in g/kg as soilKey’s %. The names are checked once for
the whole table, so a column that no key reads is named in one warning,
not once per profile. The result has one row per profile, in the order
of the table, with the class name in each system, the attributes the
keys asked for and did not find, and the error of a profile that could
not be classified (the others are classified as usual). The full
[`classify_all()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_all.md)
results and the pedons ride along as attributes. Asked for by Jelle
Janssen (ISRIC), who classifies ISIS profiles this way. No
classification changes: the 44 canonical fixtures are identical.

## soilKey 0.9.294 (2026-10-28)

### A warning for the attributes that no key reads

A horizon column that soilKey does not recognise, or a site property it
does not know, used to be kept in the `PedonRecord` and read by no key
without a word, so a misspelt column (`organic_carbon_gkg`) or a site
property given as a horizon column (`soil_moisture_regime`) went
unnoticed. `PedonRecord$new()` now warns about them when it is called
from outside the package, naming each one with the closest recognised
name: “organic_carbon_gkg (did you mean oc_pct?)”, “soil_moisture_regime
(a site property: site\$soil_moisture_regime)”.
[`read_pedon_csv()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/read_pedon_csv.md)
warns for the file it reads, and now also accepts a spreadsheet whose
columns are all aliases (`Top`, `Bottom`, `Clay`, `SOC`), which it used
to refuse. The loaders (BDsolos, FEBR, WoSIS, NatSoil, NPDB, KSSL,
LUCAS, AfSP, Redape) and the other constructions inside soilKey keep
extra columns on purpose and stay quiet. The warning has the class
`soilKey_unrecognised_attributes`;
`options(soilKey.warn_unrecognised = FALSE)` turns it off. The new
[`unrecognised_attributes()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/unrecognised_attributes.md)
returns the same list as a table, for a pedon or for a horizon table and
a site list, so a batch can be checked before it is built. Suggested by
Jelle Janssen (ISRIC).

The site properties now have a reference of their own, as the horizon
attributes have had since 0.9.266: `inst/schemas/site-attributes.yaml`,
read by the new
[`site_attribute_spec()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/site_attribute_spec.md),
gives each recognised property its type, unit, description, the values
the keys compare it with and the keys that read it, and
`inst/ATTRIBUTES.md` lists them after the horizon attributes. A test
fails when the code reads a site property that the file does not list.

In soilKey Pro, opening a session file keeps the site properties that
soilKey recognises beyond the editor’s own fields
(`soil_moisture_regime`, `drainage_class`, …): they reach the pedon and
the classification and are saved again with the session. Until now they
were dropped. A notice lists the horizon columns and site properties
that no key reads, on opening a session and on uploading a CSV. No
classification changes: the 44 canonical fixtures are identical.

## soilKey 0.9.293 (2026-10-28)

### New Zealand Soil Classification: the 15 orders

A new, experimental and opt-in system: the New Zealand Soil
Classification, 4th edition (Manaaki Whenua - Landcare Research 2026),
read from its Quarto source of 7 October 2026.
[`classify_nzsc4()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_nzsc4.md)
keys a pedon to the 15 orders of the Key to Soil Orders (Organic, Gley,
Ultic, Podzol, Allophanic, Pumice, Melanic, Semiarid, Oxidic, Granular,
Pallic, Brown, Anthropic, Recent and Raw Soils);
[`make_nzsc4_example()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/make_nzsc4_example.md)
gives one example profile per order. Groups and subgroups follow; the
Cryic Soils of the appendix are not keyed.
`classify_all(systems = "nzsc")` runs it.

The diagnostics read the New Zealand horizon notation (Bw, Bt, Bg, Bh,
Bs, Bo, Bx, Bw(g), the pans Bhm, Bsm, Blm, Bfm, CR, an e prefix for
anthropic soil material), moist colours, texture groups, pH, P
retention, bulk density, volcanic glass, coarse fragments and their
origin, structure and clay coatings, and the New Zealand field tests, as
five new horizon attributes: `naf_test` (reactive aluminium),
`childs_test`, `sensitivity_class`, `fluidity_class` and `stickiness`.
From the site: drainage class, parent material (Melanic Soils), human
truncation and an overthickened A horizon (the note to the key).

Three readings are Hugo’s decisions: a reductimorphic horizon in a
designated profile is read from its notation (g, r, or peat), as pale B
horizons of Pallic Soils have low chroma without being reduced; a
measured P retention decides allophanic soil material, the field tests
standing in only when it is not measured; and a reductimorphic horizon
that reaches the base of the B horizon meets the depth condition of the
Gley Soils. The other readings are in `inst/rules/nzsc4/readings.yaml`.
WRB, SiBCS, USDA, Canadian and Australian results do not change.

## soilKey 0.9.292 (2026-10-27)

### Australian classification: the families

`classify_asc3(include_family = TRUE)` now places a soil in the family
classes of its order and writes them after the name, as the book does:
“Bleached, Eutrophic, Red Chromosol; thick, non-gravelly, loamy/clayey,
deep”. The new
[`classify_asc3_family()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_asc3_family.md)
returns each criterion as a `FamilyAttribute` with its code (YY when the
data cannot decide the class, ZZ when no class of the order fits); the
result keeps them in `trace$family`, `trace$family_label` and
`trace$family_code`. `classify_all(include_family = TRUE)` passes the
option on when the Australian key is run. Without the option nothing
changes.

The criteria are those of each order page: the thickness of the A1, or
of the whole A in the Kurosols, Sodosols and Chromosols and in the
Kurosolic, Sodosolic and Chromosolic Hydrosols (the book’s general rule,
where the order pages disagree); gravel (2-60 mm) of the surface and A1,
the larger of the two estimates; the field texture of the A1 and the
most clayey one of the B; soil depth (to rock, a cemented pan or
saprolite; otherwise to the C under the B, or the depth described in a
soil without a B); and water repellence. The Vertosols use laboratory
clay, the Calcarosols the depth of the Bk, the Arenosols and Rudosols
the surface soil, the Organosols their organic materials. The
Anthroposols and the tidal Hydrosols have none. The classes and the
criteria of each order are in `inst/rules/asc3/families.yaml`, the
readings in `readings.yaml`.

Two horizon attributes: `gravel_pct` (gravel-sized fragments) and
`water_repellence`. The NatSoil reader fills them, with the coarse
fragments of the ground surface and the surveyors’ family codes, and
`benchmark_natsoil(family = TRUE)` compares each criterion. On the
NatSoil profiles whose order agrees, the decided classes agree with the
surveyors for 85 % of the thicknesses, 87 % of the A1 textures, 97 % of
the B textures, 83 % of the depths and 75 % of the gravel classes. The
Vertosol clay classes are mostly undecided: only 29 of 291 NatSoil
Vertosols have laboratory clay.

No order, suborder, great group or subgroup changes on NatSoil. WRB,
SiBCS and USDA results do not change.

## soilKey 0.9.291 (2026-10-27)

### Australian classification: subgroups of the Rudosolic and Tenosolic Hydrosols

The Hydrosol page points the Rudosolic and Tenosolic great groups of the
Redoxic and Oxyaquic Hydrosols to the subgroup lists of the Rudosols and
Tenosols.
[`classify_asc3()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_asc3.md)
now keys such a soil, apart from wetness, through the Rudosol or Tenosol
suborders, and takes the list of the suborder it keys to: “Basic,
Rudosolic, Oxyaquic Hydrosol”. Those lists are the same for every great
group of a suborder, so the soil is keyed to the suborder only. Apart
from wetness, the Hypersalic Rudosol suborder is read by its salinity
alone (its other conditions, no water table and no mottling, are
wetness). A suborder with no list (Shelly, Carbic) gives no subgroup. A
suborder left undecided before the one assigned makes the subgroup
provisional only when it would lead to another list. The Salic Rudosolic
and Tenosolic Hydrosols keep the Salic list.

The rules name these great groups under `subgroups_from` in the Hydrosol
subgroup file, with site fields set for the walk only
(`.apart_from_wetness`);
[`load_rules()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/load_rules.md)
reads such blocks, the rule validator checks them, and the key walks the
other order as the main key would, only as deep as the choice of list
needs. The walk shows in the trace as a phase of its own (“suborders, as
a Rudosol”).

On 9,700 licensed NatSoil profiles only the five that key to these great
groups change: two get a subgroup, two stay undecided for lack of data,
and one fits none of the three Rudosol subgroups (exactly half of its
soil is strongly acid). Nothing else changes, at any level. WRB, SiBCS
and USDA results do not change.

## soilKey 0.9.290 (2026-10-26)

### Australian classification: carbonate segregations recorded as none

A horizon whose carbonate segregations are recorded as none (0 %), with
no effervescence or CaCO3 recorded, was left undecided by the test of
“calcareous”, although the same horizon with nothing recorded is read by
its pH (a pHw below 7.0 is not calcareous, as free carbonate holds the
pH higher). A recorded 0 % of segregations says nothing of the
fine-earth carbonate, so the pH rule now applies to it too. Found in the
review of 0.9.289.

On 9,700 licensed NatSoil profiles no order or suborder changes, and 32
more orders are decided (1,305, at 74.5 %). 98 great groups change,
nearly all to Eutrophic, which needs B and BC horizons that are not
calcareous; the great groups that agree with the survey go from 1,076 to
1,140 and the subgroups from 499 to 555. WRB, SiBCS and USDA results do
not change.

## soilKey 0.9.289 (2026-10-26)

### Australian classification: subgroups of the Hydrosols, Arenosols, Rudosols and Tenosols (experimental)

[`classify_asc3()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_asc3.md)
keys the subgroups of the last four orders, so every order that has
great groups now keys its subgroups. WRB, SiBCS and USDA results do not
change, nor do the Australian orders, suborders and great groups, nor
the subgroups of the ten orders keyed before.

- Hydrosols: Fibric, Hemic and Sapric for the Histic-Hypersulfidic and
  Histic-Hyposulfidic Intertidal Hydrosols; Episulfidic-Petrocalcic,
  Episulfidic and Petrocalcic for the Salic ones; 40 subgroups for the
  Redoxic and Oxyaquic ones, without the acidic subgroups for the
  Kurosolic great groups and without the sodic and natric ones for the
  Sodosolic, as the page says. The page sends the Rudosolic and
  Tenosolic great groups to the Rudosol and Tenosol lists; that is not
  keyed yet, and they keep the great group’s name.
- Arenosols: 13 subgroups for the Chernic, Bleached and coloured
  suborders, read over the upper 1.0 m of the profile; the carbonate
  great groups take the list without Humose-Calcareous,
  Melanic-Calcareous and Calcareous, as the page says.
- Rudosols: Acidic, Basic and Calcareous, read over the soil above any
  rock, pan or buried soil; for every suborder but the Shelly and
  Carbic. The Hypergypsic, Lutic and Stratic Rudosols have no great
  groups, and their subgroups follow the suborder (“Basic, Lutic
  Rudosol”): the hierarchical key skips a level only when the next one
  has a list named by the exact path.
- Tenosols: one list per suborder (4, 9, 6, 3, 12, 7 and 13 subgroups):
  chernic horizons with the acidity and carbonate of the B, the A2 or
  the solum; Subpeaty, Subhumose, Submelacic and Submelanic (every
  requirement but the thickness); Lithocalcic, Supracalcic and
  Hypercalcic for the Calcenic Tenosols, read on the Calcenic horizon.
- Readings decided with Hugo: the Salic Hydrosols take only the three
  subgroups listed; in the coloured Tenosols Basic is read as no part of
  the solum calcareous (the page’s “the A2 horizon” read as a misprint);
  in the Chernic Tenosols “the B horizon (if present)” with no B fails.
- [`benchmark_natsoil()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/benchmark_natsoil.md)
  reads the survey’s subgroup of a suborder with no great groups from
  its great-group column.
- The readings are in `inst/rules/asc3/readings.yaml` (57).

On 9,700 licensed NatSoil profiles, 195 of the 414 profiles of these
four orders that reach a subgroup list get a subgroup (75 decided). Only
20 can be compared with the survey (5 agree): most survey labels of
these orders use older codes, and many profiles stop at a great group
the survey does not give.

## soilKey 0.9.288 (2026-10-26)

### Australian classification: subgroups of the Vertosols, Calcarosols, Podosols and Organosols (experimental)

[`classify_asc3()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_asc3.md)
keys the subgroups of the Vertosols, Calcarosols, Podosols and
Organosols, one list per order as the order pages give them (43, 12, 15
and 8 subgroups). WRB, SiBCS and USDA results do not change, nor do the
Australian orders, suborders and great groups, nor the subgroups of the
six orders keyed before.

- Vertosols: the acid sulfate subgroups as for the acid sulfate great
  groups; Salic as for the Salic Hydrosols; Duric and Petrocalcic; the
  upper 0.1 m of the solum sodic (Episodic, by its weighted average
  ESP); the upper 0.5 m of the solum and the solum below it strongly
  acid, calcareous, mottled or with an ESP of 15 or more (Epiacidic,
  Endocalcareous, Epihypersodic and their combinations); Magnesic over
  the B. The solum is read as described, pans left out, rows of unknown
  role and horizons of unknown depth tried every way they may go.
- Calcarosols: Melanic, Vertic, Subplastic and Gypsic; Epibasic and
  Hypervescent as for the Calsilic Arenosols; Supravescent;
  Epihypersodic and Endohypersodic; Ceteric for the others. The
  Carbonatic Calcarosols take the list without Supravescent and
  Hypervescent, as the page says they are not required there.
- Podosols: a strongly or weakly coherent B (Parapanic, Fragic), a
  densipan in the A2 (Densic), a thin ironpan in or under the B
  (Placic), a siliceous pan under the B, a ferric horizon in the B, with
  the peaty, humose, melacic and melanic combinations.
- Organosols: what the organic materials directly overlie (Lithic,
  Paralithic, Marly, Rudaceous, Modic), a thin ironpan below them, and
  layers of unconsolidated mineral material within or below them (Terric
  within 0.8 m, Regolithic below).
- The examples of the four orders key to a subgroup (“Endocalcareous,
  Self-mulching, Black Vertosol”).
- The readings are in `inst/rules/asc3/readings.yaml` (56).

On 9,700 licensed NatSoil profiles, 424 of the 533 profiles keyed to
these four orders with a great group get a subgroup. Of the 347 whose
order, suborder and great group agree with the survey and whose survey
gives a subgroup of the key, 261 get one and 113 (43 %) the survey’s
(Vertosols 100 of 239). Nearly every Vertosol subgroup stays
provisional: the Sulfuric subgroup needs the pH of the upper 1.5 m, and
the Sulfidic one a sulfide test, rarely recorded (read as absent, a test
not done would decide 11 more Vertosols and leave the agreement
unchanged).

## soilKey 0.9.287 (2026-10-26)

### Australian classification: subgroups of the Dermosols, Kandosols and Ferrosols (experimental)

[`classify_asc3()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_asc3.md)
keys the subgroups of the Dermosols, Kandosols and Ferrosols, one list
per order as the order pages give them (33, 29 and 14 subgroups). WRB,
SiBCS and USDA results do not change.

- These pages read the B2 horizon where the Kurosols, Sodosols and
  Chromosols read the B2t: mottled, whole coloured, and strongly acid
  (Acidic, Humose-Acidic, Melanic-Acidic, Ferric-Acidic,
  Manganic-Acidic, Acidic-Sodic, Bleached-Acidic, Acidic-Mottled: the
  major part of the B2 with a pHw below 5.5, or a pHCa below 4.6 without
  pHw).
- New in the Kandosols: an argic or a bauxitic horizon within the B
  (Argic, Bauxitic). New in the Ferrosols: Snuffy (an A horizon with a
  very fine granular structure, peds under 2 mm, and a weak or very weak
  dry strength), and Sodic read on the lower part of the B2, as printed.
- The Kandosol page says the acidic subgroups are not required for the
  calcareous great groups: the Hypocalcic, Lithocalcic, Supracalcic,
  Hypercalcic and Calcic Kandosols take the list without them, as the
  Natric Kurosols take theirs without the Sodic ones.
- The examples of the three orders record organic C, mottles and the
  CEC, and key to a subgroup (“Haplic, Eutrophic, Brown Dermosol”).
- The dark horizon of the Chernic suborders (melacic or melanic) is now
  decided over every extent it may have, as the subgroups read it since
  0.9.286. Before, a horizon 0.2 m thick in its surely black rows was
  read on those rows only, though rows that may be black below could
  change its major part, and a gap in the record directly above the
  first row that may not be black was not counted as possibly black.
  Such a gap may likewise be organic material (the peaty horizon, where
  the mineral surface lies) or fusic material (Fusic Anthroposols);
  where the mineral surface may lie at more than one depth, a verdict
  holds only when it holds at each. Over a clear or abrupt textural B, a
  row of unknown role between two A horizons is now read as an A horizon
  (before, as not black).
- The readings are in `inst/rules/asc3/readings.yaml` (55).

On 9,700 licensed NatSoil profiles the orders and great groups do not
change. The Chernic test becomes undecided on five profiles, where a
suborder was already provisional, and decided on one: a Tenosol whose A1
(17.6 % organic C) may or may not be organic material gives a humose
horizon either way, and is now Chernic. Of the 799 profiles keyed to
these three orders with a great group, 549 get a subgroup. Of the 278
whose order, suborder and great group agree with the survey and whose
survey gives a subgroup of the key, 213 get one and 113 (53 %) the
survey’s (Dermosols 32 of 65, Kandosols 80 of 137, Ferrosols 1 of 11).
Most of the others stop at Humose-Mottled, which needs organic C in the
upper 0.2 m. The Ferrosol disagreements come from one survey whose
profiles have 5 to 9 % organic C (combustion, a method the glossary
names) at the surface, a humose horizon, but were surveyed Haplic or
Acidic.

## soilKey 0.9.286 (2026-10-26)

### Australian classification: subgroups of the Kurosols, Sodosols and Chromosols (experimental)

[`classify_asc3()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_asc3.md)
now keys a fourth level, the subgroups, for the Kurosols, Sodosols and
Chromosols; the other orders follow. WRB, SiBCS and USDA results do not
change, nor do the Australian orders, suborders and great groups, but
their names now take the book’s form.

- The names follow the general form the book gives, “Subgroup, Great
  Group, Suborder Order”: “Bleached, Eutrophic, Red Chromosol”. The
  great groups carry the same comma (“Eutrophic, Red Chromosol”; before,
  “Eutrophic Red Chromosol”).
- One list per order, as the order pages give it, applied under every
  great group of the order: chernic horizons (peaty, humose, melacic,
  melanic), a conspicuously bleached A2, a B with at least 0.3 m of
  vertic properties, ferric and manganic horizons within the solum, the
  lower part of the B sodic, the B2t mottled or whole coloured, a
  reticulate horizon below the B2t, a gypsic horizon in the B or BC, a
  siliceous pan in the lower A or upper B, Magnesic, base status, the
  carbonate classes and Effervescent, combined as the lists combine them
  (Bleached-Sodic, Mottled-Sodic, Ferric-Sodic and so on).
- The hierarchical key finds a list for every class under a part of the
  path (“CH-\*“) and writes a name on the name of the class above
  (”Bleached, {parent}“); other systems do not change.
- [`benchmark_natsoil()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/benchmark_natsoil.md)
  reports the subgroups (`$subgroups`).
- The readings are in `inst/rules/asc3/readings.yaml` (54).

On 9,700 licensed NatSoil profiles the orders, suborders and great
groups do not change. Of the 560 profiles keyed to these three orders
with a great group, 294 get a subgroup. Of the 173 whose order, suborder
and great group agree with the survey and whose survey gives a subgroup
of the key, 79 get one and 37 (47 %) the survey’s; most of the others
stop at Humose, which needs organic C in the upper 0.2 m, rarely
measured. The disagreements checked are survey practice: B horizons of
heavy clay with many slickensides and lenticular peds surveyed Haplic
rather than Vertic.

## soilKey 0.9.285 (2026-10-24)

### Australian classification: great groups of the Hydrosols, Arenosols, Rudosols and Tenosols (experimental)

[`classify_asc3()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_asc3.md)
now keys the great groups of every order that has them (the Anthroposols
have none in the text). WRB, SiBCS and USDA results do not change; three
Australian orders change on NatSoil, because an AC horizon is now part
of the solum (see below).

- Hydrosols: the acid sulfate groups as for the Organosols (with
  Histic-Hypersulfidic and Histic-Hyposulfidic), then by suborder:
  Histic, Faunic, Epicalcareous and the particle-size groups for the
  tidal and subaqueous soils; Gypsic, Halic, Epicalcareous, Mottled and
  Haplic for the Supratidal and Hypersalic; and for the Extratidal,
  Salic, Redoxic and Oxyaquic, Petroferric and the order the soil would
  key to apart from wetness (Calcarosolic to Rudosolic).
- Arenosols, Rudosols and Tenosols: what the soil directly overlies
  (hard rock, saprolite, marl, unconsolidated material, a red-brown
  hardpan, a calcrete pan, ferricrete, a siliceous pan, a reticulate
  horizon, coquina), “overlie” being read as “directly overlie”; ferric,
  bauxitic and manganic horizons; gypsic and argic horizons; Inceptic (a
  C/B), Tephric, Andic, Gritty, Gravic, Halic and Subhalic; the
  carbonate classes; Kandic, Tenic and Palic Arenosols; Epibasic and
  Hypervescent Calsilic Arenosols; Arenic Tenosols; Colluvic, Fluvic and
  Lithosolic Clastic Rudosols. In the Arenosols hard layers count only
  below 1.0 m.
- Nodules not recorded are read as absent (more than 20 % of nodules
  shows); this also applies to the Sesqui-Nodular Tenosols, which read
  them as unknown since 0.9.282. A gritty feel, heavy minerals, halite
  and gypsum not recorded are absent too.
- What the soil directly overlies, shared with the Calcarosols: a C or D
  horizon of unrecorded origin is no longer read as possibly hard rock,
  nor is sandy material read as possibly marl (Lithic and Marly
  Calcarosols included); a cemented layer that is no pan may still be
  rock, while one whose origin names saprolite is saprolite; a horizon
  recorded as a pan that makes up the layer (ferricrete, calcrete and
  the like) is a pan whatever its designation, and ferricrete or
  silcrete named by the layer or rock origin counts; an AC horizon is
  part of the solum, which moves three NatSoil profiles from Tenosols or
  Rudosols to Vertosols and Calcarosols, all three now as surveyed.
- New horizon attributes: `manganiferous_nodules_pct`,
  `gypsum_visible_pct`, `halite_visible_pct`, `gritty`,
  `heavy_minerals_pct`. The NatSoil reader fills the first three from
  the segregations, counting only those recorded as nodules or
  segregations of that kind (NaN where the recorded classes leave the
  amount on either side of the limit, which the key reads as undecided).
- The readings are in `inst/rules/asc3/readings.yaml` (52).

On 9,700 licensed NatSoil profiles, three orders change, all three now
as surveyed (1,273 decided, 74.8 % of them agreeing), and 51 fewer
suborders are provisional, from the Sesqui-Nodular reading. Of the 3,536
profiles keyed to these four orders, 398 get a great group; most stop at
the suborder, which is itself undecided for many Tenosols, and the
Hydrosols wait on the sulfide test. Only 42 can be compared with the
survey (order and suborder agreeing, a great group of the key): 21 get
the survey’s great group. Most Tenosol labels use the suborder codes of
the editions before 2021.

## soilKey 0.9.284 (2026-10-24)

### Australian classification: great groups of the Vertosols, Calcarosols, Podosols and Organosols (experimental)

[`classify_asc3()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_asc3.md)
now keys the great groups of four more orders, ten in all. WRB, SiBCS
and USDA results do not change, nor do the Australian orders, suborders
and the great groups of 0.9.283.

- Vertosols, by the surface: Self-mulching (a moderately or strongly
  self-mulching surface in the site record, as the text asks that the
  group be used only when the condition is not in doubt), Epipedal (a
  pedal A, blocky or polyhedral), Crusty (a surface crusty horizon over
  pedal clay: a surface crust in the site record, or a surface horizon
  30 mm thick or less that is massive or weakly structured), Massive
  (massive or weak blocky), Peaty. The site record is read item by item,
  negations included; a thin organic layer at the top is passed over.
- Calcarosols: Duric and Petrocalcic (a pan directly under the soil),
  Rendic (the A directly over a Bk of more than 80 % soft carbonate,
  Hypercalcic only), Argic (clay lamellae in the B), Pedal, and what the
  soil directly overlies (Lithic, Paralithic, Marly, Regolithic), read
  from the designation, the layer or rock origin and any pan; a C of
  unrecorded origin, a description that stops at the base of the solum,
  or a row of unknown role that may be part of it, leaves them
  undecided.
- Podosols, by the kinds of Podosol B in the designations (Bs, Bhs, Bh,
  and a Basi under a Bh), with each suborder’s own list as printed, and
  Pipey where an A2 has a tongued boundary. The NatSoil reader now keeps
  the boundary shape (`boundary_topography`).
- Organosols: Folic (freely drained, organic materials as in Definition
  (ii)), Sulfuric, Sulfidic and the groups that replace them only with
  the evidence (Hypersulfidic, Hyposulfidic; no monosulfidic test is
  recorded), then Calcareous, Basic, Acidic. The upper 1.5 m includes
  buried horizons, and a part of it not described may hold acid sulfate
  material; sulfidic material not tested leaves the great group
  provisional.
- The readings are in `inst/rules/asc3/readings.yaml` (48).

On 9,700 licensed NatSoil profiles, of the 465 of these orders whose
order and suborder agree and whose survey gives a great group of the
key, 75.5 % get the survey’s great group, and 76.4 % of the 301 decided
(the Vertosols: 324 of 418, and 220 of the 281 decided). Several surveys
record the crust of a Crusty Vertosol as a thin A11 over a pedal A12,
which is read as the text describes it. The Calcarosols and Organosols
stay provisional for want of data: the suborder or what lies under the
solum for the first, the sulfide test for the second.

## soilKey 0.9.283 (2026-10-23)

### Australian classification: great groups of the Kurosols, Sodosols, Chromosols, Ferrosols, Dermosols and Kandosols (experimental)

[`classify_asc3()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_asc3.md)
now keys a third level, the great groups, for the six orders with a B
horizon of their own; the name is the great group’s (“Eutrophic Red
Chromosol”). The other orders follow. WRB, SiBCS and USDA results do not
change, nor do the Australian orders and suborders.

- Pans in or under the B: Duric (red-brown hardpan), Petroferric
  (ferricrete), Petrocalcic (a calcrete pan under a B that is not
  calcareous), Placic (thin ironpan), from a new attribute `pan_type`
  (NatSoil records it, “none” included) or the designation (km, sm, qm,
  cm). A pan the record does not show is absent, as the order reads hard
  layers; a cemented layer of unknown kind leaves it undecided.
- The B2t or B2: Pedaric, Subplastic, Magnesic (exchangeable Ca/Mg below
  0.1), Natric, base status (Dystrophic, Mesotrophic, Eutrophic, from
  the exchangeable bases and clay, the clay range of the field texture
  where no lab clay), the Sodosol ESP classes with their Mottled forms,
  and the carbonate classes as for the Calcarosols.
- Ferrosol Calcareous, Kandosol Leptic, Mellic and Andic.
- Hypocalcic now needs some carbonate in the solum (the class is of
  weakly calcareous soils); this does not change the Calcarosols.
- The hierarchical key finds the list under a class by the codes of the
  path to it (“CH-AA”), since the Australian suborder codes repeat from
  order to order; other systems do not change.
- [`benchmark_natsoil()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/benchmark_natsoil.md)
  reports the great groups (`$great_groups`).
- The readings are in `inst/rules/asc3/readings.yaml` (44).

On 9,700 licensed NatSoil profiles, of the 2,160 of these orders whose
order and suborder agree and whose survey gives a great group of the
key, 21.6 % get the survey’s great group, and 80.6 % of the 98 decided.
Most stay provisional for want of laboratory data: exchangeable Ca and
Mg (Magnesic, before the base status classes), the bases and clay,
mottles (the Mottled Sodosols) and, for the Kandosols, the porosity the
Mellic great group asks.

## soilKey 0.9.282 (2026-10-23)

### Australian classification: the suborders of the Anthroposols, Arenosols, Rudosols and Tenosols (experimental)

[`classify_asc3()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_asc3.md)
now keys the suborders of all fifteen orders. WRB, SiBCS and USDA
results do not change, nor do the Australian orders.

- Peaty, humose, melacic and melanic horizons (Chernic suborders), as
  the glossary defines them: organic C against clay for the humose
  horizon; black moist colour, a dry value of 5 or less, pH and
  structure for the melacic and melanic ones. Without organic C or a dry
  colour they are undecided.
- The conspicuously bleached A2: an e (not a j) in the Australian
  notation, or the dry colour of the glossary (80 % bleached: mottles
  not recorded leave it undecided).
- Leptic suborders: rock, a hard layer or a calcrete pan, or a C horizon
  of saprolite, with its top within 0.5 m; a C of unrecorded origin, or
  a description that stops at 0.5 m or above, is undecided.
- Arenosols: Hypergypsic, Hypersalic (EC of a 1:5 extract above 2 dS/m,
  no water table, no mottles), Chernic, Carbonatic, Calsilic, Stratic,
  Bleached, then the colour of the upper 1.0 m of the profile.
- Rudosols: Hypergypsic, Hypersalic, Shelly, Carbic, Leptic, Arenic
  (loose or weakly coherent sands), Lutic, Stratic, Clastic (gravelly).
- Tenosols: Chernic-Leptic, Chernic, Sesqui-Nodular (a ferric or
  bauxitic horizon over more than half of the solum), Calcenic,
  Bleached-Leptic, Leptic, Bleached, then the colour of the upper 0.5 m
  of the profile.
- Anthroposols: the kind of human-made material, from the layer origin.
- A soil with no salinity record (no EC, no saline surface) is read as
  not highly saline; shells, carbic materials and fusic material the
  record does not mention are read as absent, as for the Hydrosol
  settings.
- New horizon attributes `ec_1to5_dS_m`, `strength_dry`,
  `strength_moist`, `ped_size_max_mm`, `ferric_nodules_pct`,
  `bauxitic_nodules_pct`.
- [`load_natsoil_pedons()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/load_natsoil_pedons.md)
  reads them (EC method 3A1, strength classes, ped size, nodules from
  the segregations). Abundance classes are now added as ranges, each
  class strictly between its limits, so two records of 2-10 % and 10-20
  % make 12-30 % (undecided at 20 %); before, their middles were added.
  This also applies to the soft and hard carbonate of 0.9.281.
- The readings are in `inst/rules/asc3/readings.yaml` (39).

On 9,700 licensed NatSoil profiles the orders are as before (43.9 %,
1,270 decided at 74.8 %). Of the 3,691 profiles of the fifteen orders
whose order agrees and whose survey gives a 3rd-edition suborder, 75.9 %
get the survey’s suborder, and 95.7 % of the 679 decided. Rudosols: 20
of 61, and the 10 decided agree; Arenosols 1 of 12 and Tenosols 15 of
222, none decided. Most Tenosols stay provisional because the organic C
of the upper 0.2 m, the dry colours, the nodules or the origin of a
shallow C horizon are not recorded; many surveyed Leptic Tenosols are
described below 0.5 m with no rock, and the text does not make them
leptic.

## soilKey 0.9.281 (2026-10-22)

### Australian classification: suborders of the Organosols, Podosols, Hydrosols and Calcarosols (experimental)

[`classify_asc3()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_asc3.md)
now keys the suborders of eleven of the fifteen orders. The four added
here are read from the order pages and the glossary; the suborders of
the Anthroposols, Arenosols, Rudosols and Tenosols follow. WRB, SiBCS
and USDA results do not change, nor do the Australian orders.

- Organosols: the kind of peat (fibric, hemic, sapric) with the greatest
  thickness; when kinds tie, the most decomposed (the Comment). The kind
  comes from the squeeze test of the glossary, then the rubbed fibre
  content, a peat field texture or an Oi, Oe or Oa designation.
- Podosols: the saturation of the B horizon, from its days of saturation
  or from the drainage class. Rapidly drained is Aeric (the suborders
  define free drainage so); moderately well and imperfectly drained are
  Semiaquic; very poorly drained is Aquic; a well drained site stays
  undecided between Aeric and Semiaquic. Sulfuric material (at least 15
  cm, pH below 4 with jarosite or hypersulfidic material below) and
  hypersulfidic material (incubation test) as the glossary defines them;
  without the test they are undecided.
- Hydrosols: the setting of the soil from the site record (tidal zone,
  inland water, landform, a saline surface). A setting the record does
  not mention is read as absent, as the order key already reads tidal
  flooding. Then Redoxic (more than half of the profile mottled: more
  than 10 % distinct or prominent mottles) or Oxyaquic (more than half
  whole coloured).
- Calcarosols: Hypergypsic (gypsum over 50 % in the solum; read as
  absent when no gypsum is recorded), Carbonatic (more than 40 %
  fine-earth carbonate in the upper 0.1 m), Hypocalcic, then the
  carbonate classes of a calcareous horizon (Bk, BCk or 10 % or more
  carbonate segregations): Lithocalcic, Supracalcic, Hypercalcic,
  Calcic.
- New horizon attributes `carbonate_soft_pct` and `carbonate_hard_pct`
  (visual soft and hard pedogenic carbonate); `mottle_contrast` is now
  read by the ASC too.
- [`load_natsoil_pedons()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/load_natsoil_pedons.md)
  reads the landform pattern, mottles (abundance and contrast) and the
  soft and hard carbonate of the segregations and calcrete fragments.
  Where a segregation of unknown form or a fragment of unknown lithology
  leaves the amount spanning two carbonate classes, it is unknown.
- The readings are in `inst/rules/asc3/readings.yaml` (30).

On 9,700 licensed NatSoil profiles the orders are as before (43.9 %,
1,270 decided at 74.8 %). Of the 3,396 profiles of the eleven orders
whose order agrees and whose survey gives a 3rd-edition suborder, 81.4 %
get the survey’s suborder, and 95.7 % of the 669 decided. For the four
orders added here: Organosols 4 of 10 (the 4 decided agree), Podosols 27
of 48 (26 of the 33 decided), Hydrosols 14 of 49 (6 of the 7 decided),
Calcarosols 33 of 175 (the 2 decided agree). Most of these stay
provisional for want of data in NatSoil: the kind of peat, the contrast
of the mottles, the form of the carbonate segregations and laboratory
carbonate.

## soilKey 0.9.280 (2026-10-22)

### Australian classification: the colour suborders (experimental)

[`classify_asc3()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_asc3.md)
now keys the suborders of seven orders: the Kurosols, Sodosols and
Chromosols (the colour of the upper 0.2 m of the B2t), the Ferrosols,
Dermosols and Kandosols (the upper 0.5 m of the B2) and the Vertosols
(Aquic, then the colour of the upper 0.5 m of the solum). The name is
the suborder’s (“Red Chromosol”); `rsg_or_order` keeps the order. The
other suborders follow. WRB, SiBCS and USDA results do not change.

- Colour classes as the ASC defines them (Red, Brown, Yellow, Grey,
  Black), from the moist matrix colour matched to the nearest chip; a
  colour half way between chips of different classes is of unknown
  class.
- The dominant class covers more than half of the window; when no class
  does, the one with the largest share, as the surveyors read it (a tie
  is undecided).
- Aquic Vertosols: saturation days of the upper 0.5 m, otherwise the
  drainage class as for the Hydrosols.
- An imperfectly drained site (some horizons wet for several weeks, in
  the Field Handbook) now counts as not saturated for 2-3 months, for
  the Hydrosols and the Aquic Vertosols; before, it was undecided. No
  order changes, but more are decided. Organic materials keep their own
  limit: “saturated for long periods” is 30 days, as in Soil Taxonomy,
  whose definition the glossary adopts, so poorly and imperfectly
  drained sites stay undecided there.
- [`benchmark_natsoil()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/benchmark_natsoil.md)
  also reports the suborders (`$suborders`).
- The readings are in `inst/rules/asc3/readings.yaml` (24).

On 9,700 licensed NatSoil profiles: the order agrees for 43.9 % as
before, and 1,270 are now decided (was 1,052), 74.8 % in agreement. Of
the 3,114 profiles of these seven orders whose order agrees and whose
survey gives a suborder, 86.3 % get the survey’s suborder, and 96.6 % of
the 623 decided.

## soilKey 0.9.279 (2026-10-22)

### Australian classification: the field texture first in the textural B (experimental)

The clear or abrupt textural B of
[`classify_asc3()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_asc3.md)
(Kurosols, Sodosols, Chromosols) now reads each horizon by its field
texture grade, and by its lab clay only when it has none. The glossary
gives the limits in clay “and/or” field texture and notes that where the
two disagree the field texture may be the better guide to how the soil
behaves; before, lab clay on both sides decided. The reading is in
`inst/rules/asc3/readings.yaml`.

On the 9,700 licensed NatSoil profiles with an ASC order, 255 change
order: 104 of them now agree with the surveyors, 56 did before.
Agreement goes from 43.4 % to 43.9 % (45.7 % counting the Arenosols as
Tenosols or Rudosols), with 1,052 decided at 77.4 % (78.6 %). WRB, SiBCS
and USDA results do not change.

## soilKey 0.9.278 (2026-10-22)

### NatSoil (CSIRO) as a benchmark for the Australian key (experimental)

NatSoil, the national soil site database of CSIRO, can now be read
through its public API and used to check
[`classify_asc3()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_asc3.md)
against the orders the surveyors gave. The data are licensed per site,
most under CC BY 4.0, and are not shipped:
[`fetch_natsoil()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/fetch_natsoil.md)
saves them to a folder of your choice. WRB, SiBCS and USDA results do
not change.

- [`fetch_natsoil()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/fetch_natsoil.md)
  downloads every public site (about 150 pages) and then the horizons,
  samples and laboratory results of each licensed site with an ASC order
  (one request per site, about 9,800), with a pause between requests.
  Files already on disk are kept, so a run can be resumed. Sites not
  licensed for external use are skipped.
