- [`load_natsoil_pedons()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/load_natsoil_pedons.md)
  turns the files into pedons: designations in the Australian notation,
  field texture grades, structure, moist and dry colours, slickensides,
  cracks, coarse fragments, calcareous segregations (records with only
  their nature are templates and are not read), pans, effervescence,
  plasticity type, the moisture when described, and laboratory pH, clay,
  exchangeable cations, CEC and effective CEC (whatever the extraction
  method, the “not recorded” methods included), ESP, organic C, free
  iron and carbonate. Samples count for the horizons they overlap,
  weighed by the overlap. A value below the detection limit (“\<x”) is
  read as half the limit, unless the limit lies above one the keys read.
  The field pH stands in only where the laboratory has no pH, and the
  loss on ignition gives organic C only in peat. The site keeps the
  surveyors’ classification and confidence, the drainage class, the
  surface condition, coordinates, the licence and the citation.
- [`benchmark_natsoil()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/benchmark_natsoil.md)
  compares the orders: agreement for all pedons and for the decided
  ones, by the surveyors’ confidence, recall by order, the confusion
  table and the first order left undecided. The surveys predate the 2021
  Arenosols, so an Arenosol given to a surveyed Tenosol or Rudosol is
  also counted as agreement in the edition figures.
- New horizon attribute `esp_pct`: the exchangeable sodium percentage as
  the laboratory reports it.
  [`classify_asc3()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_asc3.md)
  reads it for the sodic condition when exchangeable Na or the CEC is
  not given.

On 9,700 licensed NatSoil profiles with an ASC order, the order agrees
for 43.4 % (45.3 % counting the Arenosols as Tenosols or Rudosols);
1,045 are decided, with 77.8 % agreement (79.1 %); of the 450 decided
with the surveyors’ highest confidence, 80.2 % agree (81.8 %).

## soilKey 0.9.277 (2026-10-22)

### Australian Soil Classification: the 15 orders (experimental)

[`classify_asc3()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_asc3.md)
keys a pedon to the orders of the Australian Soil Classification, 3rd
edition (Isbell and the National Committee on Soil and Terrain 2021),
following the online version with its errata. It is the second national
system on the registry
([`soilkey_systems()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/soilkey_systems.md),
alias `asc`) and, like the Canadian one, runs in
[`classify_all()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_all.md)
only when asked. Suborders, great groups, subgroups and families follow
in later releases. WRB, SiBCS and USDA results do not change.

- The key reads the Australian horizon notation of the Field Handbook
  (A1, A2e, B21t, B3, Bhs, 2B2b …), and FAO or USDA designations by the
  role of each horizon (an E as an A2, a Bt as a B2t).
- New horizon attributes: `field_texture` (the Field Handbook’s texture
  grades, such as SL, SCL or LMC, with + or -), `subplasticity`,
  `soil_water_status` (the moisture of the horizon when described) and
  `effervescence_class`. Where a limit is a texture grade the field
  texture decides and lab clay stands in; where it is in % clay, lab
  clay decides and the field texture stands in as the clay range of its
  grade.
- The clear or abrupt textural B (Kurosols, Sodosols, Chromosols) reads
  the glossary’s clay figures, or its field-texture equivalents when lab
  clay is missing on either side of the boundary.
- From the site the key reads the drainage class and tidal flooding
  (Hydrosols), a cracking surface condition (Vertosols) and the notation
  of the designations.
- [`make_asc3_example()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/make_asc3_example.md)
  gives one small profile per order.
- The choices where the text is silent are listed in
  `inst/rules/asc3/readings.yaml` (21 readings). Two were settled on the
  survey data below: only a very poorly drained site counts as saturated
  for the Hydrosols (poorly drained is undecided), and the Vertosols’
  cracks are not required in a solum described moist (the key’s “unless
  too moist”).

Checked against NatSoil (CSIRO, NatSoil v13, CC BY 4.0; the data are not
shipped, and a reader will follow): of 9,698 profiles with an order from
the surveys, 42.9 % get the same order (44.8 % counting the 2021
Arenosols against the Tenosols and Rudosols of earlier editions). 988
are decided, with no earlier order left open, and 78.6 % of them agree
(80.1 %; 82.9 % of the 404 decided with the surveyors’ highest
confidence). Most profiles stay provisional for missing data: the
drainage class (Hydrosols), the designations (Podosols), the cracks
(Vertosols), free iron (Ferrosols), carbonate records (Calcarosols) and
exchangeable sodium (Sodosols).

## soilKey 0.9.276 (2026-10-21)

### Canadian classification: the colour of the Chernozemic great groups (experimental)

The key’s chroma limits for the Chernozemic great groups say “usually”.
[`classify_cssc3()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_cssc3.md)
now reads them at two more places, each written down in
`inst/rules/cssc3/readings.yaml`:

- a dry value of exactly 3.5, the limit of both the Black Chernozems
  (“darker than 3.5”, Ch 5, p. 68) and the Dark Brown (3.5 to 4.5), is
  Black when the dry chroma is 1.5 or less, the chroma of the Black,
  unless an Ahe, Aej or Ae marks the eluviation of the Dark Gray, whose
  range holds 3.5;
- in a cultivated soil, an Ap whose own dry chroma is 1.5 or less counts
  as the sign of eluviation of the Dark Gray Chernozems, whose Ahe the
  plough has mixed in (the key gives that Ap its own value limit, and Ch
  5, p. 69, admits a mixed Ap); an Ahe, Aej or Ae in the profile still
  counts, and a buried one no longer does.

The colour means are rounded to the millionth before they meet a limit.
On the NPDB scenario of 0.9.275, of the 348 Chernozems decided at the
order level, 116 (was 92) get the survey’s great group, 84 of them (was
63) with the great group decided. WRB, SiBCS and USDA results do not
change.

## soilKey 0.9.275 (2026-10-21)

### An NPDB scenario with the dry colour and the soil climate estimated (experimental)

The National Pedon Database of Canada records neither the dry colour of
most A horizons nor the soil climate, which the Canadian key reads for
the Chernozems (and the Gray Brown Luvisols and some subgroups). An
optional scenario now estimates them, each as a range, and
[`benchmark_npdb()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/benchmark_npdb.md)
classifies a pedon at the ends of its ranges, counting a class as
decided only where they all agree.
[`classify_cssc3()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_cssc3.md)
itself does not change, and WRB, SiBCS and USDA results do not change.

- [`fetch_aafc_normals()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/fetch_aafc_normals.md)
  reads the climate normals of Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada (Derived
  Normal Climate Data, 5 km grid, Open Government Licence - Canada) at
  given points from the AAFC map service, without downloading files.
- [`npdb_soil_climate()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/npdb_soil_climate.md)
  turns them into the soil climate of the book’s Tables 3 and 4: the
  mean annual soil temperature as the range from the air temperature to
  4 degrees above it, and the climatic moisture index (growing-season
  precipitation over potential evapotranspiration, months of April to
  October above 5 degrees) with its moisture subclass. The potential
  evapotranspiration is computed by Thornthwaite, which matches the
  zones the book gives the Chernozem great groups on the NPDB, and by
  Hargreaves, the other end of the range.
- [`npdb_dry_colour_model()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/npdb_dry_colour_model.md)
  fits the dry value and chroma of A horizons on their moist colour
  where the NPDB records both (dry value = 1.70 + 0.92 x moist value;
  error about one value unit), and
  [`npdb_scenario()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/npdb_scenario.md)
  adds the estimates to the pedons, never replacing recorded values.

On the NPDB with the 1961-1990 normals, 295 of the 899 Chernozems that
waited for the climate are decided, 292 of them in their own order:
agreement on the Chernozems goes from 0 to 24.1 % at the order level.
The error of the dry colour seldom decides the limits between the Black,
Dark Brown and Brown Chernozems (7.4 % at the great group level). The
Gray Brown Luvisols go from 0 to 228 of 265 in agreement (53 decided).
On the other orders, agreement goes from 90.6 to 90.1 % at the order
level (56 soils of other orders are now decided as Chernozems) and from
71.9 to 74.6 % at the great group level.

## soilKey 0.9.274 (2026-10-21)

### Canadian classification: three readings raised by the NPDB benchmark (experimental)

[`classify_cssc3()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_cssc3.md)
changes three readings, each written down in
`inst/rules/cssc3/readings.yaml` (now 58 readings). WRB, SiBCS and USDA
results do not change.

- **Chroma 1 or less.** Clause a of the gleying test (Ch 3 key E, p. 34)
  counts only in materials that develop higher chromas when oxidised,
  which a colour cannot show: a pale calcareous C or a grey parent
  material is grey of its own. A horizon gleyed by clause a alone is now
  read with its designation: gleyed with a strong g, not gleyed when
  designated without one (a weak gj included; with mottles unknown,
  which could pass another clause, the designation decides as for
  unknown colours), and, with no designation, gleyed unless it holds 2 %
  CaCO3 or more (then undecided). The other clauses still read the
  colours alone. The Btg of the Luvic Gleysols reads its colours the
  same way.
- **Gleying and the Bt.** In a soil with a Bt that begins within 50 cm,
  the gley colours must be in the Bt (Ch 7, p. 83: a Luvic Gleysol when
  they are in the Btg within 50 cm, a Gleyed Luvisol when they are only
  in the Aeg or below 50 cm). Soils with a solonetzic B are left out,
  since Ch 7 places them in the Gleysolic order by their gleying. The 10
  cm minimum of Ch 7 (p. 81), which is not in the key, stays unapplied:
  on the NPDB it turned away 64 Gleysols the survey confirms, mostly
  because the depth recorded for the deepest horizon is the sampling
  depth.
- **Base saturation (neutral salt).** Criterion 6 of the chernozemic A
  is read as by an unbuffered salt, as the range each horizon’s data
  allow: the bases over the effective CEC are the value; the bases over
  the bases plus the exchangeable Al are an upper bound (the H is left
  out); a base saturation at pH 7 is a lower bound (the unbuffered value
  is higher); a pH in CaCl2 of 5.5 or more (without it, 6.0 in water)
  places it above 80 %. Only a value known to be 80 % or less fails; the
  rest is undecided. Negative amounts, pH values outside 0-14 and
  contradictory bounds count as no data, and the KCl Al stands in for
  the exchangeable Al.

On the NPDB (Chernozems apart), agreement with the survey goes from 89.8
% to 90.6 % at the order level (90.5 % to 91.5 % when decided), from
70.7 % to 71.8 % at the great group level (82.1 % to 83.9 %) and from
56.3 % to 56.6 % at the subgroup level (71.3 % to 72.3 %). Decided
disagreements in which the key puts a surveyed soil in the Gleysolic
order fall from 317 to 178 (Luvisols 141 to 72, Brunisols 51 to 29). In
turn, 32 surveyed Gleysols are now decided in the Luvisolic order, 30 of
them by the Bt rule, mostly Luvic Gleysols whose Btg or Btgj does not
have gley colours. Base saturation no longer decides any Chernozem
outside its order (11 still fail criterion 6 because Ca is not the
dominant cation): 340 Chernozems (was 445) are decided outside the order
on other criteria, and 899 (was 794) wait for the soil climate.

## soilKey 0.9.273 (2026-10-21)

### The National Pedon Database of Canada as a benchmark (experimental)

[`load_npdb_pedons()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/load_npdb_pedons.md)
reads the pre-packaged CSV files of the National Pedon Database of
Canada (NPDB, version 3, Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada, CanSIS; Open
Government Licence - Canada; not shipped with soilKey) into pedon
records, with the survey’s classification under the Canadian System of
Soil Classification as the reference, and
[`benchmark_npdb()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/benchmark_npdb.md)
compares
[`classify_cssc3()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_cssc3.md)
with it at the order, great group and subgroup levels.

The reader cleans what the files hold:

- it rebuilds the designations in the Canadian notation;
- it turns organic horizons recorded upward into depths above the
  mineral surface and repairs mineral horizons with reversed depths;
- it reads the coded matrix colours, telling the dry colour from the
  moist one pedon by pedon;
- it drops the no-data code and the copied values of total N and tells
  its units apart;
- it computes base saturation from the bases and the CEC where the
  recorded column says something else, and swaps back a dataset’s pH
  columns;
- it turns the survey’s words into the 1998 names where they name a
  class of the key (the Solodic subgroups as the Solonetzic ones they
  became).

The NPDB records no soil climate, which the key reads for the
Chernozemic order and the Gray Brown Luvisols: the 1,239 Chernozems are
reported apart. 794 of them are provisional; the other 445 are decided
outside the order, mostly because a measured property of the A fails the
chernozemic A, the most frequent being base saturation (neutral salt) of
80 % or less. On the other pedons with a reference:

| Level       | Pedons | Agreement | Decided | Agreement when decided |
|-------------|--------|-----------|---------|------------------------|
| Order       | 7,298  | 89.8%     | 6,524   | 90.5%                  |
| Great group | 7,272  | 70.7%     | 5,327   | 82.1%                  |
| Subgroup    | 4,041  | 56.3%     | 2,587   | 71.3%                  |

Most disagreements come with a provisional result, where the records
lack what the key reads: the mean annual soil temperature of the Gray
Brown Luvisols (all 265 are undecided), the pH in CaCl2 of the
Brunisols’ B, the organic C of the Humic Gleysols. Among the decided
ones, the largest group is the gleying of the Gleysolic order: Luvisols
and Brunisols with a g horizon within 50 cm, which the key places in the
Gleysolic order and the survey did not.

## soilKey 0.9.272 (2026-10-21)

### The Canadian orders and great groups: open bottoms, other notations, climate (experimental)

[`classify_cssc3()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_cssc3.md)
reads, at the order and great-group levels, what the subgroups already
read since 0.9.271:

- the deepest horizon with no bottom depth may go on: the Bt, the
  podzolic B, the chernozemic A, the Brunisolic B and the Btg of the
  Luvic Gleysols are undecided when their thickness could change the
  answer, so a profile such as LFH, Ae, Bt (20 cm, no bottom) is no
  longer a decided Orthic Regosol;
- the Bt is decided horizon by horizon, by its properties when they
  decide and otherwise by its designation: the clay increase is measured
  against the eluvial horizon above (Ch 2, p. 15), not against any
  lower-clay horizon; a horizon fails when its clay films are recorded
  as absent or when every clay needed shows no increase, and is
  undecided when the clay it should be compared with is missing; the 5
  cm are then reached by adjacent Bt horizons added up, a Bt “within 50
  cm” is a run that begins there, and a thin Btg on top of a Bt makes a
  Luvic Gleysol;
- the podzolic B is likewise decided layer by layer, so a Bf ruled out
  by its chemistry no longer counts by its designation;
- in the FAO and USDA notations a B with a t is a Bt and a Bs or Bh is
  podzolic B material by designation, a B with neither is not; an A, E,
  C or O is never podzolic B material nor a Bt; designations written in
  capitals (“BHS”) are read; an EB or BE is the AB of a Solod; an E is
  the Ae of the Chernozemic and Solonetzic tests, so a Chernozem
  described as A, Bw, Bk, C reaches the Chernozemic order;
- the word “and” of a split horizon (“Ae and Bt”) no longer switches the
  Canadian notation off;
- the soil moisture subclass is read whatever its spelling (“Sub-humid”,
  “semi-arid”).

In about 3,000 test profiles, 88 change order or great group: 82
described in another notation with a Bt, now a provisional Luvisol or
Luvic Gleysol instead of a Regosol or Gleysol, and 6 whose designated Bt
shows no clay increase over the eluvial horizon above, now ruled out by
that measured clay. In Canadian-notation profiles the subgroups and
great groups can also change where clay films are recorded as absent,
where clay was given on an organic layer, or where the eluvial horizon
has no clay recorded (the designation then decides). WRB, SiBCS and USDA
results do not change.

## soilKey 0.9.271 (2026-10-21)

### The Canadian subgroups: Solonetzic, Chernozemic and Luvisolic (experimental)

[`classify_cssc3()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_cssc3.md)
now keys the subgroups of the last three orders of the Canadian System
of Soil Classification, 3rd edition (Key to Soil Subgroups, Ch 3,
pp. 42-49), 101 more, so all 231 subgroups are keyed and the name goes
down to the subgroup in every order (“Dark Gray Solod”, “Calcareous
Black Chernozem”, “Gleyed Brunisolic Gray Luvisol”). The subgroups read,
as before, measured properties first and the Canadian designations
second:

- Solonetzic: the dry colour value of the A (Brown, Dark Brown, Black,
  and Gray and Dark Gray with a low chroma and a subhumid climate in the
  Solods and Solodized Solonetz), a strongly alkaline A (pH above 8.5),
  faint to distinct mottles within 50 cm;
- Chernozemic: a slickenside horizon, a weak solonetzic B (Bnj, Bnjtj,
  Btnj), eluvial horizons of 2 cm, a Bmk of 5 cm (0.5 % CaCO3 or more,
  or a k), no B of 5 cm, faint to distinct mottles within 50 cm;
- Luvisolic: a slickenside horizon, a fragipan, a podzolic B over a Bt
  within 50 cm, a Bm of chroma 3 or a thin Bf in the upper solum, an Ah
  of 5 cm, a Btnj, distinct mottles within 50 cm or prominent ones at
  50-100 cm.

The Solonetzic great groups have no residual subgroup in the key, so a
Solonetzic soil without an A stops at the great group; where an LFH lies
directly over an Ae, the Gray subgroups read the Ae, as Ch 12 words
them. The colour of the A is read over the whole A: a horizon with no
value leaves the class undecided when it could change it. The readings
where the book is silent are added to `inst/rules/cssc3/readings.yaml`
(now 57). The Solonetzic example of
[`make_cssc3_example()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/make_cssc3_example.md)
gains a dry colour and a pH, so it keys to a Dark Brown Solonetz.

Two changes reach the subgroups keyed since 0.9.269: a horizon with no
bottom depth (the deepest one, which may go on) no longer counts as 0 cm
when horizons are added up towards a thickness, so the Rego and
Eluviated subgroups are undecided instead of decided on it; and a buried
Aeb is no longer the Ae of the Eluviated Brunisols. Orders and great
groups do not change, and WRB, SiBCS and USDA results do not change.

## soilKey 0.9.270 (2026-10-21)

### The Canadian subgroups: Podzolic, Gleysolic, Brunisolic and Regosolic (experimental)

[`classify_cssc3()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_cssc3.md)
now keys the subgroups of four more orders of the Canadian System of
Soil Classification, 3rd edition (Key to Soil Subgroups, Ch 3,
pp. 40-51), 67 more, 130 of the 231 in all, so the name goes down to the
subgroup in seven orders (“Ortstein Humo-Ferric Podzol”, “Fera Humic
Gleysol”, “Gleyed Eluviated Dystric Brunisol”, “Cumulic Regosol”); the
Solonetzic, Chernozemic and Luvisolic orders still stop at the great
group. The subgroups read, as before, measured properties first and the
Canadian designations second:

- Podzolic: an ortstein (no depth limit), placic and duric horizons and
  a fragipan within the control section (cementation class, or a c in
  the designation), a deep Bt, an Ah of 10 cm, distinct to prominent
  mottles within 1 m;
- Gleysolic: a slickenside horizon, a solonetzic B, a fragipan below the
  Btg, the Humic Gleysol A, a Bgf horizon (dithionite Fe over the parent
  material, or gf), no B of 10 cm;
- Brunisolic: a duric horizon, an Ae or Aej of 2 cm, gleying mottles
  within 50 cm or at 50-100 cm;
- Regosolic: cumulic layering (colour value, organic C with depth, or a
  buried A) and faint to distinct mottles within 50 cm.

The readings where the book is silent are added to
`inst/rules/cssc3/readings.yaml` (now 54). The Vertic Solonetz great
group now reads its slickenside horizon horizon by horizon, as the
Vertic Gleysol subgroups do: a horizon with no designation and no
slickenside record is undecided instead of ‘none’, and a designation in
the FAO or USDA notation is read (an ss counts, a designation without ss
fails). The surface A of the great groups no longer takes in a buried A
(b) under it, so an Ah over an Ahb is measured by the Ah alone. WRB,
SiBCS and USDA results do not change.

## soilKey 0.9.269 (2026-10-21)

### The Canadian subgroups: Cryosolic, Organic and Vertisolic (experimental)

[`classify_cssc3()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_cssc3.md)
now keys the subgroups of three orders of the Canadian System of Soil
Classification, 3rd edition (Key to Soil Subgroups, Ch 3, pp. 37-40), 63
of the 231, so the name goes down to the subgroup there (“Terric Humic
Mesisol”, “Brunisolic Dystric Turbic Cryosol”, “Gleyed Vertisol”); the
other orders still stop at the great group. The subgroups read, as the
orders and great groups do, measured properties first and the Canadian
designations second:

- Cryosolic: ice layers, the mineral contact and the peat above it, the
  dominant peat below 40 cm, gleying, organic horizons over 15 cm, the
  pH of the B horizons, the thickness of the Bm, a Bt under an eluvial
  horizon;
- Organic: O horizons under folic ones, woody material, the dominant
  folic horizon, hydric, terric, limnic and cumulic layers, and the
  thickness of each kind of peat;
- Vertisolic: prominent, or faint to distinct, mottles within 50 cm.

The readings where the book is silent are added to
`inst/rules/cssc3/readings.yaml` (now 46). The Cryosolic example pedon
gains pH values. WRB, SiBCS and USDA results do not change.

Fixes to the orders and great groups of 0.9.267 and 0.9.268:

- the Organic great groups leave limnic and folic layers out of the peat
  tally (they are neither fibric, mesic nor humic); a limnic layer is
  not a terric contact, and a middle tier of limnic material only is
  read with the surface tier;
- gleying (Gleysolic order) is decided horizon by horizon: a horizon’s
  measured colours outrank its own g, and a horizon with no colours and
  no designation is undecided instead of ‘not gleyed’;
- the rows are read in depth order whatever the order they are given in
  (on a copy; the layer numbers of the trace follow that order);
- the thick-A rule of the gleying test reads the whole surface A
  (adjacent Ah and Ap from the mineral surface; a buried A, b, never
  counts) and tests the mineral horizon right below it, whatever it is,
  a gap in the record allowed; in another notation the A masters are
  left out of the test and the E masters as the Ae are (a thick, deep E
  is tested);
- a horizon with no bottom depth ends where the next one down begins,
  and the deepest one may go on (both options of the Organic order, the
  organic column and the peat tally read it as possibly deep);
- limnic layers are read from whole words of their recorded origin, not
  on rock, and from the L master of the FAO and USDA notations;
- in designations of another notation, W and R are never mineral
  horizons, and an O or H without organic C is organic.

## soilKey 0.9.268 (2026-10-21)

### The Canadian great groups (experimental)

[`classify_cssc3()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_cssc3.md)
now keys the 31 great groups of the Canadian System of Soil
Classification, 3rd edition (Key to Soil Great Groups, Ch 3, pp. 35-36),
under the ten orders of 0.9.267, so the name is the great group
(“Humo-Ferric Podzol”, “Dark Brown Chernozem”) and the order is in
`rsg_or_order`. The great groups read, as the orders do, measured
properties first and the Canadian designations second:

- Cryosolic: organic material over permafrost, cryoturbation (y);
- Organic: the folic thickness of Ch 9 (L, F, H), the dominant material
  of the middle tier (fibric, mesic or humic, by rubbed fibre, then
  designation), widened to the surface tier only by a terric, lithic or
  hydric layer;
- Vertisolic: surface dry value or Ah thickness, by drainage class, and
  the Ch 13 rule for the Ap of a poorly drained cultivated soil;
- Podzolic: at least 10 cm of Bh or Bhf chemistry;
- Gleysolic: a gleyed Bt (Btg), a humic Ah or Ap with at least 2 %
  organic C;
- Solonetzic: a slickenside horizon, an Ae of at least 2 cm, an AB or
  BA;
- Chernozemic: the dry value and chroma of the chernozemic A and signs
  of eluviation;
- Luvisolic: a forest mull Ah and a mean annual soil temperature of 8 C;
- Brunisolic: a thick dark Ah or Ap and the pH (CaCl2) of the upper B;
- Regosolic: an Ah or Ap of 10 cm.

The last great group of each order is the key’s “other soils”. The
readings where the book is silent are added to
`inst/rules/cssc3/readings.yaml` (now 33). The per-layer readings of
podzolic B chemistry and of gley colours are factored out of the order
diagnostics without changing them. The example pedons now reach a great
group each. WRB, SiBCS and USDA results do not change.

Fixes to the 0.9.267 order key, all in the Organic order:

- a folic layer (L, F, H) lying on peat is read as litter over peat, so
  F 0-5 cm over Om 5-160 cm is an Organic soil (it was keyed as
  Regosolic); the litter is not counted towards the peat limits;
- the kind of the surface organic layer is read from measured rubbed
  fibre before its designation (an Om with 60 % rubbed fibre is fibric);
- a layer of unknown organic status leaves the order undecided where it
  could change the answer, instead of failing it;
- in designations of another notation, the masters A, B, C and E are
  read as mineral, R as rock and W as water when organic C is missing.

## soilKey 0.9.267 (2026-10-20)

### The Canadian System of Soil Classification, to the order (experimental)

The first national system on the registry:
[`classify_cssc3()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_cssc3.md)
keys a profile through the Key to Soil Orders of the Canadian System of
Soil Classification, 3rd edition (Soil Classification Working Group
1998, Ch 3, pp. 33-34), from Cryosolic to Regosolic. Great groups and
subgroups follow in later releases, so the name is the order. The system
is experimental and opt-in:
[`classify_all()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_all.md)
and the Pro app keep running WRB, SiBCS and USDA by default;
`classify_all(systems = c("wrb2022", "sibcs5", "usda", "cssc3"))` runs
it beside them, and
[`classify_cssc3()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_cssc3.md)
alone.

The Canadian keys are written largely in terms of horizon designations,
which Chapter 2 defines partly by measurable properties. Each diagnostic
reads the measured properties first (podzolic B chemistry, the Bt clay
increase with clay films, the solonetzic B Ca/Na ratio, the chernozemic
A, the gley colours) and the designations second, in the Canadian
notation, where f is an illuvial Fe-Al-organic accumulation, m a
slightly altered B, v a vertic horizon, ss slickensides, y
cryoturbation, z permafrost and j a weak expression of the suffix before
it. Measured properties decide whenever they can, pass or fail;
designations decide only what they leave open, and only when the
profile’s notation is Canadian (declared in `site$designation_system`, a
Canadian site, or no sign of the FAO/USDA notation), because the same
letters mean other things there. The trace records which route decided,
and a warning says when the order rests on designations alone. The
chernozemic A includes a soil-climate criterion (mean annual soil
temperature at least 0 C, moisture subclass drier than humid), read from
the new site fields `mean_annual_soil_temp_C` and
`soil_moisture_subclass` or approximated from the USDA regimes; without
it, the orders keyed after Chernozemic are reported as provisional. The
choices where the book is silent are listed in
`inst/rules/cssc3/readings.yaml`.

Three horizon attributes are added for the Canadian key and read by no
other: `fe_pyro_pct` and `al_pyro_pct` (sodium-pyrophosphate-extractable
Fe and Al) and `mottle_contrast` (faint, distinct, prominent).
[`make_cssc3_example()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/make_cssc3_example.md)
builds one example profile per order. WRB, SiBCS and USDA results do not
change: the 44 canonical fixtures are identical.

## soilKey 0.9.266 (2026-10-20)

### One file of metadata for the horizon attributes

The section, unit and description of each of the 112 canonical horizon
columns now live in `inst/schemas/horizon-attributes.yaml`, and the new
[`horizon_attribute_spec()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/horizon_attribute_spec.md)
returns them as a table with each column’s type and accepted aliases.
The file also has room for what the national systems will need: the keys
that read an attribute, the values of a categorical one and the range of
a numeric one. The attribute reference `inst/ATTRIBUTES.md` is generated
from it (before, the generator parsed the comments of `R/utils.R` and
kept its own table of units), and a test fails when the file and the
reference fall out of step. The reference’s tables are unchanged. No
classification changes.

## soilKey 0.9.265 (2026-10-20)

### A generic classifier for ordered keys

Most of the national systems on the roadmap (Canada, Australia, New
Zealand, Japan, Hungary, China) are ordered keys of the USDA kind: at
each level the first class whose tests pass is assigned. Their
classifiers will be thin wrappers around a new internal engine,
`classify_hierarchical()`, that walks the levels named in the system’s
registry entry. Two rules differ from the three older keys, on purpose:
a class is assigned only when its tests pass (a `default: true` entry
passes by definition), so a level where nothing passes stays unassigned
instead of falling back to the last class of its list (with a warning
saying where the name stopped); and a class that could not be decided
for lack of data, tested before the one assigned, makes the assignment
provisional. Run on the USDA rules, it gives the same name, order and
evidence grade as
[`classify_usda()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_usda.md)
for all 44 canonical fixtures.

`ClassificationResult` gains three fields: `system_id` (the registry id;
WRB, SiBCS, USDA and SmartSolos results now carry it), `levels` (the
class assigned at each level) and `provisional_because`. Its
[`print()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/print.html) counts the classes
actually tested (for SiBCS and USDA it counted the phases of the nested
trace) and calls them RSGs only for WRB. No classification changes.

## soilKey 0.9.264 (2026-10-20)

### The rule engine reads nested blocks and `none_of`

National keys say things such as “other soils that have A, and B or C,
and not D”. The rule engine now reads that in YAML: an entry of an
`all_of`, `any_of` or `none_of` list may itself be one of these blocks,
and `none_of` (no test may pass) joins `all_of` and `any_of`, with the
same three-valued logic (an undecided test leaves the block undecided
unless the outcome is already settled). A nested block appears in the
key trace as a test of its own, with its sub-results as evidence.

The lower levels of a key are now read from the folders that the
system’s registry entry names (`great_groups` from `great-groups/`), not
from a fixed list of six folder names. The rule validator also reports
blocks that name more than one combinator (the engine reads only one of
them), combinators written as a mapping instead of a list, class codes
and names that are not quoted strings (YAML reads an unquoted `N` as a
logical and `11` as a number), codes listed twice in one list or one
level, and, for systems added after the registry, predicates without the
system’s suffix, so that a Canadian Chernozemic gate can never be WRB’s
[`chernozem()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/chernozem.md).
The helpers that every key shares (evidence grade, ambiguities, missing
attributes) move from `R/key-wrb2022.R` to `R/key-common.R`, unchanged.

No result changes: the 44 canonical fixtures give identical names, key
traces, evidence grades and warnings, and no rule of the three systems
nests, mixes combinators or uses `none_of`.

## soilKey 0.9.263 (2026-10-20)

### A registry of classification systems

Each classification system is now a folder `inst/rules/<id>/` holding
its key and a `system.yaml` entry: id, aliases, classifier, levels,
display names, edition, citation and status.
[`load_rules()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/load_rules.md),
[`classify_all()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/classify_all.md)
and the rule validator read that registry instead of repeating the three
ids, and the new
[`soilkey_systems()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/soilkey_systems.md)
lists it. This is the first step towards the national systems (Canada,
Australia, New Zealand and others): a new system will be added by adding
its folder.

Nothing else changes. The 44 canonical fixtures give the same names, key
traces, evidence grades and warnings as in 0.9.262, and every id or
alias accepted so far still works, including the partial ones such as
`"wrb"`. `classify_all(systems = "sibcs5")` is now accepted as well as
`"sibcs"`.
[`load_rules()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/load_rules.md)
now writes its default as `"wrb2022"`; it was the vector of the three
ids, of which the first was used.

## soilKey 0.9.262 (2026-10-15)

### The WRB 2022 reference points to the 2022 edition

The README and the Portuguese getting-started vignette gave, for WRB
2022 (IUSS Working Group WRB, 4th edition), an FAO OpenKnowledge PDF
that is the 2014 edition: its own title reads “World reference base for
soil resources 2014”. Both now give the 2022 edition at ISRIC,
`https://files.isric.org/public/documents/WRB_fourth_edition_2022-12-18.pdf`.
The classification keys do not change.

## soilKey 0.9.261 (2026-10-14)

### Pro app: a visitor counter in the footer

The footer of the hosted app (soilkeypro.com) says, in one line, how
many people are on the site now, how many have visited and from how many
countries; a click on the countries opens a map of them above the
footer. Asked for by the maintainer.

- **A person is counted once.** On the first visit the browser keeps a
  mark in its own storage (no identifier) and tells the server it is a
  new visitor; a later visit from the same browser counts as a session
  only. Nothing that identifies the visitor is sent or kept.

- **The country** comes from the address of the request, looked up in
  DB-IP’s *IP to Country Lite* table (CC BY 4.0), which the image
  downloads when it is built and the footer credits. The address is read
  for that and kept nowhere.

- **Not counted:** automated browsers (headless Chrome, crawlers,
  command-line clients, the capacity test, the Claude app’s browser),
  and pages that never open a Shiny session.

- **The numbers** are kept in Firestore, in the app’s own Google Cloud
  project: one document of totals (visitors, sessions, visitors by
  country, the day counting began) and one document per running instance
  with how many sessions it holds, written every 30 s. “Online now” adds
  up the instances that wrote in the last 90 s. Only soilkeypro.com
  writes to these; a tagged revision writes to separate test
  collections, and a local run to none.

- **Before the counter**, the request logs of Cloud Run (30 days) are
  read once by `deploy/cloudrun/visitors-backfill.R`: a session is a
  request to `/websocket/` answered with 101, a visitor a distinct
  address. The logs begin on 2026-10-07, when the site came back online.

- **The map waits for a click.** The footer is on screen in every tab,
  and a map in it (190 px in all) took the height the tabs’ own tables
  need: with a 790 px window the key trace of Classify had none left,
  and DT does not draw a table of height 0. The map now opens in a panel
  above the line’s “from N countries” button (below it when there is no
  room above) and closes on a second click, a click elsewhere, Escape
  or, on a phone, a scroll of the page; the footer grows by one line
  only. On a phone the map keeps its 210 px (the app’s narrow-screen
  rule sets every map’s height to “auto”).

- **Classify’s key trace** is drawn at its own height, not the height
  left over in its card (`DTOutput(fill = FALSE)`). With a short window,
  or a footer one line taller, it was 36 px or less before.

New files: `R/utils_visitors.R` and `R/mod_visitors.R` in the app, its
country table `data/countries.csv` (built by
`data-raw/visitor_countries.R`; see `inst/DATA-PROVENANCE.md`), the
image step in `deploy/fly/Dockerfile`, and eight strings in each
language. The classification keys do not change.

CARTO’s base maps now answer a request without an API key with a tile

The CRAN pre-test of 0.9.258 (2026-10-14) did not pass automatically on

## soilKey 0.9.257 (2026-10-13)

### SiBCS key: the activity of the clay and the base saturation in the larger part of the first 100 cm of the B

The key gives the Luvissolos a “horizonte B textural com argila de
atividade alta e saturação por bases alta na maior parte dos primeiros
100 cm do horizonte B (inclusive BA)” (SiBCS 2018, Cap. 4, p. 113), asks
the same section of the Nitossolos (p. 114), and the definitions of the
classes of the lower levels repeat it. Cap. 1 (p. 30) takes the activity
of the clay “no horizonte B (inclusive BA e exclusive BC) ou no
horizonte C (inclusive CA), quando não existe B”, and does not apply it
to “materiais de solo das classes texturais areia e areia franca”.

`atividade_argila_alta()` and
[`eutrofico()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/eutrofico.md)
passed with **one layer** of B or of C, anywhere in the profile:

- the C of a profile, with little clay and a high ratio of CEC to clay,
  made the clay of the whole profile one of high activity;
- one eutrophic layer, the C as often as not, made the profile
  eutrophic;
- the two did not have to be found in the same part of the profile.

With both, an Argissolo with a B of low base saturation keyed Luvissolos
(AC 10374, an Argissolo Álico of high activity: B1, B2 and B3 with V of
49, 40 and 37%, and a C with 76%). The same reading kept a B nítico from
being one, as it asks for clay of low activity, and sent to the
Luvissolos the Nitossolos that come after them in the key. Of the 260
complete profiles keyed Luvissolos in the default mode, 86 had that
reference.

Now, in a profile with a B horizon:

- The section is the first 100 cm of the B: the B layers, the BA with
  them and the BC not, that begin within 100 cm of the top of the
  uppermost one, each with the thickness it has inside the section.
- The activity is high, or the base saturation is, when the layers where
  it is so make **more than half** of the thickness of the section,
  among the layers that say. Half is not the larger part. A layer with
  no CEC, no clay or no V recorded is left out of both sides of the
  count.
- A layer of areia or of areia franca is left out of the activity. It is
  told by its sand, silt and clay. It was told by a clay under 15%,
  which also left out the franco-arenosa and the franca with little
  clay.

A profile with no B is read as before, in its C layers. The sections
that the book gives for those classes, each its own (Gleissolos: “dentro
de 100 cm a partir da superfície”), are not in this version.

The two functions are read by the Chernossolos and Luvissolos steps, by
the B nítico, and by the classes of the third level (Eutróficos,
Distróficos, Ta, Tb) of every order, which follow the same section.

#### Measured

National BDsolos export, 7,593 profiles with a reference order:

|                                  | 0.9.256                | 0.9.257       |
|----------------------------------|------------------------|---------------|
| default mode                     | 4,029 (53.1%)          | 4,098 (54.0%) |
| morphological mode               | 4,967 (65.4%)          | 5,044 (66.4%) |
| complete profiles, default       | 2,925 of 4,674 (62.6%) | 2,992 (64.0%) |
| complete profiles, morphological | 3,313 (70.9%)          | 3,386 (72.4%) |

Default mode: 110 profiles change order; 76 reach their reference, 7
leave it and 27 go from one other order to another. 84 go from
Luvissolos to Argissolos and 13 from Luvissolos to Nitossolos. Reference
Argissolos keyed so: 1,099 to 1,161 of 2,016; Nitossolos, 79 to 91 of
347; Luvissolos, 98 to 94 of 197. Morphological mode: 117 change, 84
reach their reference and the same 7 leave it.

The seven that leave their reference, by what the sheets record:

- RN 6022 and RN 7434 (one profile under two names, a Luvissolo
  Crômico): activity of 31.9 in the first 22 cm of the B, 26.7 in the
  next 50 and 29.6 below. High in 50 of the first 100 cm, which is half.
- PE 9076 (Luvissolo Crômico): 27.0 in the 10 cm of the IIB21t and 25.7
  in the 20 cm of the IIB22t.
- MG 7400 (Podzólico Vermelho-Amarelo Eutrófico Ta): 22.2, 19.8 and 24.3
  in its B, under the 27 of the book.
- RN 9776 (Argissolo equivalente eutrófico, argila de atividade alta): V
  of 36, 43 and 81% in its B; high in 39 of 83 cm.
- PR 5728 and PR 6773 (one profile, a Cambissolo Tb Eutrófico with an A

  an activity of 61.5. It was left out by its clay under 15%; read, it
  is of high activity and the profile a Chernossolo.

Third level. The name changes in 215 profiles that keep their order
(default mode). Where the reference states the base saturation and the
order is right before and after, the name agrees with it in 1,005 then
1,015 of 1,022 profiles; for the activity of the clay, in 295 then 304
of 357. Morphological mode: 1,269 then 1,284 of 1,309, and 325 then 334
of 400.

Panel of complete profiles (781): 437 to 447 and 514 to 524. Redape
(94): 79 to 81 and 84 to 87, Argissolos that were keyed Luvissolos. FEBR
(1,000): 376 and 501, unchanged. The 44 canonical profiles are identical

## soilKey 0.9.256 (2026-10-13)

### SiBCS key: more marks of the older notation of horizons

Since 0.9.250 the “A2” of a profile written in the notation in use until
1988 is read as the E of today, and its “B3” as the BC. The profile was
known to be in that notation by a B followed at once by a number (“B1”,
“B21t”) or by a “(B)”. A podzol described “A1, A21, A22, Bhir” has
neither: its A2 was read as a part of the A, and with no E above it its
Bhir was no B espódico by item (a) of the book (0.9.255).

Decided on 2026-10-13: three more marks.

- An A or a C followed at once by two figures (“A11”, “A12”, “A21”,
  “C11”). The older notation numbers the parts of a horizon after the
  figure of the horizon; the present one counts them from 1 after the
  letters.
- The suffix “ir” in a B (“Bir”, “Bhir”, “B2ir”), the illuvial iron that
  is written “s” today.
- The suffix “pl” in a B or a C (“Bpl”, “B21pl”, “Cpl”), the plinthite
  that is written “f” today.

**The suffix “cn” of the concretions is not a mark.** It was measured
with the other three and is found in profiles otherwise written in the
present notation: GO 12592, a Latossolo Vermelho described “A1, A2, AB,
BA, Bw1, Bw2, BC, C1, Ccn, C2”, whose A2 has 43% of clay and 1.6% of
organic carbon and is the second part of the A, would have had it read
as an E and left its order.

Like the correspondence of the A2 and of the B3 itself, these marks are
not in SiBCS 2018, which gives the present notation only.

#### Measured

National BDsolos export. 154 of its 7,694 classified profiles are newly
taken for the older notation (116 by the two figures, 16 by “ir”, 31 by
“pl”); 34 of them have an A2 or a B3 to read.

Of the 7,593 with a reference order:

|                                  | 0.9.255                | 0.9.256       |
|----------------------------------|------------------------|---------------|
| default mode                     | 4,022 (53.0%)          | 4,029 (53.1%) |
| morphological mode               | 4,967 (65.4%)          | 4,967 (65.4%) |
| complete profiles, default       | 2,918 of 4,674 (62.4%) | 2,925 (62.6%) |
| complete profiles, morphological | 3,313 (70.9%)          | 3,313 (70.9%) |

Default mode: 9 profiles change order; 7 reach their reference and none
leaves it. The 7 are Espodossolos keyed Neossolos, Gleissolos,
Argissolos and Planossolos, whose E is now seen above the B (AM 10913:
A1, A21, A22, Bhir; MG 8112: A1, A2, Bh, Bhir; PB 7844: A1, A2, Bp,
Bhir). Reference Espodossolos keyed so: 23 to 30 of 98. Two go from one
other order to another: DF 7017, a Podzol Hidromórfico whose Bh has 0.1%
of organic carbon, and PA 10278, a Plintossolo “A1, A2, A3, Bpl”, both
to Argissolos.

Morphological mode: no profile changes its order or its name. That mode
already read the B espódico of these profiles from the “h” and the “ir”
of its designation.

Panel of complete profiles (781): 435 to 437 in the default mode, two
Espodossolos keyed Argissolos and Planossolos; 514 unchanged in the
morphological. FEBR (1,000): 376 and 501, unchanged. Redape (94): 79 and
84, unchanged. The 44 canonical profiles are identical in the three
systems.

## soilKey 0.9.255 (2026-10-13)

### SiBCS key: item (a) of the B espódico

The B espódico (SiBCS 2018, Cap. 2, p. 62-65) is a horizon “com
acumulação iluvial de compostos organometálicos” that has one or more of
three characteristics, the first being “a) Um horizonte E (álbico ou
não) sobrejacente e cores úmidas de acordo com um dos itens a seguir: 1)
Matiz 5YR ou mais vermelho; 2) Matiz 7,5YR com valor 5 ou menor e croma
4 ou menor; 3) Matiz 10YR, com valor e croma 3 ou menor; 4) Cores
neutras com valor 3 ou menor (N 3/)”.

[`B_espodico()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/B_espodico.md)
was the spodic horizon of the WRB, which asks for aluminium and iron by
oxalate, or for a horizon named Bh or Bs under an albic one. The items
of the book were not tested. The sheets of the Brazilian surveys seldom
have the oxalate extraction: of the 98 Espodossolos of the BDsolos
export the default mode keyed 4 as such.

The colours of the item cannot stand alone. “5YR ou mais vermelho” is
the colour of the B textural of many an Argissolo that lies below an E,
and the Espodossolos come before the Argissolos in the key; what tells
the two apart is the illuvial accumulation of the heading, which the
sheets do not measure. Three ways of asking for it were measured on the
389 profiles with an E:

| the B, below an E and with a colour of the item, has | default mode | morphological mode |
|----|----|----|
| 0.5% of organic carbon or more and a pH under 5.9, the limits of the WRB, which the book cites as its source | 19 reach their reference, 17 leave it | 0 and 18 |
| 0.5% or more and at least twice that of the E | 18 and 2 | 1 and 2 |
| the same, with no cerosidade recorded | 18 and 0 | 1 and 0 |

Decided on 2026-10-13: the third. Where the WRB test does not find the
horizon, a B layer of 2.5 cm or more is a B espódico when

- an E lies above it;
- its moist colour is one of the four of item (a);
- its organic carbon is 0.5% or more and at least twice that of the
  nearest E above it, the form the book gives in item (b)(3) for
  aluminium and iron by oxalate (“valor 0,50 ou maior, sendo este valor
  pelo menos o dobro do encontrado no horizonte sobrejacente”); and
- no cerosidade is recorded in it, which is the mark of illuvial clay.

**This is a reading by analogy, not the letter of the book.** It is so
stated in the documentation of the function. Items (b) and (c), the
cementation and the ortstein, are not tested. The reading is the same in
both modes; the morphological mode goes on reading the designation as
well.

#### Measured

National BDsolos export, 7,593 profiles with a reference order:

|                                  | 0.9.254                | 0.9.255       |
|----------------------------------|------------------------|---------------|
| default mode                     | 4,003 (52.7%)          | 4,022 (53.0%) |
| morphological mode               | 4,966 (65.4%)          | 4,967 (65.4%) |
| complete profiles, default       | 2,900 of 4,674 (62.0%) | 2,918 (62.4%) |
| complete profiles, morphological | 3,312 (70.9%)          | 3,313 (70.9%) |

Default mode: 20 profiles change order, all to Espodossolos; 19 reach
their reference and none leaves it. They were keyed Neossolos (12),
Gleissolos (3), Planossolos (3) and Argissolos (1): sandy profiles with
a Bh of massive or single-grain structure (RJ 5339: Bh2 with 3% of clay;
BA 13385: E of 140 cm over a Bh 10YR 2/2 with 2.4% of organic carbon).
Reference Espodossolos keyed so: 4 to 23 of 98. Morphological mode,
where the horizon was already read from its designation: 2 change, 1
reaches its reference (RJ 13200, a Podzol whose horizon is written
“B2”); 73 to 74 of 98.

The one profile that goes from one other order to another, in both
modes: MT 11357, a Plintossolo Pétrico whose “B22cn”, 5YR 6/8, is
recorded with 3.4% of organic carbon below an “A21cn” with 0.6%.

The three Argissolos abrúpticos that the doubling of the carbon alone
took (MT 11249, SC 5444, PE 9019: a Bt of 30 to 51% of clay below a
sandy E) all have cerosidade recorded in that Bt, and stay where they
were.

Panel of complete profiles (781): 429 to 435 in the default mode, 514

Redape (94): 77 to 79 in the default mode, two Espodossolos keyed

A, AE, E, Bh, Bhs); 84 unchanged in the morphological. The 44 canonical

## soilKey 0.9.254 (2026-10-13)

### SiBCS key: an O or H layer recorded upward from the mineral soil is part of the histic horizon

The older descriptions give the organic layers that lie on a mineral
soil upward from its top: “O 120-0”, or “Hd 110-60” above “Hoj 60-0”,
over a “Cg 0-10”. With an upper depth greater than the lower one, such a
layer had a thickness below zero and was never part of the horizonte
hístico. BDsolos RJ 14357, an Organossolo Háplico whose one layer is “O
120-0” with 17% of organic carbon, keyed Neossolos.

Decided on 2026-10-13: the layer is counted.

- In `horizonte_histico()` an O or H layer whose upper depth is greater
  than its lower one lies above the mineral surface, with the thickness
  between its two figures; layers so recorded adjoin one another and the
  mineral soil as they are written.
- The 80 cm of the Organossolos step (0.9.253) are counted from the
  surface of the soil, the top of the uppermost of those layers.
- The depths of the profile are not changed, and no other test reads
  them this way. A layer that is no O or H is not read upward: a mineral
  horizon with its depths the wrong way round is a slip of the sheet.

#### Measured

National BDsolos export, 7,593 profiles with a reference order:

|                                  | 0.9.253                | 0.9.254       |
|----------------------------------|------------------------|---------------|
| default mode                     | 4,001 (52.7%)          | 4,003 (52.7%) |
| morphological mode               | 4,965 (65.4%)          | 4,966 (65.4%) |
| complete profiles, default       | 2,900 of 4,674 (62.0%) | 2,900 (62.0%) |
| complete profiles, morphological | 3,313 (70.9%)          | 3,312 (70.9%) |

Three profiles change order, to Organossolos. Two reach their reference:
RJ 14357 and RJ 5333 (Organossolo Tiomórfico: “Hd 110-60”, “Hoj 60-0”,
“Cg 0-10”). The third leaves it in the morphological mode and goes from
one other order to another in the default mode: MG 7435, a Glei Húmico
with an “O1 44-0” of 8.3% of organic carbon written over an “A 0-20”,
which may be a slip for “4-0”; as recorded it is 44 cm of organic
material. Reference Organossolos keyed so: 27 to 29 of 44.

224 profiles of the export have a layer recorded this way; in 172 of
them it is under 10 cm, the litter over a mineral soil, which is no
horizonte hístico. In the second level, RJ 13045 and RJ 13091 (“H 30-0”
over a Cg) get the class their horizonte hístico of 30 cm gives:
Gleissolos Melânicos, and for RJ 13091 in the default mode, where it
keys Neossolos, Neossolos Litólicos Hísticos.

Panel of complete profiles (781): 429 and 514, unchanged. FEBR (1,000):
376 and 501, unchanged. Redape: 77 and 84 of 94, unchanged. The 44
canonical profiles are identical in the three systems.

## soilKey 0.9.253 (2026-10-13)

### SiBCS key: the histic horizon with the whole of its thickness, and the thickness the key asks of it

The horizonte hístico (SiBCS 2018, Cap. 2, p. 49-50) results from plant
residues laid down at the surface, “ainda que, no presente, possa
encontrar-se recoberto por horizontes ou depósitos minerais”, and has to
be 20 cm thick or more, or 10 cm or more over a lithic contact. The
Organossolos (Cap. 4, p. 111) have a horizonte hístico of “20 cm ou
mais, quando sobrejacente a um contato lítico”, or of “40 cm ou mais,
contínuo ou cumulativo nos primeiros 80 cm a partir da superfície do
solo”.

Two things in the code were not that:

- **Only a layer that starts within 5 cm of the surface was looked at.**
  A horizon described in sub-horizons counted the first of them alone
  (BDsolos ES 8651: Oo1 0-15, Oo2 15-32, Oo3 32-80 cm, with 39 to 45% of
  organic carbon, keyed Neossolos by the 15 cm of its Oo1), and a buried
  horizon was not seen (SE 6560: 2Hdz from 22 cm down).
- **Any horizonte hístico made an Organossolo.** One of 20 to 39 cm over
  a mineral horizon did, although the key asks 40 cm of it and places
  those soils further down (Gleissolos Melânicos, Cambissolos Hísticos).

Now:

- `horizonte_histico()` takes the organic layers wherever they lie;
  adjoining ones make one horizon, with the thickness of all of them; a
  horizon passes with 20 cm, or with 10 cm when the layer right below it
  is an R or a Cr. What makes a layer organic is as before. The evidence
  lists each run of adjoining organic layers with its limits and its
  thickness.
- The Organossolos step asks (a) 20 cm or more of a horizon that lies on
  a lithic contact, or (b) 40 cm or more of horizonte hístico within the
  first 80 cm, in one section or added up.
- Not tested, as before: the volume of plant tissue is no column of the
  profile, so the greater thickness asked where it makes 75% or more of
  the horizon (40 cm in the horizon, 60 cm in the key) is not asked. The
  earlier code read it from the column of worm holes, which is not that,
  in a test that could not change the result.

#### Measured

National BDsolos export, 7,593 profiles with a reference order:

|                                  | 0.9.252                | 0.9.253       |
|----------------------------------|------------------------|---------------|
| default mode                     | 3,989 (52.5%)          | 4,001 (52.7%) |
| morphological mode               | 4,949 (65.2%)          | 4,965 (65.4%) |
| complete profiles, default       | 2,886 of 4,674 (61.7%) | 2,900 (62.0%) |
| complete profiles, morphological | 3,297 (70.5%)          | 3,313 (70.9%) |

27 profiles change order in each mode. Default: 16 reach their
reference, 4 leave it, 7 move between two other orders. Morphological:
20, 4 and 3. The Organossolos of the reference that are keyed so go from
17 to 27 of 44, and the profiles keyed Organossolos that are of another
order from 13 to 4.

The four that leave their reference, by what the sheet records:

- MG 7482 (Solo Orgânico): 20 cm at the surface and organic layers again
  from 61 cm down, 39 cm within the first 80.
- PR 6848 (Solo Orgânico): one layer described, of 20 cm.
- SC 13649 (Organossolo Háplico): 20 cm at the surface, nothing
  described from 20 to 80 cm.
- RJ 13006 (Glei Húmico): an H recorded from 30 to 80 cm, inside a 2Cgn
  recorded from 20 to 80 cm.

In the second level, 2 profiles (default) and 3 (morphological) go from
Gleissolos Háplicos to Gleissolos Melânicos, by a horizonte hístico that
was not seen.

Panel of complete profiles (781): 428 to 429 and 513 to 514, one
Latossolo with an A of 14.5% of organic carbon that was keyed
Organossolos. FEBR (1,000): 376 and 501, unchanged. Redape: 77 and 84 of
94, unchanged. The 44 canonical profiles are identical in the three
systems.

## soilKey 0.9.252 (2026-10-13)

### SiBCS key: item (c) of the Neossolos step by its letter

The Neossolos are soils with no diagnostic B that satisfy, among others
(SiBCS 2018, Cap. 4, p. 112), “c) Ausência de horizonte vértico
imediatamente abaixo de horizonte A”. The step tested a vertic horizon
that begins within 50 cm, whatever lay between it and the A.

Decided on 2026-10-13: by the letter.

- The first layer of the vertic horizon has to be right below an A. The
  horizons of transition from the A (AB, AC) count with the A, as they
  do in the thickness of the A chernozêmico (p. 51).
- A vertic horizon that begins at the surface is there too.
- A profile with no horizon designation is tested as before.

|----------------------------------|------------------------|---------------|

| morphological mode               | 4,958 (65.3%)          | 4,949 (65.2%) |
| complete profiles, default       | 2,895 of 4,674 (61.9%) | 2,886 (61.7%) |
| complete profiles, morphological | 3,306 (70.7%)          | 3,297 (70.5%) |

**The agreement goes down, by the book.** Default mode: 13 profiles
change order, all to Neossolos; none reaches its reference, 9 leave it
and 4 go from one wrong order to another. The 9 are reference
Vertissolos with a C between the A and the first vertic layer, a C1 with
few slickensides or with none recorded (BA 8974: A, C1, then the vertic
C2 from 35 cm). Reference Vertissolos agreed 41 to 32 of 72.
Morphological mode: 11 change, the same 9 leave their reference; 45 to
36 of 72.

Two of the four others had no order of their own: with a vertic horizon
within 50 cm they were kept out of the Neossolos, met no later step and
fell to the last one, Argissolos (CE 8114, MA 9946).

Panel of complete profiles (781): 432 to 428 and 517 to 513. FEBR
(1,000): 376 and 501, confusion matrices identical. Redape (94): 77 and
84, no profile changes. The 44 canonical profiles keep their class in
the three systems, in both modes.

#### Tried and left out

The vertic horizon “tem precedência diagnóstica sobre os horizontes B
incipiente, B nítico e glei” (Cap. 2, p. 73). Taking the layers of the
vertic horizon out of the glei and of the B nítico was measured: one
profile changed order, from one wrong order to another, and Vertissolos
Hidromórficos lost their suborder, which asks for a horizonte glei in
the layers that are also vertic. At the first level the precedence is
already that of the order of the key. It is not in this version.

## soilKey 0.9.251 (2026-10-13)

### BDsolos: the cerosidade written in the text of the horizon is read

The export has the cerosidade in two structured columns, its amount and
its grade, and also as the survey wrote it, in the text of the horizon
(“Descrição Original”). The key asks for both: the B textural by its
cerosidade (SiBCS 2018, Cap. 2, p. 56, item i), the B nítico “em
quantidade no mínimo comum e com grau forte ou moderado” (p. 62), the B
latossólico “no máximo pouca e fraca” (p. 59). In 142 horizons the text
names the cerosidade and the two columns are empty.

[`load_bdsolos_csv()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/load_bdsolos_csv.md)
reads the amount and the grade from the text, each where its own cell is
empty, by the rule decided on 2026-10-13 for the slickensides: what is
written beside the term.

- The words right after “cerosidade” are read as long as they are
  amounts, grades or words that join them (“cerosidade comum e
  moderada”, “cerosidade fraca e pouca”), or the one word right before
  it (“pouca cerosidade”). Two grades or two amounts are a range (“fraca
  a moderada”).
- Nothing is read from a bare mention (“presença de cerosidade”), a
  denial (“sem cerosidade”), or words that are of something else (“cor
  da cerosidade (10YR 4/4) com mosqueado pouco”, “comum e moderada muito
  firme”).
- The spellings of the export are read (“serosidade”, “crosidade”).

The reader was checked against the structured columns, in the horizons
that have both: the amount is the same in 2,150 of 2,190 (98.2%) and the
grade in 2,172 of 2,208 (98.4%). Where they differ the text and the cell
say different things (“comum e fraca” beside a cell “Pouca”); the cell
is kept. In the horizons with empty cells every phrase was read: the
loader fills the amount in 123 layers and the grade in 123, 127 layers
of 111 profiles in all.

#### Measured

|--------------------|---------------|---------------|
| default mode       | 3,993 (52.6%) | 3,998 (52.7%) |
| morphological mode | 4,956 (65.3%) | 4,958 (65.3%) |

Default mode: 13 profiles change order, 6 reach their reference (4

it (a Latossolo with “cerosidade comum e fraca” in its B, RS 8704) and 6
go from one wrong order to another. Morphological mode: 6 change, 3 to

Panel of complete profiles (781): 432 and 517, as before (one profile of
the default mode goes from one wrong order to another). FEBR (1,000):
376 and 501, confusion matrices identical. Redape (94): 77 and 84, no
profile changes. The 44 canonical profiles keep their class in the three
systems, in both modes.

## soilKey 0.9.250 (2026-10-13)

### SiBCS key: in a profile of the older notation the A2 is the E and the B3 is the BC

The notation in use in Brazil until 1988 named the eluvial horizon “A2”
and the horizon of transition from the B to the C “B3”; the present
notation writes them “E” and “BC”. The book asks about both by their
present names: an E above the B makes a B textural (SiBCS 2018, Cap. 2,
p. 55, item f), and the BC is left out of the B in the textural ratio
(p. 56, note 4). The key read the A2 as an A and the B3 as a B.

Decided on 2026-10-13: both are read by what they name.

- A profile is taken to be in the older notation when one of its
  horizons is a B followed at once by a number (“B1”, “B21t”, “IIB3”) or
  a “(B)”. In the present notation the number comes after the letters
  (“Bt1”), and “A1, A2” beside “Bt1, Bt2” stay two parts of an A. Of the
  7,593 profiles of the national BDsolos export with a reference order,
  3,167 are in the older notation; 250 of them have an A2 and 853 a B3.
- In such a profile “A2”, “A21” and “B3t” are read “E”, “E1” and “BCt”,
  by every test of the SiBCS key that reads a designation. The horizon
  data keep the designation as written, and WRB and USDA are not
  changed.

That the A2 is the eluvial horizon and the B3 the transition to the C is
the notation as I know it from the surveys; SiBCS 2018 does not state
the correspondence, and it is for confirmation.

|----------------------------------|------------------------|---------------|

| morphological mode               | 4,953 (65.2%)          | 4,956 (65.3%) |
| complete profiles, default       | 2,882 of 4,674 (61.7%) | 2,890 (61.8%) |
| complete profiles, morphological | 3,301 (70.6%)          | 3,304 (70.7%) |

Default mode: 45 profiles change order, 18 reach their reference, 9
leave it and 18 go from one wrong order to another.

- The A2 read as E, measured alone on 0.9.247: 22 profiles change, 14
  reach their reference and none leaves it. They are mostly reference
  Argissolos that keyed Latossolos or Neossolos, with an eluvial horizon

- The B3 read as BC, measured alone: 24 change, 5 reach their reference
  and 9 leave it. The 9 are reference Argissolos whose B3 has more clay
  than their B2: without it the mean of the B no longer makes the ratio,
  and 8 of them have no cerosidade recorded.

The lower levels change in 67 profiles that keep their order.

Morphological mode: 27 change, 11 to their reference and 8 from it.

(1,000): 376 and 501, confusion matrices identical. Redape (94): 77 and

## soilKey 0.9.249 (2026-10-13)

### SiBCS key: the horizons the B latossólico does not present take out their own layers

The book (SiBCS 2018, Cap. 2, p. 59): “o horizonte B latossólico é um
horizonte subsuperficial que não apresenta características diagnósticas
de horizontes glei, B textural, B nítico e plíntico”. The sentence is
about the horizon.
[`B_latossolico()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/B_latossolico.md)
voided the B latossólico of the whole profile when one of three things
was found in any layer: the gleyic properties of WRB (mottles of 5% or
more in a layer that begins within 50 cm), the plinthic horizon of WRB,
or a B nítico.

Decided on 2026-10-13: those horizons take out their own layers only.

- The layers of a horizonte glei, of a horizonte plíntico and of a B
  nítico, as SiBCS defines them, are no part of the B latossólico, with
  those of the B textural, which were already left out. The layers that
  are left make the horizon if they make its 50 cm.
- Mottles alone make no horizonte glei, so that a red B with common
  mottles keeps its B latossólico.
- `latossolo()` applies to the B nítico the rule it applied to the B
  textural (Cap. 4, p. 110): a B latossólico below a B nítico makes no
  Latossolo.

#### Measured

|----------------------------------|------------------------|---------------|

| morphological mode               | 4,922 (64.8%)          | 4,953 (65.2%) |
| complete profiles, default       | 2,866 of 4,674 (61.3%) | 2,882 (61.7%) |
| complete profiles, morphological | 3,274 (70.0%)          | 3,301 (70.6%) |

reach their reference (Latossolos that keyed Neossolos, 9, and
Cambissolos, 8), 2 leave it (reference Cambissolos) and 22 go from one
wrong order to another: 12 reference Argissolos, 6 Plintossolos, 2
Cambissolos and 2 Gleissolos that keyed Neossolos or Cambissolos. Of the
profiles keyed Latossolos, 72.4% had that reference before (1,007 of

Morphological mode: 48 change, 35 reach their reference (30 Latossolos,

latossólico, which leaves 30 and 40 cm of it (GO 6062, PA 8626).

## soilKey 0.9.248 (2026-10-13)

### SiBCS key: the “p1” of B and C horizons is the “pl” of plinthite

The surveys before the present notation wrote plinthite “pl” (B21pl,
Cpl), which the morphological mode reads as the horizonte plíntico since
0.9.234. The BDsolos export has it also as “p1”, the letter “l” written
as the figure 1: B2tp1, B22tp1, Cp1, B2tp1cn, in 219 horizons of 145
profiles. Of those profiles, 135 have “plíntico”, “laterita” or
“concrecionário” in their reference name, and 95 have a reference in
Plintossolos.

`horizonte_plintico()` reads the “p1” of a B or C horizon as “pl”, in
the morphological mode only, with the same 15 cm. It is not read where
the profile numbers such horizons on (“Bp1” beside “Bp2”): no B or C of
the export is written with “p2”, so that the “p1” there is not the first
of a series. “Ap1” is a ploughed layer and stays one.

#### Measured

morphological mode: 4,860 to 4,922 (64.0% to 64.8%); complete profiles
3,248 to 3,274 of 4,674 (69.5% to 70.0%). Reference Plintossolos agreed
118 to 195 of 331; profiles keyed Plintossolos 178 to 273.

96 profiles change order: 77 reach their reference, all of them
Plintossolos (44 keyed Argissolos, 14 Planossolos, 10 Luvissolos, 9

are 13 reference Argissolos and 2 reference Cambissolos, every one

plíntico”): their plinthic horizon, once read, meets the position the

profile. The panel of complete profiles (428 and 511 of 781), FEBR (376
and 501 of 1,000), Redape (77 and 84 of 94) and the 44 canonical
profiles are identical in both modes.

## soilKey 0.9.247 (2026-10-13)

### SiBCS key: the “ir” of the older surveys is a B espódico in the morphological mode

The surveys that predate the present horizon notation write the illuvial
iron of a B horizon “ir” (Bir, B2ir, B22irx), where the present notation
writes “s”. The morphological mode, which reads the diagnostic horizon
from the designation where the analyses do not show it, read “h” and “s”
as the B espódico. A B with “ir” and no “h” was not read.

[`B_espodico()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/B_espodico.md)
reads it now, in that mode only. In the national BDsolos export 26
profiles carry “ir” in a horizon designation, and all 26 have a
reference in Espodossolos. In the morphological mode 19 of them keyed
there already and 25 do now; the other one, with 16.5% of organic carbon
in an A of 40 cm, keys Organossolos (AM 10502).

The reading is that of SiBCS only:
[`spodic()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/spodic.md),
which serves WRB and USDA, is not changed.

#### Measured

National BDsolos export, 7,593 profiles with a reference order,
morphological mode: 4,854 to 4,860 (63.9% to 64.0%). Six profiles change
order, all six to their reference: Espodossolos that keyed Cambissolos
(3), Neossolos (2) and Gleissolos (1). Reference Espodossolos agreed 66
to 72 of 98.

The default mode does not read designations and is identical, profile by
profile. The panel of complete profiles (428 and 511 of 781), FEBR (376
and 501 of 1,000), Redape (77 and 84 of 94) and the 44 canonical
profiles are identical in both modes.

## soilKey 0.9.246 (2026-10-13)

### SiBCS key: the minimum thickness of a horizon is that of its adjoining sub-horizons

The book states each minimum of the horizon: the B incipiente “deve ter
no mínimo 10 cm de espessura” (SiBCS 2018, Cap. 2, p. 60), the B nítico
“Espessura de 30 cm ou mais” (p. 62), the horizonte glei “com espessura
de 15 cm ou mais” (p. 69), the concrecionário “no mínimo 30 cm de
espessura” (p. 68), the sulfúrico “15 cm ou mais de espessura” (p. 72).
Each was asked of one layer of the description, so that a horizon
described in two sub-horizons thinner than the minimum did not pass,
whatever the two made together. The B latossólico is read by its
adjoining sub-horizons since 0.9.241 and the vertic horizon since
0.9.245; the five above are now read the same way.

The horizonte sulfúrico is read so on its two paths: with jarosite, and
with sulfidic material, which is tested by the WRB
[`thionic()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/thionic.md).
That function takes a new argument, `adjoining`, `FALSE` by default: the
WRB thionic horizon is tested as before.

The horizons that reach SiBCS through a WRB function (plíntico,
espódico, cálcico) are not changed.

#### A correction to 0.9.244

[`mudanca_textural_abrupta()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/mudanca_textural_abrupta.md)
and
[`B_planico()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/soilKey/reference/B_planico.md)
took a BC for the first B sub-horizon when it came before any other B.
The note of 0.9.244 says that the BC is left out of the B, as in item
(h) of the B textural; the code did not leave it out, and now does. Of
the national export, 7 profiles have a BC as their first B; none had an
abrupt change or a B plânico by it, and no figure of 0.9.244 changes.

#### Measured

the default mode and 4,854 in the morphological mode, as before. The
agreement is the same and the profiles are not: 10 change order in the
default mode, 4 reach their reference, 4 leave it and 2 go from one
wrong order to another.

- 9 by the horizonte glei, all keyed Gleissolos now. In each a glei
